jurisdictions.title: Connecticut (US-CT)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. Soliciting a ride from the traveled portion of any public highway is an infraction. The statute expressly allows it from the shoulder of any public highway except a limited-access highway. On limited-access highways and parkways, state regulations ban hitchhiking and pedestrians across the entire right-of-way, and they also ban picking up hitchhikers.

sections.summary:
Connecticut's statute, Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53-181, is unusually clear for hitchhikers:

- Soliciting a ride "while on or within the limits of the traveled portion of any public highway" is an infraction with a $35 fine.
- But "any person may, while on or within the shoulder portion of any public highway, except a limited access highway, solicit such a ride."

So on ordinary roads, hitchhiking from the shoulder is expressly lawful.

Limited-access highways (state highways designated under § 13b-27; the regulations also name "parkways") are governed by Office of the State Traffic Administration regulations, which apply to the whole "highway right-of-way":

- Pedestrians are prohibited except in emergencies or on facilities provided for them (§ 14-298-238).
- "Hitchhiking, soliciting of rides and loitering are prohibited within the highway right of way", and "the picking up of hitchhikers within the highway right of way is prohibited" (§ 14-298-243).

Section 14-300e of the General Statutes confirms that the pedestrian-rights statutes do not override § 53-181 or any regulation barring pedestrians from a highway.

In practice: hitchhike from the shoulder of the local road or the approach to an interstate on-ramp. Do not stand on the ramp itself or anywhere inside the limited-access right-of-way.
sections.laws:
### Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53-181: Soliciting rides in motor vehicles

**Source:** [LawServer mirror of Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53-181](https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/connecticut/ct-laws/connecticut_statutes_53-181) (unofficial mirror, labelled "Current as of: 2024"). The official site, [cga.ct.gov, Chapter 943](https://www.cga.ct.gov/current/pub/chap_943.htm), could not be retrieved in this session because of TLS errors and HTTP 503.

> Any person who, while on or within the limits of the traveled portion of any public highway, solicits a ride in a motor vehicle, other than a public service motor bus or taxicab, except in case of accident or emergency, shall be deemed to have committed an infraction and be fined thirty-five dollars, except that any person may, while on or within the shoulder portion of any public highway, except a limited access highway, solicit such a ride.

**What it means:** Shoulder: allowed. Travel lanes: a $35 infraction. Limited-access highways: the shoulder exception does not apply, and the regulations below ban hitchhiking there entirely.

### Conn. Gen. Stat. § 14-1: Definitions ("Limited access highway", "Shoulder")

**Source:** [LawServer mirror of Conn. Gen. Stat. § 14-1](https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/connecticut/ct-laws/connecticut_statutes_14-1) (unofficial mirror, "Current as of: 2024")

> (50) "Limited access highway" means a state highway so designated under the provisions of section 13b-27 [...]
>
> (90) "Shoulder" means that portion of a highway immediately adjacent and contiguous to the travel lanes or main traveled portion of the roadway;

**What it means:** The shoulder is the strip right next to the travel lanes, and that is where § 53-181 lets you stand. Limited-access highways are the routes designated under § 13b-27. CTDOT publishes the list, which was not retrieved for this page. Treat any interstate or expressway with on-ramps as limited-access.

### Regs. Conn. State Agencies § 14-298-243: Hitchhiking

**Source:** [Regs. Conn. State Agencies § 14-298-243, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/connecticut/Regs-Conn-State-Agencies-SS-14-298-243) (unofficial mirror; effective June 3, 1976). The rule is part of "Use of Limited Access State Highways", §§ 14-298-235 to 14-298-260k.

> (a) Hitchhiking, soliciting of rides and loitering are prohibited within the highway right of way.
> (b) The picking up of hitchhikers within the highway right of way is prohibited.

**What it means:** On interstates, parkways and other limited-access state highways, hitchhiking is banned everywhere inside the right-of-way, including ramps and shoulders. Drivers may not pick you up there either.

### Regs. Conn. State Agencies § 14-298-238: Restricted use of limited access state highways

**Source:** [Regs. Conn. State Agencies § 14-298-238, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/connecticut/Regs-Conn-State-Agencies-SS-14-298-238) (unofficial mirror; effective June 3, 1976)

> The following are prohibited from entry upon and use of the highway right of way of the parkways and other limited access state highways; (a) Pedestrians, except during emergencies or except on facilities specifically provided therefore; [...]

**What it means:** Walking on an interstate or parkway, or on its ramps, is prohibited unless you are in an emergency.

### Regs. Conn. State Agencies § 14-298-236(5): "Highway right-of-way"

**Source:** [Regs. Conn. State Agencies § 14-298-236, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/connecticut/Regs-Conn-State-Agencies-SS-14-298-236) (unofficial mirror; amended December 27, 2017)

> (5) "Highway right-of-way" means the entire area, including highways, bridges, buildings, structures and lands encompassed by the lateral property lines purchased and owned by the state for the construction and maintenance of highways, bridges and access to service facilities. Where "highway" is used herein, it shall be interpreted as meaning or including the highway right-of-way;

**What it means:** The ban reaches everything the state owns for the highway, including state-owned service areas. Stay on local roads or private property.

### Regs. Conn. State Agencies § 14-298-242: Picking up or discharging passengers

**Source:** [Regs. Conn. State Agencies § 14-298-242, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/connecticut/Regs-Conn-State-Agencies-SS-14-298-242) (unofficial mirror; effective June 3, 1976)

> Picking up or discharging passengers within the highway right-of-way is prohibited except in areas designed for such purposes.

**What it means:** Drivers may not stop on a limited-access highway or its ramps to let you in or out, except in designated areas.

### Conn. Gen. Stat. § 14-300e: Application of pedestrian rights to solicitation of rides and walking on limited access highways

**Source:** [LawServer mirror of Conn. Gen. Stat. § 14-300e](https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/connecticut/ct-laws/connecticut_statutes_14-300e) (unofficial mirror, "Current as of: 2024")

> Nothing contained in sections 14-299, 14-300 or 14-300b to 14-300d, inclusive, shall be construed to limit the provisions of section 53-181 or to permit any pedestrian to walk upon or along any highway where pedestrians are prohibited by any provision of the general statutes or any regulations issued thereunder.

**What it means:** General pedestrian rights do not override the hitchhiking statute or the limited-access pedestrian ban.

### Conn. Gen. Stat. § 14-300c(a): Pedestrian use of roads and sidewalks

**Source:** [LawServer mirror of Conn. Gen. Stat. § 14-300c](https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/connecticut/ct-laws/connecticut_statutes_14-300c) (unofficial mirror, "Current as of: 2024")

> (a) No pedestrian shall walk along and upon a roadway where a sidewalk adjacent to such roadway is provided and the use thereof is practicable. Where a sidewalk is not provided adjacent to a roadway each pedestrian walking along and upon such roadway shall walk only on the shoulder thereof and as far as practicable from the edge of such roadway. [...]

**What it means:** Use the sidewalk if there is one. Otherwise walk on the shoulder, away from the lane.
sections.unverified-open-questions:
- **Official text:** The § 53-181, § 14-1, § 14-300c and § 14-300e text above comes from an unofficial mirror (LawServer, "current as of 2024"), because cga.ct.gov was unreachable. Recheck it against the official [Connecticut General Statutes](https://www.cga.ct.gov/current/pub/chap_943.htm).
- **Actual fine:** The statute says $35, but Connecticut infraction amounts may also be set by the Superior Court's infractions schedule plus fees. The amount actually charged was not confirmed.
- **Penalty for violating the § 14-298 regulations** (for example, walking on an interstate) was not confirmed.

jurisdictions.title: Maine (US-ME)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. Hitchhiking is a traffic infraction on the traveled portion of a public way, anywhere on a limited-access highway (including the Maine Turnpike), and anywhere on a public way at night. In daytime, standing off the traveled portion of an ordinary road is lawful unless signs prohibit it.

sections.summary:
Maine has a dedicated statute, 29-A M.R.S. § 2110, "Hitchhiking forbidden". It defines "hitchhike" broadly ("by words, gestures or otherwise") and bans it in three situations:

1. **On the traveled portion of a public way.** The shoulder is not the traveled portion.
2. **On a limited-access highway, including the Maine Turnpike.** This applies to the whole highway, not only the travel lanes.
3. **On any portion of a public way during the nighttime.** Nighttime is any time outside "daytime", which runs from half an hour before sunrise to half an hour after sunset.

In practice: hitchhike in daylight, from the shoulder of an ordinary road or from the local road before an interstate or turnpike entrance. Cities and towns may regulate or ban hitchhiking by ordinance, and MaineDOT may ban it at unsafe spots on state highways. Restricted areas must be signed.

The fine is a forfeiture of up to $50.

Pedestrians are not permitted anywhere on the Maine Turnpike (I-95 from Kittery to Augusta), its interchanges or its toll plazas under the Turnpike Authority's rules. Elsewhere, MaineDOT and municipalities may close a way to pedestrians by posting signs (§ 2052(5) and (5-A)).
sections.laws:
### 29-A M.R.S. § 2110: Hitchhiking forbidden

**Source:** [Maine Legislature, Office of the Revisor of Statutes, 29-A M.R.S. § 2110](https://legislature.maine.gov/statutes/29-A/title29-Asec2110.html) (data extracted 10/05/2026)

> 1. Definition. As used in this section, "hitchhike" means to endeavor by words, gestures or otherwise to beg, invite or secure transportation in a motor vehicle not engaged in carrying passengers for hire, unless the hitchhiker is known to the driver or a passenger.
>
> 2. Violation. A person commits a traffic infraction if that person hitchhikes on:
> A. The traveled portion of a public way;
> B. A limited access highway, including but not limited to the Maine Turnpike; or
> C. Any portion of a public way during the nighttime.

**What it means:** In daytime, stand on the shoulder, not in the lane. Never hitchhike on the Turnpike or on interstates, ramps included. After dark, you may not hitchhike from any part of a public way, so move to private property such as a gas station lot (with permission) or stop for the night.

> 3. Exception. This section does not prohibit solicitation of aid in the event of an accident or by persons who are sick or seeking assistance for the sick, if the sickness is bona fide and an emergency exists.
>
> 4. Regulation. A municipality may regulate or prohibit hitchhiking on a public way by ordinance. The Department of Transportation may regulate or prohibit hitchhiking on a state or state aid highway in the interest of safety at those locations where accidents may be a problem, limited visibility exists or severe traffic conflicts or other safety factors may occur.
>
> 5. Posting. An area in which hitchhiking has been regulated or prohibited must be clearly identified by posted signs.
>
> 6. Forfeitures. For a violation of subsection 2, a forfeiture not to exceed $50 may be adjudged.

**What it means:** Watch for "No Hitchhiking" signs, which mark local or MaineDOT bans. The penalty is a civil fine of up to $50.

### 29-A M.R.S. § 101: Definitions ("Daytime", "Nighttime", "Public way", "Way")

**Source:** [Maine Legislature, 29-A M.R.S. § 101](https://legislature.maine.gov/statutes/29-A/title29-Asec101.html)

> Daytime. "Daytime" means any time from 1/2 hour before sunrise to 1/2 hour after sunset.
>
> Nighttime. "Nighttime" means a time other than daytime.
>
> Public way. "Public way" means a way, owned and maintained by the State, a county or a municipality, over which the general public has a right to pass.
>
> Way. "Way" means the entire width between boundary lines of a road, highway, parkway, street or bridge used for vehicular traffic, whether public or private.

**What it means:** The night ban covers the "entire width" of the way, shoulders included, from half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise.

### 29-A M.R.S. § 2052(5) and (5-A): Limiting use of a way to pedestrians

**Source:** [Maine Legislature, 29-A M.R.S. § 2052](https://legislature.maine.gov/statutes/29-A/title29-Asec2052.html)

> 5. Limiting use. The Department of Transportation or a municipality, with respect to a way under that authority's jurisdiction, may prohibit the use of a way by:
> A. Pedestrians; or
> B. Bicycles, roller skis or other nonmotorized traffic, scooters, motorized bicycles or tricycles or motorized scooters.
>
> 5-A. Limiting use sign restrictions. On limiting the use of a way, the authority shall erect and maintain official signs stating the prohibition. A person may not disobey the restrictions stated on those signs.

**What it means:** Where you see a "No Pedestrians" sign, for example at an interstate ramp, walking past it is an offense.

### 29-A M.R.S. § 2056(1)-(2): Pedestrians

**Source:** [Maine Legislature, 29-A M.R.S. § 2056](https://legislature.maine.gov/statutes/29-A/title29-Asec2056.html)

> 1. Pedestrian traffic. When use of a sidewalk next to a public way is practicable, a pedestrian may not walk on that public way.
>
> 2. Pedestrian on way. Where sidewalks are not provided, a pedestrian shall walk facing approaching traffic on the left side of the public way or the way's shoulder when practicable. [...]

**What it means:** Use sidewalks where they exist. Otherwise walk on the left, facing traffic.

### Maine Turnpike Authority Rules: Section 6 (Pedestrians) and Section 14 (Penalties)

**Source:** [Maine Turnpike Authority, Policies & Rules](https://www.maineturnpike.com/business-with-mta/policies-rules)

> Section 6 Pedestrians
> Pedestrians are not permitted on the Turnpike, on any Interchange or at any Toll Plaza. Solicitation of any kind, including but not limited to solicitation of rides, signatures or donations, passing of hand bills, displaying of signs, and attempts to sell merchandise are prohibited on Authority property. [...] Loitering on any Authority property is prohibited.

> Section 14 Penalties
> In accordance with 23 M.R.S.A. §1980, any violation of these rules shall constitute a traffic infraction, except that operation of a motor vehicle which exceeds, by 30 miles an hour or more, the speed fixed by the Authority, and failure to pay tolls, fares or charges for use of the Turnpike shall constitute Class E crimes.

**What it means:** The Turnpike (I-95 from Kittery to Augusta) is off-limits on foot, and soliciting rides is banned anywhere on Authority property, including service plazas. A violation is a traffic infraction.

- **Ramps:** That interstate on-ramps count as part of a "limited access highway" for § 2110(2)(B) is likely but was not confirmed by a definition.
- **Local ordinances** (e.g. Portland) were not researched.

jurisdictions.title: Massachusetts (US-MA)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. Massachusetts has no General Laws section on hitchhiking. MassDOT regulations ban it in two places: anywhere on the Mass Pike (Turnpike) and the Boston Metropolitan Highway System, and in the roadway of state highways. Hitchhiking from the shoulder of an ordinary state highway is not covered by these rules.

sections.summary:
Massachusetts regulates hitchhiking through MassDOT regulations, not a statute:

- **Turnpike and Metropolitan Highway System (700 CMR 7.00).** "No individual may engage in the solicitation of a ride, commonly known as 'hitchhiking', on a way." For these rules, "way" means the Turnpike, the Metropolitan Highway System (the Central Artery and the Boston tunnels), and their service and rest areas. Pedestrians are banned outright. Someone who displays a sign, signals a vehicle, or stands on Department property in view of a ramp or roadway to get a ride "may be arrested without a warrant." The fine is $50.
- **State highways (700 CMR 9.00).** "No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride [...]". Here "roadway" excludes the shoulders.
- **Limited-access and express state highways (700 CMR 9.08).** Pedestrians are banned "where official signs have been erected at the approaches."

M.G.L. c. 85, § 17A, sometimes cited as a hitchhiking law, targets signaling vehicles to solicit alms or to sell merchandise or tickets. It does not mention rides.

In practice: stay off the Mass Pike entirely, ramps and service plazas included. Don't walk past "No Pedestrians" signs at interstate ramps. On other roads, stand on the shoulder or sidewalk.

In March 2024, MassDOT re-issued its state-highway rules as 700 CMR 9.00. Older guides cite the same text as 720 CMR 9.00 (see History).
sections.laws:
### 700 CMR 7.06(5) and (7): Turnpike and Metropolitan Highway System, limitations on use of ways

**Source:** [700 CMR 7.06, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/massachusetts/700-CMR-7-06) (unofficial mirror; amended eff. 10/21/2016, 2/8/2019 and 4/15/2022)

> (5) Pedestrians and Animals. No pedestrian may enter or use a way, and no person may allow a horse or other animal not properly contained in an appropriate vehicle to enter or use a way.
>
> (7) Hitchhiking and Loitering. No individual may engage in the solicitation of a ride, commonly known as "hitchhiking", on a way. An individual who, for the purpose of soliciting a ride on a way, displays a sign, signals a moving vehicle, causes the stopping of a vehicle, or stands on property of the Department in view of a ramp or roadway of a way, may be arrested without a warrant. No person may loiter in or about a way for the purpose of "hitchhiking" or for any other purpose.

**What it means:** On the Mass Pike (I-90) and the Boston Metropolitan Highway System, you may not walk or hitchhike at all. Standing on MassDOT land in view of a ramp with a sign can get you arrested, so stand on a local street or private property instead.

### 700 CMR 7.02: Definition of "Way" (for 700 CMR 7.00)

**Source:** [700 CMR 7.02, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/massachusetts/700-CMR-7-02) (unofficial mirror)

> Way is defined as the Turnpike, the Metropolitan Highway System, tunnels, a service or rest area, that is located on property owned or controlled and under the jurisdiction of the Department, and includes the areas appurtenant to said way that are necessary for the operation, construction and maintenance of the way.

> Metropolitan Highway System (MHS) refers to the highway system that consists of the Boston Extension, the Callahan Tunnel, the Central Artery, the Central Artery North Area, the Sumner Tunnel, and the Ted Williams Tunnel, as defined in M.G.L. c. 6C, § 1.

**What it means:** The Turnpike rules cover the Mass Pike, the Boston tunnels and Central Artery, and their service and rest areas. They do not cover every interstate in the state.

### 700 CMR 7.13: Penalties (Table 12)

**Source:** [700 CMR 7.13, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/massachusetts/700-CMR-7-13) (unofficial mirror; amended eff. 4/15/2022)

> (3) Fines. (a) Fines by Reference to 700 CMR 7.00. Whoever violates any provision of 700 CMR 7.00 is subject to a fine not exceeding the amount indicated in 700 CMR 7.13(3): Table 12, in addition to other penalties as the laws of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts or federal law may provide. [...]
>
> [Table 12, "Prohibited Entry to or Use of a Way: Non-vehicle":] 700 CMR 7.06(5) Pedestrians and animals $50 [...] 700 CMR 7.06(7) Hitchhiking or loitering $50

**What it means:** Walking or hitchhiking on the Pike carries a fine of up to $50. The no-warrant arrest power in 7.06(7) is a separate issue from the fine.

### 700 CMR 9.09(6): Pedestrians soliciting rides or business (state highways)

**Source:** [700 CMR 9.09, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/massachusetts/700-CMR-9-09) (unofficial mirror; adopted by Mass Register Issue 1516, eff. 3/1/2024)

> (6) Pedestrians Soliciting Rides or Business. No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment or business from the operator or occupant of any vehicle without the written permission of the board or officer having control of such roadway or highway.

**What it means:** On state highways, don't stand in the travel lanes to hitchhike. The shoulder is not "roadway" (see the definition below).

### 700 CMR 9.01: Definitions ("Roadway", "Highway", "Limited Access Highway")

**Source:** [700 CMR 9.01, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/massachusetts/700-CMR-9-01) (unofficial mirror; eff. 3/1/2024)

> Highway. The entire width between property lines of any state highway or lawful through way designated by the Department.
>
> Limited Access Highway. An express state highway with full control of access.
>
> Roadway. That portion of a highway between regularly established curb lines or that part, exclusive of shoulders, improved and intended to be used for vehicular traffic.

**What it means:** 700 CMR 9.00 governs state highways, and its "roadway" excludes shoulders.

### 700 CMR 9.08(1) and (2)(c): Limited access and express state highways

**Source:** [700 CMR 9.08, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/massachusetts/700-CMR-9-08) (unofficial mirror; eff. 3/1/2024)

> (1) Effect of 700 CMR 9.00. 700 CMR 9.08(2) shall be effective on all limited access State Highways and express state highways where official signs have been posted prohibiting bicycles, pedestrians and/or horsedrawn vehicles.
>
> (2) Limited Access and Express State Highway Regulations. [...] (c) Pedestrians. No person shall use any highway for pedestrian or foot traffic purposes except in emergency, where official signs have been erected at the approaches of said highway prohibiting such traffic.

**What it means:** Where a "No Pedestrians" sign is posted at the start of a limited-access highway or ramp, you may not walk past it except in an emergency.

### M.G.L. c. 85, § 17A: Soliciting from vehicles on public ways

**Source:** [Massachusetts Legislature, M.G.L. c. 85, § 17A](https://malegislature.gov/Laws/GeneralLaws/PartI/TitleXIV/Chapter85/Section17A)

> Section 17A. Whoever, for the purpose of soliciting any alms, contribution or subscription or of selling any merchandise, except newspapers, or ticket of admission to any game, show, exhibition, fair, ball, entertainment or public gathering, signals a moving vehicle on any public way or causes the stopping of a vehicle thereon, or accosts any occupant of a vehicle stopped thereon at the direction of a police officer or signal man, or of a signal or device for regulating traffic, shall be punished by a fine of not more than fifty dollars. [...]

**What it means:** This statute covers panhandling and street sales, not ride solicitation. It is included here because it is often misquoted as a hitchhiking ban.
sections.history:
### 2024: 720 CMR 9.00 re-issued as 700 CMR 9.00

**Source:** [700 CMR 9.09, via Cornell LII (notes: "Adopted by Mass Register Issue 1516, eff. 3/1/2024")](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/massachusetts/700-CMR-9-09), compared with [720 CMR 9.09, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/massachusetts/720-CMR-9-09)

The ride-solicitation text of 700 CMR 9.09(6) is identical to that of the older 720 CMR 9.09(6), and so is the pedestrian rule in 9.08(2)(c). Older guides and Hitchwiki cite 720 CMR. The operative citation is now 700 CMR 9.00.
sections.unverified-open-questions:
- **Penalty for 700 CMR 9.00 violations** (ride solicitation in a state-highway roadway, pedestrians past posted signs) was not confirmed. M.G.L. c. 85, § 2 authorizes penalties of up to $20 for rules on vehicle movements, and M.G.L. c. 90, § 18A sets $1 to $2 fines for pedestrian rules adopted under it. Which applies to 700 CMR 9.09 was not determined.
- **Whether every interstate outside the Turnpike is signed** "No Pedestrians" under 700 CMR 9.08 was not checked.
- **Municipal rules:** Cities and towns may adopt pedestrian rules (M.G.L. c. 90, § 18A). These were not researched.

jurisdictions.title: New Hampshire (US-NH)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not stand on the travelled portion of a roadway to solicit a ride. The statute expressly says hitchhiking is lawful on any road, including limited-access highways, as long as you are not standing on the paved portion.

sections.summary:
New Hampshire's RSA 265:40 has the usual rule ("No person shall stand on the travelled portion of a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride [...]"). Paragraph III goes further than most states and affirmatively permits hitchhiking:

> "It shall be lawful for any person to hitchhike or solicit a ride from the occupant of any vehicle upon any road or way, or limited access road and highway provided that the individual is not, when so doing, standing on the paved portion of the road or way."

So in New Hampshire you may hitchhike even along an interstate or turnpike, provided you stand off the pavement, on the grass or gravel beyond any paved shoulder. Note the difference between the two paragraphs. The paragraph I ban covers only the "travelled portion", but the paragraph III safe harbor requires you to be off the "paved portion". A paved shoulder is safest treated as off-limits.

Breaking a Chapter 265 rule is classed as a "violation" (RSA 265:2), not a misdemeanor.

No New Hampshire statute or NHDOT rule banning pedestrians from limited-access highways was found for this page, so `freeway_pedestrians` is marked unclear. Obey any posted signs.
sections.laws:
### RSA 265:40: Pedestrians Soliciting Rides or Business

**Source:** [New Hampshire General Court, RSA 265:40](https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/XXI/265/265-40.htm). The official page refused direct downloads in this session. The text below was retrieved from the official page through a fetch tool in short consecutive quoted pieces and reassembled. See open questions.

> I. No person shall stand on the travelled portion of a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment, business or contributions from the occupant of any vehicle.
> [...]
> III. It shall be lawful for any person to hitchhike or solicit a ride from the occupant of any vehicle upon any road or way, or limited access road and highway provided that the individual is not, when so doing, standing on the paved portion of the road or way.
>
> Source. RSA 262-A:38. 1963, 330:1. 1971, 532:1. 1974, 31:1. 1981, 146:1; 479:8, 38. 1999, 243:1, eff. July 9, 1999.

**What it means:** Stay off the pavement and you may hitchhike on any road in the state, interstates and turnpikes included. Standing in a travel lane is a violation. Paragraph II (soliciting to watch parked cars) and paragraph IV (selling event tickets to moving vehicles) do not affect hitchhikers.

### RSA 259:92: Roadway

**Source:** [New Hampshire General Court, RSA 259:92](https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/XXI/259/259-92.htm) (retrieved the same way as RSA 265:40)

> "Roadway" shall mean that portion of a way improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the sidewalk, berm or shoulder even though such sidewalk, berm or shoulder is used by persons riding bicycles or other human powered vehicles. In the event a way includes 2 or more separate roadways, the term "roadway" as used herein shall refer to any such roadway separately but not to all such roadways collectively.
>
> Source. 1981, 146:1, eff. Jan. 1, 1982.

**What it means:** The shoulder is not part of the roadway, so standing on it does not break paragraph I. To fit the paragraph III safe harbor, though, you must also be off the paved portion.

### RSA 265:39, I: Pedestrians on Roadway

**Source:** [New Hampshire General Court, RSA 265:39](https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/XXI/265/265-39.htm) (retrieved the same way as RSA 265:40)

> I. Where sidewalks are provided it shall be unlawful for any pedestrian to walk along and upon an adjacent roadway.

**What it means:** Use the sidewalk where there is one. Paragraph II of the same section tells pedestrians without a sidewalk to use the shoulder, or else the left edge of the road.

### RSA 265:2: Required Obedience to Traffic Laws; Penalty

**Source:** [New Hampshire General Court, RSA 265:2](https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/XXI/265/265-2.htm) (retrieved the same way as RSA 265:40)

> 265:2 Required Obedience to Traffic Laws; Penalty. – Unless otherwise declared in this chapter with respect to particular offenses, any person who commits any act forbidden or fails to perform any act required in this chapter shall be guilty of a violation.
>
> Source. RSA 262-A:2. 1963, 330:1. 1973, 529:47. 1981, 146:1, eff. Jan. 1, 1982.

**What it means:** Breaking RSA 265:40 is classed as a "violation", not a misdemeanor.

All New Hampshire text above was obtained through a summarizing fetch tool that returned the statute in exact quoted pieces of up to 120 characters, which were then joined. The text is believed exact, but a raw-HTML cross-check was not possible. Paragraphs II and IV of RSA 265:40 were not quoted.
- **Pedestrians on interstates and turnpikes:** No RSA section or NHDOT administrative rule banning pedestrians from limited-access highways or the turnpike system was found. RSA 265:40, III implies that standing off the pavement of a limited-access highway is lawful for hitchhiking. Posted signs or turnpike rules may still restrict walking. Unconfirmed.
- **Fine amount** for a violation of RSA 265:40 was not confirmed.
- **Local ordinances** were not researched.

jurisdictions.title: Rhode Island (US-RI)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. Hitchhiking is banned anywhere on a freeway. On other roads it is banned only in the roadway or traveled portion, so the shoulder is allowed. Each violation carries a $100 civil fine.

sections.summary:
Rhode Island has two hitchhiking statutes:

- **§ 24-10-17(a): freeways.** Trying "by words, gestures, or otherwise" to get a ride "on any freeway" is prohibited. The ban is not limited to the travel lanes.
- **§ 24-10-17(b) and § 31-18-12: all other roads.** You may not solicit a ride on the "traveled portion" of a public highway (§ 24-10-17(b)) or "stand in a roadway" to solicit one (§ 31-18-12). Section 31-1-23(h) defines "roadway" to exclude the berm and the shoulder.

So on ordinary roads, standing on the shoulder or curb with your thumb out is lawful. On a freeway, including its shoulders and, presumably, its ramps (see open questions), it is not.

Both sections carry a $100 fine on the Traffic Tribunal violations schedule (§ 31-41.1-4). In 2021 the General Assembly removed the words "shall be guilty of a misdemeanor" from § 24-10-17 (see History), so freeway hitchhiking is no longer a misdemeanor.

Pedestrians may not cross a freeway except in an emergency (§ 31-18-17). No Rhode Island statute was found that bans walking along a freeway, but soliciting a ride there is banned anyway.
sections.laws:
### R.I. Gen. Laws § 24-10-17: Soliciting rides in motor vehicles

**Source:** [Rhode Island General Assembly, R.I. Gen. Laws § 24-10-17](https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE24/24-10/24-10-17.htm)

> (a) Any person who endeavors by words, gestures, or otherwise to beg, invite, or secure transportation in any motor vehicle on any freeway within the state, except in the case of a bona fide emergency or in the case of sickness, is subject to fines enumerated in § 31-41.1-4.
> (b) Any person who endeavors to solicit a ride in a motor vehicle in the manner described in this section on the traveled portion of any other public highway in this state shall be subject to fines enumerated in § 31-41.1-4.
>
> History of Section. P.L. 1966, ch. 69, § 1; P.L. 2002, ch. 58, § 1; P.L. 2002, ch. 292, § 102; P.L. 2008, ch. 100, art. 12, § 4; P.L. 2021, ch. 49, § 1, effective June 14, 2021; P.L. 2021, ch. 50, § 1, effective June 11, 2021.

**What it means:** On a freeway (for example the interstates), any attempt to get a ride is an offense, wherever you stand. On other public roads, only soliciting from the traveled portion is an offense. Stay on the shoulder.

### R.I. Gen. Laws § 24-10-1: "Freeway" defined

**Source:** [Rhode Island General Assembly, R.I. Gen. Laws § 24-10-1](https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE24/24-10/24-10-1.htm)

> A "freeway" is a way especially designed for through traffic over which abutters have no easement or right of light, air, or access by reason of the fact that their property abuts upon the way.

**What it means:** A "freeway" is a limited-access highway that adjoining properties cannot connect to directly. Interstates and expressways qualify.

### R.I. Gen. Laws § 31-18-12: Hitchhiking in road

**Source:** [Rhode Island General Assembly, R.I. Gen. Laws § 31-18-12](https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE31/31-18/31-18-12.htm)

> No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any vehicle. Violations of this section are subject to fines enumerated in § 31-41.1-4.
>
> History of Section. P.L. 1950, ch. 2595, art. 29, § 6; G.L. 1956, § 31-18-12; P.L. 2002, ch. 292, § 113.

**What it means:** This is the standard Uniform Vehicle Code rule. Don't stand in the travel lanes to hitchhike.

### R.I. Gen. Laws § 31-1-23(h): "Roadway"

**Source:** [Rhode Island General Assembly, R.I. Gen. Laws § 31-1-23](https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE31/31-1/31-1-23.htm)

> (h) "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, excluding the sidewalk, berm, or shoulder even when used by persons riding bicycles. In the event a highway includes two (2) or more separate roadways, "roadway" refers to the roadway separately and not the roadways collectively.

**What it means:** The shoulder, berm and sidewalk are not "roadway". Hitchhiking from them is outside § 31-18-12, except on freeways, where § 24-10-17(a) applies everywhere.

### R.I. Gen. Laws § 31-18-17: Pedestrians on freeways

**Source:** [Rhode Island General Assembly, R.I. Gen. Laws § 31-18-17](https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE31/31-18/31-18-17.htm)

> Any pedestrian who shall cross any freeway as defined by § 24-10-1, except in an emergency or to render assistance in case of an accident or unforeseen cause, shall be deemed to be guilty of a civil violation.

**What it means:** Crossing a freeway on foot is a civil violation. The statute does not mention walking along one, but you cannot hitchhike there in any case.

### R.I. Gen. Laws § 31-41.1-4: Schedule of violations

**Source:** [Rhode Island General Assembly, R.I. Gen. Laws § 31-41.1-4](https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/Statutes/TITLE31/31-41.1/31-41.1-4.htm)

> (a) The penalties for violations of the enumerated sections, listed in numerical order, correspond to the fines described. [...]
>
> 24-10-17 Soliciting rides in motor vehicles 100.00
> [...]
> 31-18-12 Hitchhiking 100.00

**What it means:** Hitchhiking where it is prohibited is a $100 civil fine, payable through the Traffic Tribunal.
sections.history:
### 2021: "guilty of a misdemeanor" removed from § 24-10-17

**Source:** [P.L. 2021, ch. 49 (2021-S 0681), enacted 06/14/2021](https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/PublicLaws/law21/law21049.htm) and [P.L. 2021, ch. 50 (2021-H 5977), enacted 06/11/2021](https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/PublicLaws/law21/law21050.htm)

The enacted text of chapter 49 shows these words struck through in both subsections (a) and (b) of § 24-10-17: "shall be guilty of a misdemeanor. Violations of this section are". The sentence now ends "is subject to fines enumerated in § 31-41.1-4" (a) and "shall be subject to fines enumerated in § 31-41.1-4" (b).

**What it means:** Older guides that call Rhode Island freeway hitchhiking a misdemeanor describe the pre-2021 law. It is now a civil traffic fine.
sections.unverified-open-questions:
- **Ramps:** Whether freeway on-ramps and off-ramps count as part of the "freeway" under § 24-10-17(a) was not confirmed by statute or case law. Assume they do.
- **Pedestrians walking along freeways:** No statute or RIDOT regulation banning this was found. Posted signs may apply.
- **Local ordinances** were not researched.

jurisdictions.title: Vermont (US-VT)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not stand in the roadway to solicit a ride, and the shoulder is not part of the roadway. On limited-access highways (the interstates and their ramps), a Traffic Committee rule with the force of law bans both hitchhiking and pedestrians.

sections.summary:
Vermont's statute, 23 V.S.A. § 1056(a), follows the Uniform Vehicle Code pattern: "no person may stand within the roadway of a highway [...] for the purpose of soliciting a ride." Section 4(32) defines "roadway" as the part used for vehicular traffic, "exclusive of the shoulder." On ordinary roads, standing on the shoulder with your thumb out is lawful.

Limited-access highways are different. The Vermont Traffic Committee's "Regulations Governing Use of State Highways with Limited Access Facilities" apply to the whole right-of-way, including "all ramps and highways provided for approach thereto". These rules:

- prohibit "soliciting of rides on limited access highways, commonly known as 'hitchhiking'", and loitering there for hitchhiking; and
- prohibit pedestrians "except in areas specifically designated for that purpose."

The rule makes an exception for Agency of Transportation commuter parking areas inside a limited-access right-of-way, except on the Interstate system.

Penalties: a violation of § 1056 or of the Traffic Committee rule is a civil "traffic violation" under 23 V.S.A. § 2302, with a maximum penalty of $1,000. The usual waiver (ticket) amount was not confirmed.
sections.laws:
### 23 V.S.A. § 1056: Highway solicitations

**Source:** [Vermont General Assembly, 23 V.S.A. § 1056](https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/section/23/013/01056)

> (a) Except as provided in subsection (b) of this section, no person may stand within the roadway of a highway as defined in subdivision 4(32) of this title for the purpose of soliciting a ride, contributions, employment, or business from the occupant of any vehicle.
> (b) Not-for-profit and municipal organizations may solicit contributions on the roadway of a highway, other than limited access highways, provided that approval is granted by the local legislative body [...]
>
> (Added 1971, No. 258 (Adj. Sess.), § 3, eff. March 1, 1973; amended 1973, No. 20, eff. March 7, 1973; 1989, No. 212 (Adj. Sess.).)

**What it means:** Don't stand in the travel lanes to hitchhike. The shoulder, sidewalk or a pull-off are fine on ordinary roads.

### 23 V.S.A. § 4(32): "Roadway"

**Source:** [Vermont General Assembly, 23 V.S.A. § 4](https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/section/23/001/00004)

> (32) "Roadway" is that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular traffic, exclusive of the shoulder.

**What it means:** The shoulder is expressly excluded, so § 1056(a) does not reach a hitchhiker standing on it.

### 23 V.S.A. § 1055(b): Pedestrians on roadways

**Source:** [Vermont General Assembly, 23 V.S.A. § 1055](https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/section/23/013/01055)

> (a) [Repealed.]
> (b) Any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall, when practicable, walk only on the left side of the roadway or its shoulder facing the direction of possible oncoming traffic. (Added 1971, No. 258 (Adj. Sess.), § 3, eff. March 1, 1973; amended 2023, No. 165 (Adj. Sess.), § 45, eff. July 1, 2024.)

**What it means:** Walk on the left, facing traffic. Subsection (a) was repealed by 2023, No. 165 (Adj. Sess.), effective July 1, 2024. Its former text was not retrieved for this page.

### Code Vt. R. 14-053-004: Regulations Governing Use of State Highways with Limited Access Facilities

**Source:** [Code Vt. R. 14-053-004, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/vermont/14-004-Code-Vt-R-14-053-004-X) (unofficial mirror; effective November 28, 1971, last amended September 13, 1983 per the notes shown; statutory authority 23 V.S.A. § 1004)

> B. Penalties These regulations, together with alterations and amendments thereto, made under this Act shall have the force of law and violations thereof shall be penalized under Title 23, Vermont Statutes Annotated, Section 2205(c).
>
> C. Definition Limited access highways shall mean any portion of the right of way of a limited access facility as defined under Title 19, Vermont Statutes Annotated, Section 1862, and shall include but not be limited to the National System of Interstate and Defense Highways, and shall include all ramps and highways provided for approach thereto.

> Article 1. 8. Limitations on Use of Highway [...] b. Use of limited access highways and entry thereon by the following is prohibited at all times: (1) Vehicles drawn by animals. (2) Pedestrians except in areas specifically designated for that purpose. [...]

> Article 2. 9. Hitchhiking and Loitering Prohibited
> Soliciting of rides on limited access highways, commonly known as "hitchhiking," is prohibited. Loitering in or about limited access highways for the purposes of hitchhiking or participating in a "car pool," or as part of a demonstration or protest, or for any other purpose, is prohibited. Nothing contained in the above wording shall prohibit the use of commuter parking areas, constructed by the Agency of Transportation, within the right of way of a limited access highway, except for the National System of Interstate and Defense Highways.

**What it means:** On I-89, I-91, I-93 and other limited-access highways, you may not hitchhike or walk, and that includes the ramps. Stand on the local road before the ramp starts.

### 23 V.S.A. § 2302(a): Traffic violation defined

**Source:** [Vermont General Assembly, 23 V.S.A. § 2302](https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/section/23/024/02302)

> (a) As used in this chapter, "traffic violation" means:
> (1) a violation of any provision of this title or rule adopted under this title for which no term of imprisonment is provided by law and for which a penalty of no more than $1,000.00 is provided; [...]

**What it means:** Hitchhiking violations are civil traffic tickets, not crimes.

- **Penalty amount:** The Cornell copy of the rule cites 23 V.S.A. § 2205(c) for penalties. That section was not retrieved. The waiver (ticket) amount for § 1056 under the Judicial Bureau schedule was not confirmed.
- **Local ordinances** (e.g. Burlington) were not researched.

jurisdictions.title: Delaware (US-DE)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Illegal. Delaware bans standing "in a highway" to solicit a ride, and "highway" covers the entire public right-of-way, shoulders included. The law also says nobody may be jailed solely for this offense. Walking on controlled-access highways is prohibited except in an emergency.

sections.summary:
Delaware's rule is stricter than the common Uniform Vehicle Code wording. Most states ban standing "in a roadway" (the travel lanes) to solicit a ride. Delaware's 21 Del. C. § 4147(c) says "highway" instead, and § 101 defines a highway as "the entire width between boundary lines" of a public way. Read literally, that includes the shoulder and the grass verge inside the right-of-way, so thumbing from the shoulder is not a safe harbor here.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Asking for a ride while standing in the highway right-of-way is an offense.** The safest places to ask are off the public right-of-way, such as a gas station or parking lot (with the owner's permission).
- **No jail for hitchhiking alone.** § 4147(d) says no one may be jailed solely for violating the ride-soliciting rule. The fine under the general penalty section is $25 to $75 for a first offense.
- **It does not go on a driving record.** § 4140 keeps convictions under the pedestrian sections, including § 4147, off a driver's motor vehicle record.
- **Highways DelDOT designates as controlled-access (such as the interstates) are closed to pedestrians** except to get help after a crash, breakdown or other emergency (§ 4126(a)(11)).
- **Walk facing traffic** on the shoulder if there is no sidewalk (§ 4146).
sections.laws:
### 21 Del. C. § 4147: Pedestrians soliciting rides or business

**Source:** [Delaware Code Online, Title 21, Chapter 41, Subchapter V](https://delcode.delaware.gov/title21/c041/sc05/index.html)

> (a) No person shall stand in a highway for the purpose of soliciting any employment, business or contributions from the occupant of any vehicle.
>
> (b) No person shall stand on or in proximity to a highway for the purpose of soliciting the watching or guarding of any vehicle while parking or about to be parked on a highway.
>
> (c) No person shall stand in a highway for the purpose of soliciting a ride.
>
> (d) No person shall at any time be jailed solely for violation of subsection (c) of this section.

**What it means:** You may not stand anywhere within the public highway, including the shoulder, to ask drivers for a ride. Subsection (d) means the worst outcome for hitchhiking alone is a fine, not jail.

### 21 Del. C. § 101: Definitions ("Highway", "Roadway")

**Source:** [Delaware Code Online, Title 21, Chapter 1](https://delcode.delaware.gov/title21/c001/index.html)

> (29) "Highway" means the entire width between boundary lines of every way or place of whatever nature open to the use of the public as a matter of right for purposes of vehicular travel, but does not include a road or driveway upon grounds owned by private persons, colleges, universities or other institutions.
>
> [...]
>
> (71) "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the berm or shoulder. [...]

**What it means:** The "roadway" is just the travel lanes, but § 4147(c) uses the broader word "highway," which runs from boundary line to boundary line. Shoulders and roadside strips inside the public right-of-way are part of the highway.

### 21 Del. C. § 4126: Unlawful use of controlled-access highways; penalties

**Source:** [Delaware Code Online, Title 21, Chapter 41, Subchapter III-A](https://delcode.delaware.gov/title21/c041/sc03a/index.html)

> (a) On any state highway designated by the Department of Transportation as a "controlled-access highway," no person shall:
>
> [...]
>
> (11) Walk as a pedestrian except to contact aid in the event of an accident, breakdown or other emergency;
>
> (12) Operate a vehicle of any type or kind prohibited by traffic-control devices at the entrances;
>
> (13) Disobey the restriction stated on any traffic-control device erected at the entrances.
>
> (b) Whoever violates subsection (a) of this section shall for the first offense be fined not less than $25 nor more than $75. For each subsequent like offense, the person shall be fined not less than $50 nor more than $95. [...]

**What it means:** Don't walk on Delaware's controlled-access highways at all, shoulders included, unless you are going for help after an emergency. The fine is $25 to $75 for a first offense.

### 21 Del. C. § 4146: Pedestrians on highways; penalty

**Source:** [Delaware Code Online, Title 21, Chapter 41, Subchapter V](https://delcode.delaware.gov/title21/c041/sc05/index.html)

> (a) Where a sidewalk is provided and is accessible, it shall be unlawful for any pedestrian to walk along and upon an adjacent roadway.
>
> (b) Where a sidewalk is not available, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall walk facing traffic only on a shoulder, as far as practicable from the edge of the roadway.
>
> (c) Where neither a sidewalk nor a shoulder is available, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall walk as near as practicable to an outside edge of the roadway, and shall walk facing traffic.
>
> [...]
>
> (f) Whoever violates this section shall for the first offense be fined not less than $10 nor more than $28.75. For each subsequent like offense, the person shall be fined not less than $25 nor more than $50.

**What it means:** Walking along a road is allowed. Use the sidewalk; if there isn't one, walk on the shoulder facing oncoming traffic.

### 21 Del. C. § 4140: Certain offenses not entered on motor vehicle record

**Source:** [Delaware Code Online, Title 21, Chapter 41, Subchapter V](https://delcode.delaware.gov/title21/c041/sc05/index.html)

> Arrests and or convictions for offenses in §§ 4141, 4143, 4145-4150 of this title shall not be entered on a driver's motor vehicle record.

**What it means:** A hitchhiking ticket under § 4147 will not show up on your Delaware driving record.

### 21 Del. C. § 4205: Penalties

**Source:** [Delaware Code Online, Title 21, Chapter 42](https://delcode.delaware.gov/title21/c042/index.html)

> (a) Whoever violates this chapter or Chapter 41 of this title shall for the first offense be fined not less than $25 nor more than $75. For each subsequent like offense, the person shall be fined not less than $57.50 nor more than $95. All second offenses, before being punishable as such, shall have been committed within 24 months after the commission of the first offense unless otherwise specifically provided.
>
> (b) Subsection (a) of this section shall not apply to violations for which penalties are prescribed elsewhere in this chapter or Chapter 41 of this title.

**What it means:** § 4147 has no penalty of its own, so this general rule applies: $25 to $75 for a first offense, and $57.50 to $95 for a repeat within 24 months.
sections.unverified-open-questions:
- I did not find Delaware court decisions on whether a hitchhiker standing on the shoulder is "in a highway" under § 4147(c). The reading above follows the plain statutory definition.
- A 2002 Delaware Attorney General opinion reportedly addressed the constitutionality of parts of § 4147 (the contributions clause). I saw this only in search snippets and did not retrieve the opinion, so it is not relied on here.
- The § 4147 history note on the official site ends with 67 Del. Laws c. 39; I found no 2023 to 2026 amendment, but did not search every recent bill.

jurisdictions.title: District of Columbia (US-DC)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. D.C. traffic regulations ban standing *in a roadway* to solicit a ride from a driver. The civil fine is $10. Hitchhiking is also banned on National Park Service land in the city unless the park has designated an area for it.

sections.summary:
The District's rule is in the D.C. Municipal Regulations (DCMR), Title 18, not in the D.C. Code: "No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any vehicle" (18 DCMR § 2305.4). "Roadway" is the part of the highway "improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel." Unlike many states, the D.C. definition does not expressly mention shoulders. A sidewalk or curb is still clearly outside the roadway, so asking for a ride from the sidewalk is not covered by § 2305.4.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Don't step into the street to flag cars.** Stand on the sidewalk or curb. The fine for "soliciting rides while standing in roadway" is $10 (§ 2603.1).
- **Federal park land is different.** Large parts of D.C. are National Park Service property (for example the National Mall and Rock Creek Park). There, federal rule 36 C.F.R. § 4.31 prohibits "hitchhiking or soliciting transportation" except in designated areas, wherever you stand.
- **Freeways:** D.C. regulations let the DDOT Director restrict "any class or kind of traffic" on controlled-access roadways by posting signs. When signs are posted, disobeying them is a violation. I did not find a regulation that bans pedestrians from all D.C. freeways outright (see open questions), but expect signed bans at ramps. Stay off the interstates and other freeways on foot.
- **Walk on the sidewalk** if there is one; otherwise on the left side facing traffic (§ 2305.2, § 2305.3).
sections.laws:
### 18 DCMR § 2305: Walking and standing on sidewalks and roadways

**Source:** [D.C. Office of Documents and Administrative Issuances, DCRegs, 18 DCMR § 2305](https://dcregs.dc.gov/Common/DCMR/SectionList.aspx?SectionNumber=18-2305) (current text, as amended by Final Rulemaking at 68 DCR 7212, July 23, 2021)

> 2305.2 Where a paved sidewalk is provided, a pedestrian shall not walk upon a roadway adjacent to the sidewalk, except as appropriate to avoid a risk to the pedestrian's, or another individual's, safety or health.
>
> 2305.3 Where sidewalks are not provided, any pedestrian walking along and upon a street or highway shall, when practicable, walk only on the left side of the roadway or its shoulder facing traffic, which may approach from the opposite direction.
>
> 2305.4 No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any vehicle.

**What it means:** You may not stand in the street itself to ask for a ride. From the sidewalk or curb is not covered by this rule. If you walk where there is no sidewalk, walk on the left facing traffic.

### 18 DCMR § 9901: Definitions ("Highway", "Roadway", "Controlled Access Highway")

**Source:** [DCRegs, 18 DCMR § 9901](https://dcregs.dc.gov/Common/DCMR/SectionList.aspx?SectionNumber=18-9901)

> Controlled Access Highway - a highway, street, or roadway with respect to which owners or occupants of abutting property or lands and other persons have no legal right of access to or from the same, except at such points only and in such manner as may be determined by the Council.
>
> [...]
>
> Highway - the entire width between the boundary lines of every publicly maintained way, when any part thereof is open to the use of the public for purposes of vehicular or pedestrian travel. (Reg. No. 71-26)
>
> [...]
>
> Roadway - that portion of a highway which is improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel. In the event a highway includes two or more separate roadways, the term roadway as used herein shall refer to any such roadway separately, but not to all such roadways collectively. (Reg. No. 71-26)

**What it means:** The roadway is the part of the street cars drive on. The sidewalk is not part of it. D.C.'s definition, unlike Pennsylvania's or Maryland's, does not expressly carve out the shoulder, so on the few D.C. roads with paved shoulders it is less certain that the shoulder is safe ground.

### 18 DCMR § 2201.13 and § 2201.14: Restrictions on controlled-access roadways

**Source:** [DCRegs, 18 DCMR § 2201](https://dcregs.dc.gov/Common/DCMR/SectionList.aspx?SectionNumber=18-2201) (Final Rulemaking at 42 DCR 3064, June 16, 1995)

> 2201.13 The Director may regulate or prohibit the use of any controlled-access roadway or highway by any class or kind of traffic which is found to be incompatible with the normal and safe movement of traffic.
>
> 2201.14 The Director shall erect and maintain official traffic control devices on the controlled access highway on which such prohibitions are applicable and, when in place, no person shall disobey restrictions on such devices.

**What it means:** DDOT closes freeways to classes of traffic (such as pedestrians) by posting signs. If a sign at the ramp bars pedestrians, walking past it is a violation.

### 18 DCMR § 2603: Pedestrian infractions (fines)

**Source:** [DCRegs, 18 DCMR § 2603](https://dcregs.dc.gov/Common/DCMR/SectionList.aspx?SectionNumber=18-2603) (as amended by Final Rulemaking at 66 DCR 56, January 4, 2019)

> 2603.1 The following civil infractions and their respective fines set forth in this section refer to pedestrians:
>
> [...]
>
> Roadway [...] Walking in (sidewalk provided) [§ 2305.2] $ 10.00
>
> Walking on wrong side (no sidewalk) [§ 2305.3] $ 10.00
>
> Soliciting rides while standing in roadway [§ 2305.4] $ 10.00

**What it means:** Hitchhiking from the street is a civil infraction, like a parking ticket, with a $10 fine. It is not a crime.
sections.notable-local-rules:
### 36 C.F.R. § 4.31: Hitchhiking in National Park Service areas (federal)

**Source:** [eCFR, 36 C.F.R. § 4.31](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-36/chapter-I/part-4/section-4.31) (last amended 2016-12-21)

> § 4.31 Hitchhiking.
>
> Hitchhiking or soliciting transportation is prohibited except in designated areas and under conditions established by the superintendent.

**What it means:** On roads and land run by the National Park Service, hitchhiking is banned outright unless the park has set aside an area for it. In D.C. this covers a lot of ground, including the National Mall and Rock Creek Park and their parkways. This is federal law enforced by the U.S. Park Police, and it applies whether or not you are standing in the roadway.

jurisdictions.title: Maryland (US-MD)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. Maryland bans standing *in a roadway* to solicit a ride. "Roadway" is defined to exclude the shoulder, so the shoulder and sidewalk are outside this rule. Pedestrians are banned from controlled access highways, their ramps and their access roads.

sections.summary:
Maryland Transportation Article § 21-507(a) says a person "may not stand in a roadway to solicit a ride." Section 11-151 defines "roadway" as the part of the highway used for vehicle travel, "other than the shoulder." So the statewide hitchhiking rule covers the travel lanes, not the shoulder.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stay out of the travel lanes.** Stand on the shoulder or sidewalk, with room for a driver to pull fully off the road.
- **A stranded motorist may flag down help.** The ban expressly does not apply to "the occupant of a disabled vehicle who seeks the aid of another vehicle."
- **Interstates and other controlled access highways are off limits on foot, and so are their ramps and access roads** (§ 21-509). This is broader than many states: you can't stand on the on-ramp. Ask for rides on the local road before the ramp begins.
- **Walk on the left, facing traffic** where there is no sidewalk (§ 21-506).
- **Penalty:** A Maryland Vehicle Law violation is technically a misdemeanor with a fine of up to $500 (§ 27-101).
sections.laws:
### Md. Code, Transp. § 21-507: Solicitation of rides, business, or contributions

**Source:** [Maryland General Assembly, Transportation § 21-507](https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Laws/StatuteText?article=gtr&section=21-507&enactments=false)

> (a) Except for the occupant of a disabled vehicle who seeks the aid of another vehicle, a person may not stand in a roadway to solicit a ride, employment, or business from the occupant of any vehicle.
>
> (b) A person may not stand on or near a highway to solicit any other person to watch or guard any vehicle while it is parked or about to be parked on a highway.

**What it means:** You may not stand in the traffic lanes to hitchhike. The rule uses "roadway," which leaves out the shoulder (see § 11-151 below), so thumbing from the shoulder or sidewalk is not covered. If your own car has broken down, you may flag down help.

### Md. Code, Transp. §§ 11-127 and 11-151: Definitions of "Highway" and "Roadway"

**Source:** [Maryland General Assembly, Transportation § 11-127](https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Laws/StatuteText?article=gtr&section=11-127&enactments=false); [Transportation § 11-151](https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Laws/StatuteText?article=gtr&section=11-151&enactments=false)

> §11-127. "Highway" means: (1) The entire width between the boundary lines of any way or thoroughfare of which any part is used by the public for vehicular travel, whether or not the way or thoroughfare has been dedicated to the public and accepted by any proper authority; [...]

> §11-151. (a) "Roadway" means that part of a highway that is improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, other than the shoulder.

**What it means:** The "highway" is the whole public strip; the "roadway" is just the lanes cars drive in. The shoulder is expressly not part of the roadway.

### Md. Code, Transp. § 21-509: Pedestrians on controlled access highways

**Source:** [Maryland General Assembly, Transportation § 21-509](https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Laws/StatuteText?article=gtr&section=21-509&enactments=false)

> (a) Except as provided in subsection (j) of this section, a pedestrian may not walk along a controlled access highway.
>
> (b) Except as provided in subsection (j) of this section, a pedestrian may not walk on a controlled access highway.
>
> (c) Except as provided in subsection (j) of this section, a pedestrian may not walk along a ramp leading to or from a controlled access highway.
>
> (d) Except as provided in subsection (j) of this section, a pedestrian may not walk on a ramp leading to or from a controlled access highway.
>
> (e) Except as provided in subsection (j) of this section, a pedestrian may not walk along an access road leading to or from a controlled access highway.
>
> (f) Except as provided in subsection (j) of this section, a pedestrian may not walk on an access road leading to or from a controlled access highway.
>
> [...]
>
> (j) This section does not apply to a person if an emergency prevents the movement of a vehicle in which he is riding and the person goes only to the nearest telephone or other source of assistance, nor to a person boarding or leaving a bus within a bus stop approved by the State Highway Administration.

**What it means:** No walking on or along interstates and other controlled access highways, their ramps, or the access roads leading to them. The only exceptions are walking to get help when your vehicle is stuck, and getting on or off a bus at an approved stop. Get dropped off and picked up on surface streets, before the ramp.

### Md. Code, Transp. § 21-506: Pedestrians on roadways

**Source:** [Maryland General Assembly, Transportation § 21-506](https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Laws/StatuteText?article=gtr&section=21-506&enactments=false)

> (a) Where a sidewalk is provided, a pedestrian may not walk along and on an adjacent roadway.
>
> (b) Where a sidewalk is not provided, a pedestrian who walks along and on a highway may walk only on the left shoulder, if practicable, or on the left side of the roadway, as near as practicable to the edge of the roadway, facing any traffic that might approach from the opposite direction.

**What it means:** Use the sidewalk. Without one, walk on the left shoulder facing oncoming traffic.

### Md. Code, Transp. § 27-101: Penalties

**Source:** [Maryland General Assembly, Transportation § 27-101](https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Laws/StatuteText?article=gtr&section=27-101&enactments=false)

> (a) A person who violates a provision of the Maryland Vehicle Law is guilty of a misdemeanor unless the violation: (1) Is a felony under the Maryland Vehicle Law; or (2) Is punishable by a civil penalty under the applicable provision of the Maryland Vehicle Law.
>
> (b) Except as otherwise provided in the Maryland Vehicle Law, a person convicted of a misdemeanor for a violation of a provision of the Maryland Vehicle Law is subject to a fine not exceeding $500.

**What it means:** Violating § 21-507 or § 21-509 is legally a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $500. The statute quoted here sets only a fine, not jail, for these sections.
sections.notable-local-rules:
§ 21-507 itself contains county-specific subsections (c) through (j) for Calvert, Carroll, Charles, Harford, Washington, Prince George's, Anne Arundel, Allegany, Cecil, Montgomery, Baltimore, Howard and Frederick Counties. These deal with **soliciting money or donations** (and, in Anne Arundel, advertising), not rides. Two of them define "highway" very broadly (rights-of-way, shoulders, medians and more), for example Prince George's County:

> (d) (1) This subsection applies to Prince George's County. (2) (i) A person may not stand in a highway to solicit money or donations of any kind from the occupant of a vehicle. [...]

**What it means:** Holding a sign asking for money is restricted much more tightly in these counties than holding a sign asking for a ride. Don't combine the two (for example, asking for gas money from the roadside).

jurisdictions.title: New Jersey (US-NJ)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Illegal. New Jersey bars standing "in a highway" to solicit a ride, and "highway" means the full width of the public way, so the shoulder is included. Pedestrians and ride solicitation are also banned on the New Jersey Turnpike and the Garden State Parkway.

sections.summary:
New Jersey's rule, N.J.S.A. 39:4-59 ("Begging rides prohibited"), is stricter than the usual Uniform Vehicle Code wording. Most states say "roadway", which excludes the shoulder. New Jersey says "highway", which § 39:1-1 defines as "the entire width between the boundary lines of every way publicly maintained." So thumbing from the shoulder of a public road is covered. Only a ride from a bus or streetcar is exempt.

What this means in practice:

- **Don't stand anywhere in a public highway to solicit a ride,** shoulder included. Private property next to the road, such as a gas station, truck stop or parking lot (with the owner's permission), is outside the "highway".
- **New Jersey Turnpike and Garden State Parkway:** pedestrians are prohibited and "soliciting of rides on the Roadway is prohibited" (N.J.A.C. 19:9-1.9 and 19:9-1.13). Here "Roadway" is defined to mean the whole Turnpike and Parkway, including service areas and interchanges.
- **Other limited-access highways:** the Commissioner of Transportation and counties may prohibit pedestrians by regulation (N.J.S.A. 27:7A-6). The text of the state rule was not retrieved for this page.

Penalty: § 39:4-59 does not set its own penalty, so the general penalty in § 39:4-203 applies. That is a fine of up to $50 or up to 15 days in jail, or both. A higher range applies to some articles of the chapter. On Turnpike Authority property, a violation is punishable by a fine of up to $500, up to 30 days, or both (N.J.A.C. 19:9-1.33).
sections.laws:
### N.J.S.A. 39:4-59: Begging rides prohibited

**Source:** [New Jersey Legislature, official statutes text download (STATUTES-TEXT.zip, file dated 2026-11-01)](https://pub.njleg.gov/statutes/STATUTES-TEXT.zip)

> 39:4-59. Begging rides prohibited
> No person shall stand in a highway for the purpose of or while soliciting a ride from the operator of any vehicle other than an omnibus or a street car.
>
> Amended by L.1951, c. 23, p. 78, s. 34.

**What it means:** Asking for a ride while standing anywhere in a public highway is an offense, shoulder included (see the definition below). The only exception is asking a bus or streetcar driver. Solicit rides from private property off the highway instead, with permission, for example at gas stations, truck stops or diners where drivers are already stopped. Turnpike and Parkway service areas do not count (see below).

### N.J.S.A. 39:1-1: Definitions ("Highway", "Roadway", "Limited-access highway")

**Source:** [New Jersey Legislature, official statutes text download](https://pub.njleg.gov/statutes/STATUTES-TEXT.zip)

> "Highway" means the entire width between the boundary lines of every way publicly maintained when any part thereof is open to the use of the public for purposes of vehicular travel.
>
> "Limited-access highway" means every highway, street, or roadway in respect to which owners or occupants of abutting lands and other persons have no legal right of access to or from, except at such points only and in such manner as may be determined by the public authority having jurisdiction over such highway, street, or roadway; and includes any highway designated as a "freeway" or "parkway" by authority of law.
>
> "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the berm or shoulder. [...]

**What it means:** "Highway" covers the whole public right-of-way, including shoulders and sidewalks. "Roadway" excludes the shoulder, but § 39:4-59 uses "highway", not "roadway". That is why New Jersey is rated illegal here, not merely restricted.

### N.J.S.A. 39:4-203: General penalty for violations of chapter

**Source:** [New Jersey Legislature, official statutes text download](https://pub.njleg.gov/statutes/STATUTES-TEXT.zip)

> For a violation of a provision of this chapter or any supplement thereto for which no specific penalty is provided, the offender shall be liable to a penalty of not more than $50.00 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding 15 days, or both; except that for a violation of a section of article 11, 13, 14 or 17 of this chapter or any supplement thereto for which no specific penalty is provided, the offender shall be liable to a penalty of not less than $50.00 or more than $200.00 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding 15 days, or both.

**What it means:** A violation of § 39:4-59 carries a fine of up to $50 (or up to $200 if the section falls in one of the listed articles), and theoretically up to 15 days in jail.

### N.J.S.A. 27:7A-6: Restricted use of limited access highways

**Source:** [New Jersey Legislature, official statutes text download](https://pub.njleg.gov/statutes/STATUTES-TEXT.zip)

> The commissioner, with respect to limited access highways under his jurisdiction, and the governing body of a county, with respect to limited access highways under its jurisdiction, shall have the authority to restrict the use of roadways in limited access highways to passenger motor vehicles, to prohibit the use of any roadway in limited access highways by certain classes of vehicles or by pedestrians, bicycles or other nonmotorized traffic [...]

**What it means:** NJDOT and counties can ban pedestrians from limited-access highways by regulation. Expect "no pedestrians" signs at interstate ramps. Even without them, § 39:4-59 already bans hitchhiking anywhere in a highway.

### N.J.A.C. 19:9-1.9 and 19:9-1.13: New Jersey Turnpike Authority rules (Turnpike and Garden State Parkway)

**Source:** [N.J.A.C. 19:9-1.9, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-jersey/N-J-A-C-19-9-1-9) and [N.J.A.C. 19:9-1.13, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-jersey/N-J-A-C-19-9-1-13) (unofficial mirror; both last amended by 57 N.J.R. 55(c), effective 1/6/2025)

> 19:9-1.9 (a) Use of the Roadway and entry thereon by the following, unless otherwise authorized by the Authority, is prohibited: 1. Pedestrians; [...]

> 19:9-1.13 (a) Soliciting of alms or contributions on the Roadway is prohibited. (b) Soliciting of rides on the Roadway is prohibited. [...]

**What it means:** On the Turnpike and the Parkway you may not be on foot or solicit rides at all. The definition below shows that this includes service areas, toll plazas and interchanges.

### N.J.A.C. 19:9-1.1: Definitions ("Roadway", "Turnpike", "Parkway")

**Source:** [N.J.A.C. 19:9-1.1, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-jersey/N-J-A-C-19-9-1-1) (unofficial mirror)

> "Roadway" means, collectively, the Turnpike and the Parkway.
>
> "Turnpike" means the express highway, superhighway, or motorway known as the New Jersey Turnpike, owned and operated by the Authority pursuant to the provisions at N.J.S.A. 27:23-1 et seq., and shall include, but not be limited to, the Turnpike right-of-way, all bridges, tunnels, underpasses, interchanges, entrance plazas, approaches, toll houses, service areas, service stations, service facilities, [...]

**What it means:** Unlike the ordinary statutory meaning, "Roadway" in these rules covers the entire Turnpike or Parkway property. Service areas count, so asking for rides at a Turnpike service plaza is prohibited.

### N.J.A.C. 19:9-1.33: Violations and penalties

**Source:** [N.J.A.C. 19:9-1.33, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-jersey/N-J-A-C-19-9-1-33) (unofficial mirror)

> (a) If the violation of this chapter would have been a violation of law or ordinance if committed on any public road, street, or highway in the municipality in which such violation occurred, it shall be tried and punished in the same manner as if it had been committed in such municipality. (b) Except as set forth at (a) above and N.J.A.C. 19:9-9.3(a), any violation of this chapter shall be punishable by a fine not exceeding $ 500.00 or by imprisonment not exceeding 30 days or by both such fine and imprisonment. [...]

**What it means:** Hitchhiking on the Turnpike or Parkway is punished like the equivalent offense on a public road. Other violations of the Authority's rules carry up to $500 and/or 30 days.
