jurisdictions.title: New York (US-NY)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not stand in the roadway (the travel lanes) to solicit a ride. The shoulder is not part of the "roadway". Pedestrians are banned from state expressways and interstates, including their ramps, and hitchhiking is banned everywhere on the New York State Thruway.

sections.summary:
New York follows the Uniform Vehicle Code pattern. Vehicle and Traffic Law § 1157(a) says "No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride." Section 140 defines "roadway" as the part of the highway used for vehicle travel, "exclusive of the shoulder and slope." So hitchhiking from the shoulder or curb of an ordinary road is not covered by § 1157(a).

What still applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stay out of the travel lanes.** Stand on the shoulder, curb or sidewalk where a car can pull fully off the road.
- **No walking on state expressways or interstates, or their entrance and exit ramps** (§ 1229-a), except at rest areas, in emergencies, or on a provided sidewalk or path. This rules out standing on an interstate on-ramp. Stand on the local road before the ramp begins.
- **No hitchhiking anywhere on the Thruway system, including toll plazas** (21 NYCRR § 102.4). Drivers may not stop to pick up or drop off hitchhikers there either.
- **Outside cities and villages,** § 1157(c) bars occupying any part of a state highway "for the purpose of selling or soliciting". See the open question below on whether this reaches ride solicitation.

A violation of the Vehicle and Traffic Law is a traffic infraction. Under § 1800(b), a first conviction carries a fine of up to $150, up to 15 days in jail, or both.
sections.laws:
### N.Y. Vehicle and Traffic Law § 1157: Pedestrians soliciting rides, or business

**Source:** [NY State Senate, Consolidated Laws, VAT § 1157](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/VAT/1157)

> § 1157. Pedestrians soliciting rides, or business. (a) No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, or to solicit from or sell to an occupant of any vehicle.
> (b) No person shall stand on or in proximity to a street or highway for the purpose of soliciting the watching or guarding of any vehicle while parked or about to be parked on a street or highway.
> (c) No person shall occupy any part of a state highway, except in a city or village, in any manner for the purpose of selling or soliciting.

**What it means:** Subsection (a) is the hitchhiking rule. It applies only to the "roadway", meaning the travel lanes. Thumbing from the shoulder of a normal road is not covered. Subsection (c) is broader ("any part of a state highway"), but it is aimed at selling and soliciting outside cities and villages. It does not mention rides. Avoid lingering on state highway rights-of-way in rural areas if police object.

### N.Y. Vehicle and Traffic Law § 140: Roadway

**Source:** [NY State Senate, Consolidated Laws, VAT § 140](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/VAT/140)

> § 140. Roadway. That portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the shoulder and slope. In the event a highway includes two or more separate roadways the term "roadway" as used herein shall refer to any such roadway separately but not to all such roadways collectively.

**What it means:** The shoulder and the slope beside it are not "roadway". This is why § 1157(a) does not reach a hitchhiker standing on the shoulder.

### N.Y. Vehicle and Traffic Law § 1229-a: Pedestrians prohibited on state expressway and interstate highways

**Source:** [NY State Senate, Consolidated Laws, VAT § 1229-A](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/VAT/1229-A)

> § 1229-a. Pedestrians, animals, and non-motorized vehicles prohibited on state expressway highways or state interstate route highways including the entrances thereto and exits therefrom. No person, unless otherwise directed by a police officer shall: (a) As a pedestrian, occupy any space within the limits of a state expressway highway or state interstate route highway, including the entrances thereto and exits therefrom, except: in a rest area, parking area, or scenic overlook; in the performance of public works or official duties; as a result of an emergency caused by an accident or breakdown of a motor vehicle or to obtain assistance; where a sidewalk, footpath or pedestrian crossing of such a highway is provided; [...]

**What it means:** On interstates and state expressways you may not be on foot anywhere within the highway limits, including the ramps. Rest areas and parking areas are an exception, so asking drivers for a ride at a rest area is not barred by this section. Elsewhere, hitchhike from the surface street before the ramp.

### N.Y. Vehicle and Traffic Law § 1156: Pedestrians on roadways

**Source:** [NY State Senate, Consolidated Laws, VAT § 1156](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/VAT/1156)

> § 1156. Pedestrians on roadways. (a) Where sidewalks are provided and they may be used with safety it shall be unlawful for any pedestrian to walk along and upon an adjacent roadway.
> (b) Where sidewalks are not provided any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall when practicable walk only on the left side of the roadway or its shoulder facing traffic which may approach from the opposite direction. Upon the approach of any vehicle from the opposite direction, such pedestrian shall move as far to the left as is practicable.

**What it means:** Use the sidewalk if there is one. Otherwise walk on the left, facing traffic.

### N.Y. Vehicle and Traffic Law § 1800: Penalties for traffic infractions

**Source:** [NY State Senate, Consolidated Laws, VAT § 1800](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/VAT/1800)

> § 1800. Penalties for traffic infractions. (a) It is a traffic infraction for any person to violate any of the provisions of this chapter or of any local law, ordinance, order, rule or regulation adopted pursuant to this chapter, unless such violation is by this chapter or other law of this state declared to be a misdemeanor or a felony.
> (b) 1. Every person convicted of a traffic infraction for a violation of any of the provisions of this chapter [...] for which another penalty is not provided shall for a first conviction thereof be punished by a fine of not more than one hundred fifty dollars or by imprisonment for not more than fifteen days or by both such fine and imprisonment; for a conviction of a second violation, both of which were committed within a period of eighteen months, such person shall be punished by a fine of not more than three hundred dollars or by imprisonment for not more than forty-five days or by both such fine and imprisonment; upon a conviction of a third or subsequent violation, all of which were committed within a period of eighteen months, such person shall be punished by a fine of not more than four hundred fifty dollars or by imprisonment for not more than ninety days or by both such fine and imprisonment [...]

**What it means:** Violating § 1157 or § 1229-a is a traffic infraction, not a crime. The maximum is $150 and/or 15 days for a first offense, rising for repeat offenses within 18 months.

### 21 NYCRR § 102.4: Hitchhiking; loitering (New York State Thruway)

**Source:** [N.Y. Comp. Codes R. & Regs. tit. 21, § 102.4, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-york/21-NYCRR-102.4) (unofficial mirror of the Thruway Authority regulations, Title 21, Chapter III, Part 102)

> The solicitation of a ride, commonly known as hitchhiking, or stopping any vehicle for the purpose of picking up or discharging a hitchhiker, on any portion of the Thruway system, including toll plazas, is prohibited. Loitering in or about the toll plazas or any other portion of the Thruway system, for the purpose of hitchhiking or for any other purpose, is prohibited.

**What it means:** The Thruway (I-87/I-90 and its spurs) is completely off-limits for hitchhiking, including at toll plazas. This rule also covers drivers, who may not stop to pick up or drop off a hitchhiker on the Thruway.

### 21 NYCRR § 102.1: Prohibited uses of the Thruway

**Source:** [N.Y. Comp. Codes R. & Regs. tit. 21, § 102.1, via Cornell LII](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/new-york/21-NYCRR-102.1) (unofficial mirror)

> (a) Use of the Thruway system by the following is prohibited at all times, with the noted exceptions: (1) Pedestrians, except on the Grand Island Bridges sidewalks and on the Governor Mario M. Cuomo Bridge's shared use path when such sidewalks and/or shared use path are not closed or otherwise prescribed at the sole discretion of the Thruway Authority. [...]

**What it means:** You may not be on foot anywhere on the Thruway system, apart from two bridge paths.

jurisdictions.title: Pennsylvania (US-PA)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. Pennsylvania bans standing *on a roadway* to solicit a ride. The legal definition of "roadway" excludes the shoulder and berm, so thumbing from the shoulder or sidewalk is not covered by that rule. The Pennsylvania Turnpike is different: hitchhiking and all pedestrian entry onto the Turnpike right-of-way are banned there by regulation.

sections.summary:
The Vehicle Code (75 Pa.C.S. § 3545) follows the standard Uniform Vehicle Code pattern: "No person shall [...] Stand on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride." Section 102 defines "roadway" as the part of the highway used for vehicle travel, "exclusive of the sidewalk, berm or shoulder." So the statewide rule reaches people standing in the travel lanes, not people standing on the shoulder or sidewalk.

What still applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stay out of the travel lanes.** Stand on the shoulder, berm or sidewalk, and pick a spot where a driver can pull completely off the road.
- **The Pennsylvania Turnpike is off limits.** Turnpike Commission regulations prohibit hitchhiking and prohibit pedestrians from entering the Turnpike right-of-way at all, and they also prohibit drivers from stopping to let hitchhikers board. Ask for rides on a local road before the Turnpike entrance, not on the Turnpike itself.
- **Other freeways:** The Vehicle Code does not contain a blanket statutory ban on pedestrians on freeways. Instead, § 3313 lets PennDOT prohibit any "class or kind of traffic" on a limited access highway and requires it to post signs at the entrances; once signs are posted, disobeying them is a violation. In practice most interstate ramps carry signs barring pedestrians, so treat a signed ramp as closed to you.
- **Walk on the sidewalk** if there is one; otherwise on the shoulder; otherwise on the left edge facing traffic (§ 3544).

A violation of § 3545 is a summary offense with a $25 fine under § 6502. A Turnpike regulation violation is also a summary offense with a $25 fine.
sections.laws:
### 75 Pa.C.S. § 3545: Pedestrians soliciting rides or business

**Source:** [Pennsylvania General Assembly, 75 Pa.C.S. § 3545](https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?txtType=HTM&ttl=75&div=0&chapter=35&section=45&subsctn=0)

> No person shall:
>
> (1) Stand on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride.
>
> (2) Stand on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting employment, business or contributions from the occupant of any vehicle.
>
> (3) Stand on or in proximity to a highway for the purpose of soliciting the watching or guarding of any vehicle while parked or about to be parked on a street or highway.

**What it means:** You may not stand in the part of the road cars drive on to ask for a ride. The rule says "roadway," not "highway," so standing on the shoulder or sidewalk is not covered (see the definition below).

### 75 Pa.C.S. § 102: Definitions ("Roadway", "Highway", "Limited access highway", "Freeway")

**Source:** [Pennsylvania General Assembly, 75 Pa.C.S. § 102](https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?txtType=HTM&ttl=75&div=0&chapter=1&section=2&subsctn=0)

> "Freeway." A limited access highway to which the only means of ingress and egress is by interchange ramps.
>
> [...]
>
> "Highway." The entire width between the boundary lines of every way publicly maintained when any part thereof is open to the use of the public for purposes of vehicular travel. [...]
>
> [...]
>
> "Limited access highway." A highway in respect to which owners or occupants of abutting lands and other persons have no legal right of access except at points and in the manner determined by the authority having jurisdiction over the highway.
>
> [...]
>
> "Roadway." That portion of a highway improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the sidewalk, berm or shoulder even though such sidewalk, berm or shoulder is used by pedalcycles. [...]

**What it means:** The "highway" is the whole public right-of-way, edge to edge. The "roadway" is only the travel lanes, and expressly excludes the shoulder, berm and sidewalk. That is why § 3545 does not reach a hitchhiker standing on the shoulder.

### 75 Pa.C.S. § 3313: Restrictions on use of limited access highways

**Source:** [Pennsylvania General Assembly, 75 Pa.C.S. § 3313](https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?txtType=HTM&ttl=75&div=0&chapter=33&section=13&subsctn=0)

> (a) General rule.-- The department may regulate or prohibit the use of any limited access highway by any class or kind of traffic which is found to be incompatible with the normal and safe movement of traffic.
>
> (b) Traffic-control devices at entrances.-- The department, when adopting any prohibition under this section, shall erect and maintain official traffic-control devices at the entrances to the limited access highway on which the prohibitions are applicable and when in place no person shall disobey the restrictions stated on the devices.

**What it means:** PennDOT can close a limited access highway to pedestrians, but it does so with signs at the entrances. If the ramp has a "pedestrians prohibited" sign, walking past it is a violation. Stand before the sign.

### 75 Pa.C.S. § 3544: Pedestrians walking along or on highway

**Source:** [Pennsylvania General Assembly, 75 Pa.C.S. § 3544](https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?txtType=HTM&ttl=75&div=0&chapter=35&section=44&subsctn=0)

> (a) Mandatory use of available sidewalk.-- Where a sidewalk is provided and its use is practicable, it is unlawful for any pedestrian to walk along and upon an adjacent roadway.
>
> (b) Absence of sidewalk.-- Where a sidewalk is not available, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall walk only on a shoulder as far as practicable from the edge of the roadway.
>
> (c) Absence of sidewalk and shoulder.-- Where neither a sidewalk nor a shoulder is available, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall walk as near as practicable to an outside edge of the roadway and, if on a two-way roadway, shall walk only on the left side of the roadway.

**What it means:** Use the sidewalk if there is one; otherwise the shoulder; otherwise walk on the left edge facing traffic.

### 67 Pa. Code §§ 601.10, 601.11: Pennsylvania Turnpike pedestrian travel and hitchhiking

**Source:** [Pennsylvania Code, 67 Pa. Code Chapter 601 (Turnpike Commission traffic regulations)](https://www.pacodeandbulletin.gov/Display/pacode?file=/secure/pacode/data/067/chapter601/chap601toc.html)

> § 601.10. Pedestrian travel.
>
> Pedestrian travel or entry upon the right-of-way of the Turnpike System is prohibited.
>
> § 601.11. Hitchhiking.
>
> The solicitation for a ride, commonly known as "hitchhiking," is prohibited, and stopping or allowing a vehicle to be standing while hitchhikers board is also prohibited.

From § 601.1 (Definitions):

> Turnpike System—The limited access highway maintained and constructed by the Commission, extending eastward from the Ohio line to the New Jersey line and northward from a point near Norristown, Pennsylvania to a point near Scranton, Pennsylvania and other extensions thereto, which have been or may hereafter be designated as part of the Turnpike System by the Legislature.

**What it means:** On the Turnpike System, you may not walk on the right-of-way at all and you may not hitchhike, and drivers may not stop to pick you up. This includes the shoulders and ramps inside the Turnpike's boundaries.

### 75 Pa.C.S. § 6502 and 67 Pa. Code § 601.16: Penalties

**Source:** [Pennsylvania General Assembly, 75 Pa.C.S. § 6502](https://www.palegis.us/statutes/consolidated/view-statute?txtType=HTM&ttl=75&div=0&chapter=65&section=2&subsctn=0); [67 Pa. Code § 601.16](https://www.pacodeandbulletin.gov/Display/pacode?file=/secure/pacode/data/067/chapter601/chap601toc.html)

> (a) Violations of this title.-- It is a summary offense for any person to violate any of the provisions of this title unless the violation is by this title or other statute of this Commonwealth declared to be a misdemeanor or felony. Every person convicted of a summary offense for a violation of any of the provisions of this title for which another penalty is not provided shall be sentenced to pay a fine of $25.

> § 601.16. Penalties.
>
> A person violating a provision of this part for which no penalty has otherwise been provided by statute is guilty of a summary offense and shall, upon conviction, be sentenced to pay a fine of $25.

**What it means:** Breaking § 3545, § 3544, a § 3313 sign, or the Turnpike rules is a summary offense (the lowest level, like a traffic ticket) with a $25 base fine.

jurisdictions.title: Florida (US-FL)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not stand in the paved travel part of a roadway to solicit a ride. The shoulder and curb are outside the "roadway" as Florida defines it. Pedestrians are banned from limited access highways and from their ramps.

sections.summary:
Florida's hitchhiking rule is narrower than most. Fla. Stat. § 316.130(5) only bans standing "in the portion of a roadway paved for vehicular traffic" to solicit a ride. Florida defines "roadway" to exclude the berm or shoulder. Standing on the shoulder, curb or sidewalk with your thumb out is therefore not covered by this rule.

What still applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stay off limited access highways and their ramps.** Florida bans pedestrians from walking on a limited access facility (interstates, turnpikes, expressways) or on a ramp that connects one to another road. Hitchhike from the surface street before the ramp starts.
- **Don't block traffic.** A separate statute (§ 316.2045) makes it a pedestrian violation to willfully obstruct a street by standing in it or impeding traffic.
- **Walk facing traffic** on the left shoulder where there is no sidewalk.

A violation of § 316.130 is a noncriminal traffic infraction. The pedestrian penalty in § 318.18(1) is $15, plus any court costs.
sections.laws:
### Fla. Stat. § 316.130: Pedestrians; traffic regulations

**Source:** [Florida Legislature, Online Sunshine, Fla. Stat. § 316.130](http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0300-0399/0316/Sections/0316.130.html) (2026 Florida Statutes; history ends with s. 2, ch. 2008-33)

> (3) Where sidewalks are provided, no pedestrian shall, unless required by other circumstances, walk along and upon the portion of a roadway paved for vehicular traffic.
>
> (4) Where sidewalks are not provided, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall, when practicable, walk only on the shoulder on the left side of the roadway in relation to the pedestrian's direction of travel, facing traffic which may approach from the opposite direction.
>
> (5) No person shall stand in the portion of a roadway paved for vehicular traffic for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment, or business from the occupant of any vehicle.

**What it means:** The ban covers only the paved travel lanes. Standing on the shoulder, the curb or the sidewalk to solicit a ride is not prohibited by this subsection. Pick a spot where a driver can pull completely off the road. Where there is no sidewalk, walk on the left shoulder facing traffic.

> (18) No pedestrian shall walk upon a limited access facility or a ramp connecting a limited access facility to any other street or highway; however, this subsection does not apply to maintenance personnel of any governmental subdivision.

**What it means:** Interstates, Florida's Turnpike and other limited access expressways are off limits on foot, and so are their on-ramps and off-ramps. Stand on the local road before the ramp begins.

> (19) A violation of this section is a noncriminal traffic infraction, punishable pursuant to chapter 318 as either a pedestrian violation or, if the infraction resulted from the operation of a vehicle, as a moving violation.

**What it means:** A violation is a ticket, not a crime.

### Fla. Stat. § 316.003: Definitions ("roadway" and "limited access facility")

**Source:** [Florida Legislature, Online Sunshine, Fla. Stat. § 316.003](http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0300-0399/0316/Sections/0316.003.html) (2026 Florida Statutes)

> (36) LIMITED ACCESS FACILITY.—A street or highway especially designed for through traffic and over, from, or to which owners or occupants of abutting land or other persons have no right or easement, or only a limited right or easement, of access, light, air, or view by reason of the fact that their property abuts upon such limited access facility or for any other reason. Such highways or streets may be parkways from which trucks, buses, and other commercial vehicles are excluded or may be freeways open to use by all customary forms of street and highway traffic.
>
> [...]
>
> (74) ROADWAY.—That portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the berm or shoulder. If a highway includes two or more separate roadways, the term "roadway" refers to any such roadway separately, but not to all such roadways collectively.

**What it means:** The shoulder is not part of the "roadway." Section 316.130(5) goes further and limits the ban to the *paved travel* part of the roadway.

### Fla. Stat. § 316.2045: Obstruction of public streets, highways, and roads

**Source:** [Florida Legislature, Online Sunshine, Fla. Stat. § 316.2045](http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0300-0399/0316/Sections/0316.2045.html) (2026 Florida Statutes; last amended s. 2, ch. 2021-6)

> (1)(a) A person may not willfully obstruct the free, convenient, and normal use of a public street, highway, or road by:
> 1. Impeding, hindering, stifling, retarding, or restraining traffic or passage thereon;
> 2. Standing on or remaining in the street, highway, or road; or
> 3. Endangering the safe movement of vehicles or pedestrians traveling thereon.
>
> (b) A person who violates paragraph (a) shall be cited for a pedestrian violation, punishable as provided in chapter 318.

**What it means:** This is a general anti-obstruction rule, not a hitchhiking rule. It does mean that standing in the street so that cars must stop or swerve can get you a ticket. Stay clear of traffic.

### Fla. Stat. § 318.18: Amount of penalties

**Source:** [Florida Legislature, Online Sunshine, Fla. Stat. § 318.18](http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0300-0399/0318/Sections/0318.18.html) (2026 Florida Statutes)

> The penalties required for a noncriminal disposition pursuant to s. 318.14 or a criminal offense listed in s. 318.17 are as follows:
> (1) Fifteen dollars for:
> (a) All infractions of pedestrian regulations.

**What it means:** The base penalty for a pedestrian ticket is $15. Court costs and fees may be added.
sections.history:
### 2021: § 316.2045 rewritten

**Source:** [Fla. Stat. § 316.2045 history note](http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0300-0399/0316/Sections/0316.2045.html)

The section's history line shows it was last amended by chapter 2021-6, Laws of Florida. The current text makes willful obstruction a pedestrian violation. The ride-solicitation rule in § 316.130(5) itself has not changed since at least 2008.

jurisdictions.title: Georgia (US-GA)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not stand in the roadway to solicit a ride. Georgia defines "roadway" to exclude the berm and shoulder, so hitchhiking from the shoulder or curb is not covered by this rule.

sections.summary:
Georgia follows the Uniform Vehicle Code pattern. O.C.G.A. § 40-6-97(a) says "No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride." Georgia's definition of "roadway" excludes the berm or shoulder. The rule therefore targets people standing in the travel lanes.

Note the contrast with subsection (b). That subsection bans soliciting employment, business or contributions while standing anywhere "on a highway," which includes the shoulder. That broader wording does not apply to soliciting rides.

What still applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stand on the shoulder or sidewalk, not in the lanes.**
- **Use the sidewalk where there is one.** Georgia makes it unlawful to stand or walk on the roadway next to a sidewalk unless no vehicle is within 1,000 feet.
- **Where there's no sidewalk, stay on the shoulder.**
- **Interstates:** No Georgia statute banning pedestrians from controlled-access highways was found in this research (see open questions). Many interstate ramps are signed against pedestrians. Hitchhiking from the surface road before the ramp is the safer choice.

Violations of Chapter 6 of Title 40 are misdemeanors unless the chapter says otherwise (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-1).
sections.laws:
### O.C.G.A. § 40-6-97: Soliciting rides, business, or watching of vehicles

**Source:** [FindLaw, Georgia Code § 40-6-97](https://codes.findlaw.com/ga/title-40-motor-vehicles-and-traffic/ga-code-sect-40-6-97.html) (unofficial mirror, marked "Current as of March 28, 2024"). Georgia's official code is published by LexisNexis and could not be retrieved in this session. Subsection (a) also matches the Georgia Governor's Office of Highway Safety [pedestrian safety page](https://www.gahighwaysafety.org/pedestrian-safety/).

> (a) No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride.
>
> (b) Except as provided in Code Section 40-6-97.1, no person shall stand on a highway for the purpose of soliciting employment, business, or contributions from the occupant of any vehicle.
>
> (c) No person shall stand on or in proximity to a street or highway for the purpose of soliciting the watching or guarding of any vehicle while parked or about to be parked on a street or highway.

**What it means:** Don't stand in the travel lanes with your thumb out. The ride rule says "roadway," which excludes the shoulder. The business and contribution rule in (b) says "highway," which covers the whole right-of-way. Hitchhikers fall under (a), not (b).

### O.C.G.A. § 40-1-1: Definitions ("roadway," "highway," "controlled-access highway")

**Source:** [FindLaw, Georgia Code § 40-1-1](https://codes.findlaw.com/ga/title-40-motor-vehicles-and-traffic/ga-code-sect-40-1-1.html) (unofficial mirror, marked "Current as of March 28, 2024")

> (9) [...] every highway, street, or roadway in respect to which owners or occupants of abutting lands and other persons have no legal right of access to or from the same except only at such points and in such manner as may be determined by the public authority having jurisdiction over such highway, street, or roadway.
>
> [...]
>
> (19) [...] the entire width between the boundary lines of every way publicly maintained when any part thereof is open to the use of the public for purposes of vehicular travel.
>
> [...]
>
> (53) "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the berm or shoulder. In the event a highway includes two or more separate roadways, the term "roadway" shall refer to any such roadway separately, but not to all such roadways collectively.

(Paragraph (9) is the definition of "controlled-access highway" and paragraph (19) is the definition of "highway." The opening words of each were not captured verbatim.)

**What it means:** The "roadway" is the travel lanes only. The shoulder is outside it. A "highway" is everything between the boundary lines, shoulders included.

### O.C.G.A. § 40-6-96: Pedestrians on or along roadway

**Source:** [FindLaw, Georgia Code § 40-6-96](https://codes.findlaw.com/ga/title-40-motor-vehicles-and-traffic/ga-code-sect-40-6-96.html) (unofficial mirror, marked "Current as of March 28, 2024")

> (a) As used in this Code section, the term "pedestrian" means any person afoot and shall include, without limitation, persons standing, walking, jogging, running, or otherwise on foot.
>
> (b) Where a sidewalk is provided, it shall be unlawful for any pedestrian to stand or stride along and upon an adjacent roadway unless there is no motor vehicle traveling within 1,000 feet of such pedestrian on such roadway or the available sidewalk presents an imminent threat of bodily injury to such pedestrian.
>
> (c) Where a sidewalk is not provided but a shoulder is available, any pedestrian standing or striding along and upon a highway shall stand or stride only on the shoulder, as far as practicable from the edge of the roadway.
>
> (d) Where neither a sidewalk nor a shoulder is available, any pedestrian standing or striding along and upon a highway shall stand or stride as near as practicable to an outside edge of the roadway, and, if on a two-lane roadway, shall stand or stride only on the left side of the roadway.
>
> (e) Except as otherwise provided in this chapter, any pedestrian upon a roadway shall yield the right of way to all vehicles upon the roadway.

**What it means:** This section expressly covers *standing*, not just walking. If there's a sidewalk, stand on it. If there's only a shoulder, stand on the shoulder, as far from the lanes as you can. Pick a spot with a wide shoulder or pull-off where a driver can stop safely.

### O.C.G.A. § 40-6-1: Penalty

**Source:** [FindLaw, Georgia Code § 40-6-1](https://codes.findlaw.com/ga/title-40-motor-vehicles-and-traffic/ga-code-sect-40-6-1.html) (unofficial mirror, marked "Current as of March 28, 2024")

> (a) It is unlawful and, unless otherwise declared in this chapter with respect to particular offenses, it is a misdemeanor for any person to do any act forbidden or fail to perform any act required in this chapter.

**What it means:** Standing in the roadway to solicit a ride is technically a misdemeanor. In practice it is usually handled as a citation.

jurisdictions.title: North Carolina (US-NC)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. On ordinary State highways, North Carolina law expressly lets you stand on the **shoulder** to solicit a ride; only the rest of the highway is off limits. On interstates and other controlled-access highways, hitchhiking is banned outright by a Department of Transportation ordinance, and so is a driver stopping to pick you up. Breaking that ordinance is a Class 1 misdemeanor.

sections.summary:
North Carolina has two separate rules:

1. **G.S. § 20-175(a), all State highways:** "No person shall stand in any portion of the State highways, except upon the shoulders thereof, for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any motor vehicle." This is unusually clear. The shoulder is the legal place to hitchhike, and the travel lanes and median are not.
2. **19A NCAC 02E .0410, interstates and controlled-access highways:** it is unlawful "to hitchhike or to solicit rides, or for the driver of any vehicle to stop for the purpose of picking up one who is hitchhiking or soliciting a ride, on any interstate or controlled access highway." The only exception is for occupants of a broken-down vehicle and the people who stop to help them. Under G.S. § 136-18(5), violating a DOT ordinance is a Class 1 misdemeanor, which is far more serious than an ordinary pedestrian ticket.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **On regular State roads, stand on the shoulder.** That is expressly allowed by § 20-175(a).
- **Never hitchhike on an interstate or controlled-access highway, including its shoulder.** Wait on the surface road before the on-ramp. A driver who stops for you there is also breaking the rule.
- **Don't impede traffic.** Willfully standing on the highway or street "in such a manner as to impede the regular flow of traffic" is a separate Class 2 misdemeanor (§ 20-174.1).
- **Walk on the sidewalk** if there is one; otherwise on the extreme left of the roadway or its shoulder, facing traffic (§ 20-174(d)).
- **Penalty for § 20-175:** it is in Part 11 (pedestrians) of the motor vehicle article, so a violation is an infraction (a non-criminal offense) with a penalty of up to $100 (§ 20-176).
sections.laws:
### N.C. Gen. Stat. § 20-175: Pedestrians soliciting rides, employment, business or funds upon highways or streets

**Source:** [North Carolina General Assembly, G.S. § 20-175](https://www.ncleg.gov/EnactedLegislation/Statutes/HTML/BySection/Chapter_20/GS_20-175.html)

> (a) No person shall stand in any portion of the State highways, except upon the shoulders thereof, for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any motor vehicle.
>
> (b) No person shall stand or loiter in the main traveled portion, including the shoulders and median, of any State highway or street, excluding sidewalks, or stop any motor vehicle for the purpose of soliciting employment, business or contributions from the driver or occupant of any motor vehicle that impedes the normal movement of traffic on the public highways or streets: [...]
>
> (c) Repealed by Session Laws 1973, c. 1330, s. 39.
>
> (d) Local governments may enact ordinances restricting or prohibiting a person from standing on any street, highway, or right-of-way excluding sidewalks while soliciting, or attempting to solicit, any employment, business, or contributions from the driver or occupants of any vehicle. [...]

**What it means:** On a State highway you may hitchhike from the shoulder, but not from a travel lane, the median or anywhere else in the right-of-way. Note that the local-ordinance power in (d) covers soliciting employment, business or contributions, not rides. Don't ask for gas money from the roadside, because that falls under the stricter rules in (b) and (d).

### 19A NCAC 02E .0410: Hitchhiking on interstate or controlled access highways

**Source:** [North Carolina Office of Administrative Hearings, 19A NCAC 02E .0410 (PDF)](http://reports.oah.state.nc.us/ncac/title%2019a%20-%20transportation/chapter%2002%20-%20division%20of%20highways/subchapter%20e/19a%20ncac%2002e%20.0410.pdf) (readopted effective July 1, 2019)

> (a) It shall be unlawful for any person to hitchhike or to solicit rides, or for the driver of any vehicle to stop for the purpose of picking up one who is hitchhiking or soliciting a ride, on any interstate or controlled access highway.
>
> (b) This Rule shall not shall prohibit an operator or passengers in a vehicle stopped on a controlled access facility by reason of any emergency, mechanical failure, or other failure of the vehicle to operate, from requesting aid or soliciting a ride, nor does it prohibit the operator of any other vehicle from stopping to render aid or assistance and giving rides in such situations.

**What it means:** Interstates and other controlled-access highways are completely off limits for hitchhiking, shoulder and ramps included. Drivers can be charged for stopping to pick you up. The exception is if your own vehicle broke down there: then you may ask for help and others may give you a ride. ("not shall prohibit" is the rule's own wording.)

### N.C. Gen. Stat. § 136-18(5): DOT ordinances; violation is a Class 1 misdemeanor

**Source:** [North Carolina General Assembly, G.S. § 136-18](https://www.ncleg.gov/EnactedLegislation/Statutes/HTML/BySection/Chapter_136/GS_136-18.html)

> (5) To make rules, regulations, and ordinances for the use of, and to police traffic on, the State highways, and to prevent their abuse by individuals, corporations, and public corporations, [...] or by any other means whatsoever, and to provide ample means for the enforcement of the rules, regulations, and ordinances. The violation of any of the rules, regulations, or ordinances so prescribed by the Department of Transportation constitutes a Class 1 misdemeanor. [...]

**What it means:** Hitchhiking on an interstate is a crime, not just a ticket. See the sentencing section below for what a Class 1 misdemeanor can mean.

### N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-1340.23: Misdemeanor punishment limits

**Source:** [North Carolina General Assembly, G.S. § 15A-1340.23](https://www.ncleg.gov/EnactedLegislation/Statutes/HTML/BySection/Chapter_15A/GS_15A-1340.23.html)

> (b) Fines. - [...] Unless otherwise provided for a specific offense, the maximum fine that may be imposed is two hundred dollars ($200.00) for a Class 3 misdemeanor and one thousand dollars ($1,000) for a Class 2 misdemeanor. The amount of the fine for a Class 1 misdemeanor and a Class A1 misdemeanor is in the discretion of the court.

From the punishment chart (offense class, then Level I "No Prior Convictions", Level II "One to Four Prior Convictions", Level III "Five or More Prior Convictions"):

> 1 1-45 days C 1-45 days C/I/A 1-120 days C/I/A
>
> 2 1-30 days C 1-45 days C/I 1-60 days C/I/A

**What it means:** For a first-time Class 1 misdemeanor (interstate hitchhiking), the sentence range is 1 to 45 days of community punishment ("C"), and the fine is up to the judge. With prior convictions, active jail time ("A") becomes possible. Class 2 (impeding traffic under § 20-174.1) carries a fine of up to $1,000.

### N.C. Gen. Stat. § 20-174.1: Standing, sitting or lying upon highways or streets prohibited

**Source:** [North Carolina General Assembly, G.S. § 20-174.1](https://www.ncleg.gov/EnactedLegislation/Statutes/HTML/BySection/Chapter_20/GS_20-174.1.html)

> (a) A person who willfully stands, sits, or lies upon the highway or street in such a manner as to impede the regular flow of traffic is guilty of a Class 2 misdemeanor.
>
> (b) Repealed by Session Laws 2024-16, s. 4(a), effective December 1, 2024, [...]

**What it means:** Standing where cars have to slow or swerve around you is a crime on any road. Stay well back on the shoulder.

### N.C. Gen. Stat. § 20-4.01: Definitions ("Highway", "Roadway")

**Source:** [North Carolina General Assembly, G.S. § 20-4.01](https://www.ncleg.gov/EnactedLegislation/Statutes/HTML/BySection/Chapter_20/GS_20-4.01.html)

> Highway. - The entire width between property or right-of-way lines of every way or place of whatever nature, when any part thereof is open to the use of the public as a matter of right for the purposes of vehicular traffic. The terms "highway" and "street" and their cognates are synonymous.
>
> [...]
>
> Roadway. - That portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the shoulder. [...]

**What it means:** The highway is the whole right-of-way, from line to line. § 20-175(a) bans hitchhiking anywhere on that highway except the shoulder. So the grassy area beyond the shoulder, but still inside the right-of-way, is technically off limits too.

### N.C. Gen. Stat. § 20-174(d): Walking along highway

**Source:** [North Carolina General Assembly, G.S. § 20-174](https://www.ncleg.gov/EnactedLegislation/Statutes/HTML/BySection/Chapter_20/GS_20-174.html)

> (d) Where sidewalks are provided, it shall be unlawful for any pedestrian to walk along and upon an adjacent roadway. Where sidewalks are not provided, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall, when practicable, walk only on the extreme left of the roadway or its shoulder facing traffic which may approach from the opposite direction. Such pedestrian shall yield the right-of-way to approaching traffic.

**What it means:** Use the sidewalk. Without one, walk on the left edge or left shoulder facing traffic.

### N.C. Gen. Stat. § 20-176: Penalty for misdemeanor or infraction

**Source:** [North Carolina General Assembly, G.S. § 20-176](https://www.ncleg.gov/EnactedLegislation/Statutes/HTML/BySection/Chapter_20/GS_20-176.html)

> (a) Violation of a provision of Part 9, 10, 10A, or 11 of this Article is an infraction unless the violation is specifically declared by law to be a misdemeanor or felony. [...]
>
> (b) Unless a specific penalty is otherwise provided by law, a person found responsible for an infraction contained in this Article may be ordered to pay a penalty of not more than one hundred dollars ($100.00).

**What it means:** § 20-175 sits in Part 11 ("Pedestrians' Rights and Duties"), so hitchhiking from the wrong part of a State highway is an infraction with a penalty of up to $100. The interstate ordinance is the exception, as a Class 1 misdemeanor under § 136-18(5).
sections.history:

The official history line for § 20-174.1 lists Session Law 2024-16, s. 4(a), which among other things repealed subsection (b) effective December 1, 2024. The current text, including the Class 2 misdemeanor in subsection (a) and the enhanced penalties for demonstrations and for obstructing emergency vehicles in subsections (c) and (d), is what applies now.

jurisdictions.title: South Carolina (US-SC)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. South Carolina bans standing *in a roadway* to solicit a ride. The definition of "roadway" excludes the shoulder and berm, so hitchhiking from the shoulder of an ordinary road is not covered by that rule. Pedestrians are banned from the roadway and shoulder of freeways (interstate-type highways).

sections.summary:
S.C. Code § 56-5-3180(a) follows the Uniform Vehicle Code wording: "No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride." Section 56-5-460 defines the roadway as the part of the highway used for vehicle travel, "exclusive of the shoulder or berm."

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **On ordinary roads, stand on the shoulder or sidewalk, not in a travel lane.**
- **Freeways are off limits on foot.** § 56-5-3170 bars pedestrians from "any space within the limits of the roadway and shoulder of the main facility of a freeway," except in emergencies, to get help, or when directed by an officer. A freeway means an interstate-style highway with full control of access. The ban covers the "main facility"; it expressly does not apply to service roads, and it does not mention ramps. The safest place is the surface road before the on-ramp.
- **Walk on the sidewalk** if there is one; otherwise on the shoulder; otherwise on the left edge facing traffic (§ 56-5-3160).
- **Penalties:** both violations are misdemeanors. Hitchhiking from the roadway falls under the general penalty, a fine of up to $100 or up to 30 days in jail (§ 56-5-6190). Walking on a freeway has the same maximum under its own penalty clause (§ 56-5-3170(B)).
sections.laws:
### S.C. Code § 56-5-3180: Pedestrians soliciting rides or business

**Source:** [South Carolina Legislature, Code of Laws Title 56, Chapter 5](https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t56c005.php)

> (a) No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride.
>
> (b) Except when authorized by the provisions of Section 5-27-910, no person shall stand on a highway for the purpose of soliciting employment, business, or contributions from the occupant of any vehicle.
>
> (c) No person may stand on or in proximity to a street or highway for the purpose of soliciting the watching or guarding of any vehicle while parked or about to be parked on a street or highway.
>
> HISTORY: 1962 Code SECTION 46-437; 1952 Code SECTION 46-437; 1949 (46) 466; 1977 Act No. 145 SECTION 5; 1988 Act No. 373, SECTION 3.

**What it means:** Hitchhiking is barred only in the travel lanes ("roadway"). Note the contrast with (b): soliciting business or contributions is barred anywhere "on a highway," which includes the shoulder. So hold a sign asking for a ride, not one asking for money.

### S.C. Code §§ 56-5-430 and 56-5-460: Definitions of "Street or highway" and "Roadway"

**Source:** [South Carolina Legislature, Code of Laws Title 56, Chapter 5](https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t56c005.php)

> SECTION 56-5-430. Street defined; highway defined.
>
> The entire width between boundary lines of every way publicly maintained when any part thereof is open to the use of the public for purposes of vehicular travel is a "street" or "highway."

> SECTION 56-5-460. Roadway defined.
>
> A "roadway" is that portion of a highway improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the shoulder or berm. [...]

**What it means:** The shoulder and berm are part of the highway but not part of the roadway, so they are outside the hitchhiking ban in § 56-5-3180(a).

### S.C. Code § 56-5-3170: Pedestrians prohibited on freeways

**Source:** [South Carolina Legislature, Code of Laws Title 56, Chapter 5](https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t56c005.php)

> (A) No person as a pedestrian, unless otherwise directed by a law enforcement officer, shall occupy any space within the limits of the roadway and shoulder of the main facility of a freeway, except to perform public works or official duties, as a result of an emergency caused by an accident or breakdown of a motor vehicle, or to obtain assistance.
>
> The prohibitions imposed by this subsection on the use of freeways do not apply to service roads alongside the highways.
>
> (B) A person who violates the provisions of this section is guilty of a misdemeanor and, upon conviction, must be fined not more than one hundred dollars or imprisoned not more than thirty days.
>
> HISTORY: 1962 Code SECTION 46-436.1; 1971 (57) 298; 1993 Act No. 98, SECTION 2.

**What it means:** You may not stand or walk on the travel lanes or shoulder of an interstate-type freeway. Your own breakdown or crash is the exception. Frontage (service) roads are fine.

### S.C. Code § 56-5-615: Freeway defined

**Source:** [South Carolina Legislature, Code of Laws Title 56, Chapter 5](https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t56c005.php)

> A "freeway" is a multilane divided highway with full control of access, and grade separated interchanges, of the type comprising the National System of Interstate and Defense Highways, or other highways built essentially in conformance to the standards of them.

**What it means:** Interstates, and other highways built to interstate standards, count as freeways.

### S.C. Code § 56-5-3160: Pedestrians on highways

**Source:** [South Carolina Legislature, Code of Laws Title 56, Chapter 5](https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t56c005.php)

> (a) Where a sidewalk is provided and its use is practicable, it shall be unlawful for any pedestrian to walk along and upon an adjacent roadway.
>
> (b) Where a sidewalk is not available any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall walk only on a shoulder as far as practicable from the edge of the roadway.
>
> (c) Where neither a sidewalk nor a shoulder is available, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall walk as near as practicable to an outside edge of the roadway and, if on a two-way roadway, shall walk only on the left side of the roadway.

**What it means:** Use the sidewalk; otherwise the shoulder; otherwise the left edge facing traffic.

### S.C. Code § 56-5-6190: General penalty for violations of chapter

**Source:** [South Carolina Legislature, Code of Laws Title 56, Chapter 5](https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t56c005.php)

> It is a misdemeanor for any person to violate any of the provisions of this chapter unless such violation is by this chapter or other law of this State declared to be a felony.
>
> Every person convicted of a misdemeanor for a violation of any of the provisions of this chapter for which another penalty is not provided shall be punished by a fine of not more than one hundred dollars or by imprisonment for not more than thirty days.

**What it means:** Hitchhiking from a travel lane is a misdemeanor with a maximum of $100 or 30 days in jail.

jurisdictions.title: Virginia (US-VA)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. Virginia bans standing or stopping *in any roadway* to solicit rides. The Code defines "roadway" as excluding the shoulder, so hitchhiking from the shoulder or sidewalk is not covered by that rule. Pedestrians may be barred from controlled access highways where the Commonwealth Transportation Board has restricted them and posted markers.

sections.summary:
Va. Code § 46.2-929 is one sentence: "Pedestrians shall not stand or stop in any roadway for the purpose of soliciting rides." Section 46.2-100 defines "roadway" as the part of the highway used for vehicle travel, "exclusive of the shoulder." So the ban covers the travel lanes, not the shoulder.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stay out of the travel lanes.** The shoulder or sidewalk is outside § 46.2-929. Pick a spot with room for a car to pull fully off the road.
- **Interstates and other controlled access highways:** § 46.2-808 lets the Commonwealth Transportation Board prohibit pedestrians on controlled access highways "or any part thereof," with conspicuous markers at the ends of the restricted section. Where those markers are posted, walking past them is a traffic infraction. Ask for rides before the sign.
- **Posted no-loitering zones.** § 46.2-930 bans loitering on bridges or parts of the right-of-way where state or local officials have posted signs.
- **Walking along the road:** use the sidewalk; otherwise walk on the left facing traffic, or on either shoulder if it is wide enough (§ 46.2-928).
- **Penalty:** a traffic infraction (not a crime), fine of up to $250 (§ 46.2-113 with § 18.2-11).
sections.laws:
### Va. Code § 46.2-929: Pedestrians soliciting rides

**Source:** [Code of Virginia, § 46.2-929 (Virginia Law Library, law.lis.virginia.gov)](https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title46.2/chapter8/section46.2-929/)

> Pedestrians shall not stand or stop in any roadway for the purpose of soliciting rides.

**What it means:** You may not stand in a traffic lane to hitchhike. Because "roadway" excludes the shoulder (see below), standing on the shoulder or sidewalk is not covered by this section.

### Va. Code § 46.2-100: Definitions ("Highway", "Roadway", "Shoulder")

**Source:** [Code of Virginia, § 46.2-100](https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title46.2/chapter1/section46.2-100/)

> "Highway" means the entire width between the boundary lines of every way or place open to the use of the public for purposes of vehicular travel in the Commonwealth, including the streets and alleys, [...]
>
> "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the shoulder. A highway may include two or more roadways if divided by a physical barrier or barriers or an unpaved area.
>
> "Shoulder" means that part of a highway between the portion regularly traveled by vehicular traffic and the lateral curbline or ditch.

**What it means:** The shoulder is part of the "highway" but not part of the "roadway." The hitchhiking rule only reaches the roadway.

### Va. Code § 46.2-808: Commonwealth Transportation Board may prohibit certain uses of controlled access highways; penalty

**Source:** [Code of Virginia, § 46.2-808](https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title46.2/chapter8/section46.2-808/)

> A. The Commonwealth Transportation Board may, when necessary to promote safety, prohibit the use of controlled access highways or any part thereof by any or all of the following:
>
> 1. Pedestrians,
>
> [...]
>
> B. The termini of any section of controlled access highways, use of which is restricted under the provisions of this section, shall be clearly indicated by a conspicuous marker.
>
> [...] Any person violating a restriction or prohibition imposed pursuant to this section shall be guilty of a traffic infraction.

**What it means:** There is no blanket statute banning pedestrians from every Virginia freeway. Instead, the state bans them section by section and marks the restricted sections with signs. If you see a "pedestrians prohibited" sign at a ramp, stay behind it.

### Va. Code § 46.2-930: Loitering on bridges or highway rights-of-way

**Source:** [Code of Virginia, § 46.2-930](https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title46.2/chapter8/section46.2-930/)

> Pedestrians shall not loiter on any bridge or in any portion of the right-of-way of any highway where loitering has been determined by the Commissioner of Highways or the local governing body of any county, city, or town to present a public safety hazard and on which the Commissioner of Highways or the governing body of any county, city, or town has posted signs prohibiting such action. [...] Any person violating the provisions of this section shall be guilty of a traffic infraction.

**What it means:** Where there is a posted "no loitering" sign on a bridge or roadside, waiting there for a ride can be a violation even on the shoulder.

### Va. Code § 46.2-928: Pedestrians not to use roadway except when necessary; keeping to left

**Source:** [Code of Virginia, § 46.2-928](https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title46.2/chapter8/section46.2-928/) (amended 2026, c. 431)

> Pedestrians shall not use the roadways for travel, except when necessary to do so because of the absence of sidewalks which are reasonably suitable and passable for their use. If they walk on the hard surface, or the main travelled portion of the roadway, they shall keep to the extreme left side or edge thereof, or where the shoulders of the highway are of sufficient width to permit, they may walk on either shoulder thereof. Pedestrians walking on a roadway shall face oncoming traffic. However, when walking on a roadway that is part of a highway divided by a physical barrier or barriers or an unpaved area, and when there are no shoulders of the highway present, pedestrians may keep to the extreme right side or edge of the roadway, regardless of the direction of traffic they face.

**What it means:** Use the sidewalk. Without one, walk on the far left facing traffic, or on either shoulder if it is wide enough. On a divided road with no shoulder, you may keep to the right edge.

### Va. Code § 46.2-113 and § 18.2-11: Penalties

**Source:** [Code of Virginia, § 46.2-113](https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title46.2/chapter1/section46.2-113/); [Code of Virginia, § 18.2-11](https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title18.2/chapter1/section18.2-11/)

> It is unlawful for any person to violate any of the provisions of this title, or any regulation adopted pursuant to this title, or local ordinances adopted pursuant to the authority granted in this title. Unless otherwise stated, these violations shall constitute traffic infractions punishable by a fine of not more than that provided for a Class 4 misdemeanor under § 18.2-11. [...]

> (d) For Class 4 misdemeanors, a fine of not more than $250.

**What it means:** Hitchhiking from a travel lane, or walking past a freeway pedestrian ban, is a traffic infraction with a maximum fine of $250. It is not a criminal misdemeanor.

jurisdictions.title: West Virginia (US-WV)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. West Virginia bans standing *in a roadway* to solicit a ride. "Roadway" is defined to exclude the berm and shoulder, so hitchhiking from the shoulder is not covered by that rule. Pedestrians can be barred from controlled-access roads by posted signs.

sections.summary:
W. Va. Code § 17C-10-6(c) follows the Uniform Vehicle Code: "No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any vehicle." Section 17C-1-37 defines "roadway" as the part of the highway used for vehicle travel, "exclusive of the berm or shoulder."

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stay off the travel lanes.** The shoulder (berm) is outside the hitchhiking rule. Pick a place where a driver can pull completely off.
- **Interstates and the West Virginia Turnpike:** § 17C-7-13 lets the state road authority (by resolution) and local authorities (by ordinance) prohibit pedestrians on any controlled-access roadway and requires them to post signs. Where signs are up, walking past them is a violation. Stand before the sign at the on-ramp.
- **Walk on the sidewalk** if there is one; otherwise walk on the left side of the road or its shoulder, facing traffic (§ 17C-10-6(a), (b)).
- **Penalty:** a pedestrian violation is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $100 for a first offense, rising to $200 and then $500 for repeat convictions (§ 17C-10-7). The statute provides for fines only, not jail.
sections.laws:
### W. Va. Code § 17C-10-6: Pedestrians on roadways; soliciting rides

**Source:** [West Virginia Legislature, W. Va. Code § 17C-10-6](https://code.wvlegislature.gov/17C-10-6/)

> (a) Where sidewalks are provided it shall be unlawful for any pedestrian to walk along and upon an adjacent roadway.
>
> (b) Where sidewalks are not provided any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall when practicable walk only on the left side of the roadway or its shoulder facing traffic which may approach from the opposite direction.
>
> (c) No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any vehicle.

**What it means:** Don't stand in a traffic lane to hitchhike. Standing on the shoulder or berm is not covered by (c). When walking, use the sidewalk, or the left side or left shoulder facing traffic.

### W. Va. Code §§ 17C-1-35 and 17C-1-37: Definitions of "Street or highway" and "Roadway"

**Source:** [West Virginia Legislature, W. Va. Code § 17C-1-35](https://code.wvlegislature.gov/17C-1-35/); [W. Va. Code § 17C-1-37](https://code.wvlegislature.gov/17C-1-37/)

> "Street" or "highway" means the entire width between the boundary lines of every way publicly maintained when any part thereof is open to the use of the public for purposes of vehicular travel.

> "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the berm or shoulder. In the event a highway includes two or more separate roadways, the term "roadway" as used herein shall refer to any such roadway separately but not to all such roadways collectively.

**What it means:** The highway is the whole public strip; the roadway is just the travel lanes. The shoulder and berm are expressly not part of the roadway.

### W. Va. Code § 17C-7-13: Restrictions on use of controlled-access roadway

**Source:** [West Virginia Legislature, W. Va. Code § 17C-7-13](https://code.wvlegislature.gov/17C-7-13/)

> The state road commission may by resolution or order entered in its minutes and local authorities may by ordinance with respect to any controlled-access roadway under their respective jurisdictions prohibit the use of any such roadway by pedestrians, bicycles, or other nonmotorized traffic or by any person operating a motor-driven cycle. The state road commission or the local authority adopting any such prohibitory regulation shall erect and maintain official signs on the controlled-access roadway on which such regulations are applicable and when so erected no person shall disobey the restrictions stated on such signs.

**What it means:** There is no blanket statute banning pedestrians from all West Virginia freeways; the ban applies where it has been adopted and signed. Treat a "pedestrians prohibited" sign at a ramp as binding and stay on the local road side of it.

### W. Va. Code § 17C-10-7: Penalty for pedestrians violating the provisions of this article

**Source:** [West Virginia Legislature, W. Va. Code § 17C-10-7](https://code.wvlegislature.gov/17C-10-7/)

> Any person violating the provisions of this article is guilty of a misdemeanor and, upon conviction thereof, shall be fined not more than $100; upon a second conviction within one year thereafter, shall be fined not more than $200; and upon a third or subsequent conviction, shall be fined not more than $500.

**What it means:** Hitchhiking from a travel lane is technically a misdemeanor, but the penalty is a fine only: up to $100 the first time.

jurisdictions.title: Alabama (US-AL)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Illegal along state-maintained roads; restricted elsewhere. The traffic code only bans standing *in the roadway* to solicit a ride. Since 2023, however, Alabama's loitering law has made it a crime to "loiter or remain" on any state-maintained road *or its right-of-way*. Since 2024 that also covers anywhere within 30 feet of a freeway interchange. In practice, that covers the shoulders and on-ramp areas where hitchhikers usually stand.

sections.summary:
Alabama has two overlapping rules.

1. **Traffic code, Ala. Code § 32-5A-216(a):** "No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride." "Roadway" excludes the berm and shoulder. Taken alone, this would make shoulder hitchhiking lawful.
2. **Loitering, Ala. Code § 13A-11-9(a)(8):** A person commits loitering if they loiter or remain on a state-maintained public roadway, on the right-of-way of a state-maintained public roadway, or within 30 feet of any interchange involving a controlled-access or limited-access highway. The right-of-way includes shoulders and grass margins. Unlike the ride rule, this provision does not depend on your purpose.

The loitering provision was added by Act 2023-245 (2023 H.B. 24) and expanded to interchanges by Act 2024-326 (2024 S.B. 89). Its stated target is roadside panhandling and camping. Its text, though, covers anyone who "remains" in a state highway right-of-way. A hitchhiker standing on the shoulder of a U.S. or state route, or at an interstate on-ramp, is plainly within its words.

What this means for hitchhikers:

- **Interstate on-ramps are risky.** Anywhere within 30 feet of an interchange is covered by the loitering law.
- **State and U.S. highways:** Standing still on the shoulder or right-of-way is covered.
- **City and county roads** that are not state-maintained are covered only by § 32-5A-216(a). Stay off the travel lanes there.
- Before arresting someone under (a)(8), an officer *may* instruct the person to leave the right-of-way. Comply if asked.

Penalties: A first loitering offense is a "violation," punishable by a fine of up to $200 and up to 30 days in jail. A second or later offense in the same jurisdiction is a Class C misdemeanor, punishable by up to $500 and up to 3 months in jail. A first violation of § 32-5A-216 is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $100 or up to 10 days in jail.
sections.laws:
### Ala. Code § 32-5A-216: Pedestrian soliciting rides or business or fishing

**Source:** [Alabama Legislature, ALISON, Code of Alabama § 32-5A-216](https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/code-of-alabama?section=32-5A-216) (official; history: Acts 1980, No. 80-434; Acts 1981, No. 81-803)

> (a) No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride.
>
> (b) No person shall stand on a highway for the purpose of soliciting employment, business, or contributions from the occupant of any vehicle, nor for the purpose of distributing any article, unless otherwise authorized by official permit of the governing body of the city or county having jurisdiction over the highway.
>
> (c) No person shall stand on or in proximity to a street or highway for the purpose of soliciting the watching or guarding of any vehicle while parked or about to be parked on a street or highway.

**What it means:** Don't stand in the travel lanes to hitchhike. Taken alone, this section leaves the shoulder open. On state-maintained roads, though, the loitering law below applies on top of it.

### Ala. Code § 13A-11-9: Loitering

**Source:** [Alabama Legislature, ALISON, Code of Alabama § 13A-11-9](https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/code-of-alabama?section=13A-11-9) (official; history: Acts 1977, No. 607; Act 2019-465; Act 2023-245; Act 2024-326)

> (a) A person commits the crime of loitering if he or she does any of the following:
> [...]
> (8) Loiters or remains on a public roadway maintained by the state, the right-of-way of a public roadway maintained by the state, or any area within 30 feet of any interchange involving a controlled-access or limited-access highway. An "interchange" is defined as a system of interconnecting roadways providing for traffic movement between two or more roadways that do not intersect at grade.
> [...]
> (e) Loitering is a violation. A second or subsequent violation of this section in the same jurisdiction is a Class C misdemeanor.
>
> (f)(1) Prior to making an arrest for a violation of subdivision (a)(8), a law enforcement officer may instruct any person in violation of subdivision (a)(8) to immediately and peaceably exit the public roadway maintained by the state or the right-of-way of the public roadway maintained by the state.

**What it means:** Standing on the shoulder or grass beside a state or U.S. highway, or near an interstate interchange, can be charged as loitering. You don't have to be in the travel lanes. The law does not mention hitchhiking and was aimed at panhandling, but its words are broad enough to reach hitchhikers. Safer spots are private property with the owner's permission, such as a gas station or truck stop, or city streets that are not state routes.

### Ala. Code § 32-1-1.1: Definitions ("roadway," "highway," "controlled-access highway")

**Source:** [Alabama Legislature, ALISON, Code of Alabama § 32-1-1.1](https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/code-of-alabama?section=32-1-1.1) (official)

> (8) CONTROLLED-ACCESS HIGHWAY. Every highway, street, or roadway to which owners or occupants of abutting lands and other persons have no legal right of access to or from the same except at such points only and in such manner as may be determined by the public authority having jurisdiction over the highway, street, or roadway.
>
> [...]
>
> (26) HIGHWAY. The entire width between the boundary lines of every way publicly maintained when any part thereof is open to the use of the public for purposes of vehicular travel.
>
> [...]
>
> (59) ROADWAY. That portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the berm or shoulder. In the event a highway includes two or more separate roadways, the term refers to each roadway separately but not to all roadways collectively.

**What it means:** Under the traffic code, the shoulder is not part of the "roadway."

### Ala. Code § 32-5A-92: Restrictions on use of controlled-access roadway

**Source:** [Alabama Legislature, ALISON, Code of Alabama § 32-5A-92](https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/code-of-alabama?section=32-5A-92) (official)

> (a) The Department of Transportation by resolution or order entered in its minutes, and local authorities by ordinance, may regulate or prohibit the use of any controlled-access roadway (or highway) within their respective jurisdictions by any class or kind of traffic which is found to be incompatible with the normal and safe movement of traffic.
>
> (b) The Department of Transportation or the local authority adopting any such prohibition shall erect and maintain official traffic-control devices on the controlled-access highway on which such prohibitions are applicable and when in place no person shall disobey the restrictions stated on such devices.

**What it means:** There is no blanket statutory ban on pedestrians on Alabama freeways. ALDOT or a local authority can ban them by order, and the ban is enforceable where signs are posted. Obey "No Pedestrians" signs at ramps.

### Ala. Code § 32-5A-215: Pedestrians on roadways

**Source:** [Alabama Legislature, ALISON, Code of Alabama § 32-5A-215](https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/code-of-alabama?section=32-5A-215) (official)

> (a) Where a sidewalk is provided and its use is practicable, it shall be unlawful for any pedestrian to walk along and upon an adjacent roadway.
>
> (b) Where a sidewalk is not available, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall walk only on a shoulder, as far as practicable from the edge of the roadway.
>
> (c) Where neither a sidewalk nor a shoulder is available any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall walk as near as practicable to an outside edge of the roadway, and if on a two-way roadway, shall walk only on the left side of the roadway.

**What it means:** Use the sidewalk if there is one. If not, use the shoulder. If there's no shoulder either, walk on the left, facing traffic.

### Penalties: Ala. Code §§ 32-5A-8, 13A-5-7, 13A-5-12

**Source:** [Ala. Code § 32-5A-8](https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/code-of-alabama?section=32-5A-8), [§ 13A-5-7](https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/code-of-alabama?section=13A-5-7), [§ 13A-5-12](https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/code-of-alabama?section=13A-5-12) (official)

> § 32-5A-8(b) Every person convicted of a misdemeanor for a violation of any of the provisions of this chapter for which another penalty is not provided, shall for a first conviction thereof be punished by a fine of not more than $100.00 or by imprisonment for not more than 10 days; [...]
>
> § 13A-5-7(b) Sentences for violations shall be for a definite term of imprisonment in the county jail, not to exceed 30 days.
>
> § 13A-5-12(a)(3) For a Class C misdemeanor, not more than $500; [...]
> (b) A sentence to pay a fine for a violation shall be for a definite amount, fixed by the court, not to exceed $200, [...]

**What it means:** Standing in the roadway to hitch carries up to $100 or 10 days for a first offense. A first loitering offense is a violation, with up to $200 or 30 days. Repeat loitering in the same jurisdiction is a Class C misdemeanor.
sections.history:
### 2023 and 2024: loitering on state roads added

**Source:** [2023 H.B. 24, House substitute (J0BEFF-1)](https://www.legislature.state.al.us/pdf/SearchableInstruments/2023RS/J0BEFF-1.pdf); [2024 S.B. 89, House committee substitute (LLQEYYW-1)](https://www.legislature.state.al.us/pdf/SearchableInstruments/2024RS/LLQEYYW-1.pdf); codified history in [§ 13A-11-9](https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/code-of-alabama?section=13A-11-9)

Act 2023-245 (2023 H.B. 24) created the "state-maintained roadway or right-of-way" loitering offense. One draft of H.B. 24 would also have struck § 32-5A-216(b), the employment and contribution rule. The current official text of § 32-5A-216 still contains (b), and its history lists no 2023 amendment, so that part was not enacted. Act 2024-326 (2024 S.B. 89, effective June 1, 2024) added the "within 30 feet of any interchange" language and moved the offense to subdivision (a)(8). A 2026 bill (H.B. 168, introduced) would amend other parts of § 13A-11-9 (mask exemptions) and leaves (a)(8) unchanged.

jurisdictions.title: Arkansas (US-AR)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not stand in a roadway to solicit a ride from the driver of a private vehicle. Since 2023, pedestrians may not be anywhere within the property boundaries of a controlled-access highway.

sections.summary:
Ark. Code Ann. § 27-51-1205 reads: "No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any private vehicle." It follows the Uniform Vehicle Code pattern. Whether the shoulder counts as part of the "roadway" under Arkansas's own definition could not be confirmed in this research (see open questions). Standing on the grass or a pull-off beyond the shoulder is the safest choice.

What still applies to hitchhikers:

- **No freeways, including ramps and right-of-way.** Act 779 of 2023 created § 27-51-1206: "A pedestrian shall not be within the property boundaries of a controlled-access highway." The only exceptions are being directed by a police officer, construction personnel in a work zone, and people who leave a vehicle after a breakdown, crash or other emergency. The fine is up to $100. Hitchhike from the surface road before the interchange, or from a gas station or truck stop.
sections.laws:
### Ark. Code Ann. § 27-51-1205: Soliciting rides prohibited

**Source:** [FindLaw, Arkansas Code § 27-51-1205](https://codes.findlaw.com/ar/title-27-transportation/ar-code-sect-27-51-1205.html) (unofficial mirror, marked "Current as of March 28, 2024"). Arkansas's official code is published by LexisNexis and was not retrieved.

> No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any private vehicle.

**What it means:** Don't stand in the travel lanes to hitch. The rule only covers soliciting rides from *private* vehicles.

### Ark. Code Ann. § 27-51-1206: Pedestrians prohibited on controlled-access highway

**Source:** [Arkansas General Assembly, Act 779 of 2023 (SB 504)](https://arkleg.state.ar.us/Acts/FTPDocument?path=%2FACTS%2F2023R%2FPublic%2F&file=779.pdf&ddBienniumSession=2023%2F2023R) (official act text, approved April 12, 2023). The codified text matches [FindLaw, § 27-51-1206](https://codes.findlaw.com/ar/title-27-transportation/ar-code-sect-27-51-1206.html) ("Current as of March 28, 2024"), except that FindLaw reads "defense to prosecution under this section" where the act reads "of this section."

> (a) As used in this section:
> (1) "Construction personnel" means an employee of the Arkansas Department of Transportation or a contractor of the State Highway Commission;
> (2) "Controlled-access highway" means a state highway or street that:
> (A) Is designed for an unhindered flow of traffic without intersections, traffic signals, or property access; and
> (B) Regulates the ingress and egress of a motor vehicle;
> [...]
> (4)(A) "Pedestrian" means a person afoot.
> (B) "Pedestrian" does not include a person who is the driver or passenger of a motor vehicle traveling on a controlled-access highway.
>
> (b) A pedestrian shall not be within the property boundaries of a controlled-access highway unless he or she is:
> (1) Directed by a police officer; or
> (2) Construction personnel in a highway work zone.
>
> (c) A person who violates this section, upon conviction shall pay a fine not to exceed one hundred dollars ($100).
>
> (d) It is a defense to prosecution of this section that the pedestrian was first within a motor vehicle upon the controlled-access highway and exited the motor vehicle due to a mechanical breakdown, a motor vehicle accident, or other emergency.

**What it means:** The ban covers the whole property of an interstate or other freeway, not just the lanes: shoulders, ramps, medians and the grass inside the fence line. If your ride drops you on the interstate, the defense in (d) only covers leaving a vehicle because of a breakdown, crash or other emergency. Ask to be let out at an exit, off the ramp.
