jurisdictions.title: Kentucky (US-KY)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Illegal on state-maintained roads (new in 2026). A law effective **July 15, 2026** bans anyone from standing or remaining stationary anywhere in a state-maintained right-of-way that isn't designated for pedestrians. That includes shoulders, ramps, medians and the grass beside the road. The older rule against standing in the roadway to solicit a ride still applies on every road. Pedestrians are banned from fully controlled access highways.

sections.summary:
For decades Kentucky followed the Uniform Vehicle Code pattern: "A person shall not stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride" (KRS 189.570(19)). Because "roadway" excludes the shoulder, shoulder hitchhiking was lawful.

That changed in 2026. House Bill 189 (2026 Ky. Acts ch. 32) created **KRS 189.572**. It says a person "shall not sit, kneel, recline, stand, or remain physically stationary in any portion of a state-maintained right-of-way that is not designated for pedestrian use." The right-of-way expressly includes "paved and unpaved shoulders, medians, entrance and exit ramps, and adjacent grassy or drainage areas." The law does not mention hitchhiking. It was aimed at people standing beside busy roads. Standing on the shoulder of a state road to thumb a ride is squarely covered.

What this means for hitchhikers:

- **State-maintained roads** (interstates, parkways, U.S. and Kentucky numbered routes maintained by the Transportation Cabinet): no standing anywhere in the right-of-way, unless you are on a sidewalk, in a marked crosswalk or at a transit stop.
- **City and county streets** not maintained by the state: KRS 189.572 doesn't apply. The old roadway rule still does, so stay out of the travel lanes.
- **Sidewalks are exempt.** A sidewalk along a state route is a legal place to stand.
- **Interstates and parkways:** pedestrians are prohibited "within the right-of-way of a fully controlled access highway" by regulation.
- **Local exceptions:** cities and counties may create a permit process for limited exceptions.

Penalty: violations of KRS 189.570 through 189.590 carry a fine of $20 to $100 per offense (KRS 189.990(1)).
sections.laws:
### KRS 189.572: Prohibitions for pedestrians in state-maintained rights-of-way

**Source:** [Kentucky Legislature, KRS 189.572](https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=57272) (official; "Effective: July 15, 2026. History: Created 2026 Ky. Acts ch. 32, sec. 1")

> (1) As used in this section:
> (a) "Local government" means any city, county, consolidated local government, urban-county government, charter county government, or unified local government; and
> (b) "State-maintained right-of-way" means any land, property, or infrastructure under the jurisdiction or maintenance of the Kentucky Transportation Cabinet that is used by the public for transportation purposes, including but not limited to travel lanes, paved and unpaved shoulders, medians, entrance and exit ramps, and adjacent grassy or drainage areas not designated for pedestrian use.
>
> (2) Except as provided in subsection (3) or (4) of this section, a person shall not sit, kneel, recline, stand, or remain physically stationary in any portion of a state-maintained right-of-way that is not designated for pedestrian use.
>
> (3) Subsection (2) of this section shall not apply to:
> (a) Individuals experiencing a medical emergency;
> (b) Individuals involved in a vehicle-related emergency, provided they remain in the immediate area of the vehicle;
> (c) Emergency personnel or public utility workers performing their official duties; or
> (d) Persons located within a pedestrian-designated area such as a sidewalk, marked crosswalk, or transit stop.
>
> (4) A local government may by ordinance authorize limited exceptions to subsection (2) of this section if: [...]

**What it means:** On any state-maintained road, you can't stand still on the shoulder, the ramp, the median or the grass beside the road. Walking along a road that isn't a controlled access highway is not covered; standing in one place to thumb is. Sidewalks, marked crosswalks and transit stops are exempt. Find a spot on private property with permission (a gas station, truck stop or rest-area parking lot), or a sidewalk on the way out of town.

### KRS 189.570: Pedestrians

**Source:** [Kentucky Legislature, KRS 189.570](https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=57273) (official; "Effective: July 15, 2026. History: Amended 2026 Ky. Acts ch. 32, sec. 2")

> (12) Where a sidewalk is provided and its use is practicable, it shall be unlawful for any pedestrian to walk along and upon an adjacent roadway.
>
> (13) Where a sidewalk is not available, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall walk only on a shoulder, as far as practicable from the edge of the roadway.
>
> (14) Where neither a sidewalk nor a shoulder is available, any pedestrian walking on or along a highway shall walk as near as practicable to an outside edge of the roadway, and, if on a two-way roadway shall walk only on the left side of the roadway.
>
> [...]
>
> (19) A person shall not stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride.
>
> (20) A person shall not stand on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting employment or business from the occupant of any vehicle.
>
> [...]
>
> (23) A person shall not occupy any portion of a state-maintained right-of-way in violation of KRS 189.572.

**What it means:** On every road, state or local, you may not stand in the travel lanes to solicit a ride. Subsection (23) was added in 2026 to tie this section to the new state right-of-way ban.

### KRS 189.010: Definitions ("highway," "roadway")

**Source:** [Kentucky Legislature, KRS 189.010](https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=57661) (official; effective July 15, 2026)

> (3) "Highway" means any public road, street, avenue, alley or boulevard, bridge, viaduct, or trestle and the approaches to them [...]
>
> [...]
>
> (10) "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the berm or shoulder. If a highway includes two (2) or more separate roadways, the term "roadway" as used herein shall refer to any roadway separately but not to all such roadways collectively;

**What it means:** Under KRS 189.570(19), the shoulder is not part of the "roadway." KRS 189.572 has its own, much broader definition of "state-maintained right-of-way" that expressly includes shoulders.

### 603 KAR 5:025: Fully controlled access highways

**Source:** [Kentucky Legislature, 603 KAR 5:025](https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/603/005/025/) (official; history ends "Cert eff. 12-12-2024")

> Section 4. Limitations. The following shall be prohibited within the right-of-way of a fully controlled access highway:
> (1) Bicycles or motor scooters;
> [...]
> (9) Pedestrians.

**What it means:** No walking or standing anywhere within the right-of-way of interstates and fully controlled access parkways, including the ramps. Wait on the surface road outside the interchange.

### KRS 189.990: Penalties

**Source:** [Kentucky Legislature, KRS 189.990](https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=57417) (official; effective July 15, 2026)

> (1) (a) Any person who violates any of the provisions of KRS [...] 189.570 to 189.590, except 189.580(1)(b) or (6)(b), [...] shall be fined not less than twenty dollars ($20) nor more than one hundred dollars ($100) for each offense.

**What it means:** Standing in the roadway to hitch (KRS 189.570) and, by its section number, standing in a state right-of-way (KRS 189.572) each carry a fine of $20 to $100. Court costs are extra.
sections.history:
### 2026 H.B. 189: state right-of-way standing ban

**Source:** [Kentucky General Assembly, 2026 Regular Session, House Bill 189](https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/record/26rs/HB189.html); [2026 Ky. Acts ch. 32](https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/acts/26RS/documents/0032.pdf)

H.B. 189 ("AN ACT relating to pedestrians") became law without the Governor's signature on April 5, 2026, as Acts Chapter 32. Its preamble cites "individuals remaining physically stationary in narrow medians, highway shoulders, and exit ramps" as a safety risk. It created KRS 189.572 and added subsection (23) to KRS 189.570. Both take effect July 15, 2026. Before that date, Kentucky was effectively a "restricted" state: hitchhiking from the shoulder was lawful, and only standing in the roadway was banned. Guides written before mid-2026 describe the old law.

jurisdictions.title: Louisiana (US-LA)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not stand on a public roadway to solicit a ride. Louisiana defines "roadway" to exclude the berm or shoulder. Pedestrians may not use Louisiana interstate highways at all, and crossing an interstate on foot is a separate offense.

sections.summary:
La. R.S. 32:218(A) says "no person shall stand on a public roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment, or business from the occupant of any vehicle." Louisiana's definition of "roadway" excludes the berm or shoulder. Standing on the shoulder or curb is therefore outside this rule.

What still applies to hitchhikers:

- **No interstates.** "The use of any Louisiana interstate highway by pedestrians [...] is prohibited" (R.S. 32:263(C)). Crossing an interstate on foot is also unlawful except in an emergency (R.S. 32:216(C)). Hitchhike from the surface road before the on-ramp.
- **Use sidewalks where they exist.** Where there are none, walk on the left side of the highway or its shoulder, facing traffic (R.S. 32:216).

Penalty: a first violation of the traffic chapter carries a fine of up to $175, up to 30 days in jail, or both. Subsequent violations carry up to $500 and 90 days (R.S. 32:57). For violations of R.S. 32:216, a court may order community service instead.
sections.laws:
### La. R.S. 32:218: Pedestrians soliciting rides or business

**Source:** [Louisiana State Legislature, R.S. 32:218](https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?d=88193) (official; history: Acts 1962, No. 310; Acts 1999, No. 1132; Acts 2019, No. 123)

> A. Subject to Subsection B of this Section, no person shall stand on a public roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment, or business from the occupant of any vehicle.
>
> B.(1) Subject to the permission of the local municipal or parish authority in which the roadway is located, a member of a professional firefighters association, a police officer, or other public safety officer shall not be prohibited by this Section nor any other provision of state law from standing on a public roadway for the purpose of soliciting contributions on behalf of bona fide charitable or civic organizations during daylight hours, if all of the following are satisfied: [...]
>
> C. This Section shall be known as the Rivers Lacrouts Charitable Solicitation Act.

**What it means:** Don't stand in the travel lanes to hitch. The shoulder is not part of the "roadway" (see the definition below). Subsection B, added in 2019, is a carve-out for firefighters and police doing charity "boot drives" and doesn't affect hitchhikers.

### La. R.S. 32:1: Definitions ("roadway," "highway," "controlled-access highway")

**Source:** [Louisiana State Legislature, R.S. 32:1](https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?d=88016) (official; history through Acts 2025, No. 281)

> (19) "Controlled-access highway" means every highway, street, or roadway in respect to which owners or occupants of abutting lands and other persons have no legal right of access to or from the same except at such points only and in such manner as may be determined by the public authority having jurisdiction over such highway, street, or roadway.
>
> [...]
>
> (34) "Highway" means the entire width between the boundary lines of every way or place of whatever nature publicly maintained and open to the use of the public for the purpose of vehicular travel, including bridges, causeways, tunnels and ferries; synonymous with the word "street".
>
> [...]
>
> (75) "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular traffic, exclusive of the berm or shoulder. A divided highway has two or more roadways.

**What it means:** The shoulder is expressly outside the "roadway," so R.S. 32:218 does not reach someone standing on the shoulder.

### La. R.S. 32:263: Special restrictions on use of Louisiana interstate highways

**Source:** [Louisiana State Legislature, R.S. 32:263](https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?d=88213) (official; Acts 1962, No. 310; amended Acts 1964, No. 87)

> C. The use of any Louisiana interstate highway by pedestrians, bicycles, or other non-motorized vehicles is prohibited.

**What it means:** No walking or standing on interstates, including their shoulders. The text says "interstate highway." It doesn't expressly cover non-interstate expressways, but those may be signed against pedestrians.

### La. R.S. 32:216: Pedestrians on highways or interstate highways

**Source:** [Louisiana State Legislature, R.S. 32:216](https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?d=88191) (official; Acts 1962, No. 310; Acts 2001, No. 585)

> A. Where sidewalks are provided, it shall be unlawful for any pedestrian to walk along and upon an adjacent highway.
>
> B. Where sidewalks are not provided, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall, when practicable, walk only on the left side of the highway or its shoulder, facing traffic which may approach from the opposite direction.
>
> C. It shall be unlawful for any pedestrian to cross an interstate highway, except in the case of an emergency.
>
> D. Upon conviction of a violation of this Section, a court may order, in lieu of the penalty provisions provided in R.S. 32:57, that the offender perform three eight-hour days of court-approved community service activities, at least half of which shall consist of participation in a litter abatement or collection program.

**What it means:** Use sidewalks where they exist. Otherwise walk facing traffic. Never run across an interstate.

### La. R.S. 32:57: Penalties

**Source:** [Louisiana State Legislature, R.S. 32:57](https://www.legis.la.gov/Legis/Law.aspx?d=88472) (official. The page notes that this section "was included in the Unconstitutional Statutes Biennial Report to the Legislature, dated March 14, 2016"; the report's concern was not reviewed.)

> A.(1) Except as provided in Paragraph (2) of this Subsection and Subsections H and I of this Section, the first violation of the provisions of this Chapter or any regulation of the department, secretary, and commissioner made pursuant thereto shall be punished by a fine of not more than one hundred seventy-five dollars or by imprisonment for not more than thirty days, or both, unless otherwise specifically provided. A subsequent violation shall be punished by a fine of not more than five hundred dollars or by imprisonment for not more than ninety days, or both.

**What it means:** A first offense carries up to $175 and 30 days. Repeat offenses carry up to $500 and 90 days.

jurisdictions.title: Mississippi (US-MS)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not stand in a roadway to solicit a ride from the driver of a private vehicle. Mississippi Department of Transportation (MDOT) rules ban pedestrians and "hitchhikers" by name from fully controlled access highways.

sections.summary:
Mississippi Code § 63-3-1109 reads: "No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any private vehicle."

One wrinkle: Mississippi's definition of "roadway" (§ 63-3-125(c)) does **not** expressly exclude the shoulder. Most states' definitions add "exclusive of the berm or shoulder"; Mississippi's does not. The definition still limits "roadway" to the part "improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel," and a shoulder is not ordinarily used for travel. Standing well off the travel lanes is the safest reading.

What still applies to hitchhikers:

- **No interstates or other fully controlled access highways.** An MDOT rule says "The use of any fully controlled access facility by pedestrians, bicycles, hitchhikers [...] is prohibited." Hitchhike from the surface road or a gas station before the on-ramp.
- **Stand clear of the travel lanes** on ordinary highways.

A violation of § 63-3-1109 is a misdemeanor. A first conviction carries a fine of up to $100 or up to 10 days in jail (§ 63-9-11).
sections.laws:
### Miss. Code Ann. § 63-3-1109: Soliciting rides

**Source:** [FindLaw, Mississippi Code § 63-3-1109](https://codes.findlaw.com/ms/title-63-motor-vehicles-and-traffic-regulations/ms-code-sect-63-3-1109.html) (unofficial mirror; FindLaw's Title 63 pages are marked "Current as of January 01, 2025"). Mississippi's official code is published by LexisNexis and was not retrieved.

> No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any private vehicle.

**What it means:** Don't stand in the travel lanes to hitch. The rule says nothing about the shoulder, the sidewalk or the area beyond the road edge.

### Miss. Code Ann. § 63-3-125: Definitions ("street or highway," "roadway")

**Source:** [FindLaw, Mississippi Code § 63-3-125](https://codes.findlaw.com/ms/title-63-motor-vehicles-and-traffic-regulations/ms-code-sect-63-3-125.html) (unofficial mirror, "Current as of January 01, 2025")

> (a) "Street or highway" means the entire width between property lines of every way or place of whatever nature when any part thereof is open to the use of the public, as a matter of right, for purposes of vehicular traffic.
>
> [...]
>
> (c) "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel.
>
> (d) "Sidewalk" means that portion of a street between curb lines, or the lateral lines of a roadway, and the adjacent property lines intended for the use of pedestrians.

**What it means:** Unlike most states, Mississippi doesn't say in so many words that the shoulder is excluded from the "roadway." A paved shoulder is still not "ordinarily used for vehicular travel," so it is arguably outside the roadway. To be safe, stand on the grass or a pull-off beyond the shoulder edge.

### Mississippi Administrative Code, Title 37, Part 1, Rule 7501-09001-311: Fully controlled access facilities

**Source:** [Cornell LII, 37 Miss. Code. R. § 1-7501-09001-311](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/mississippi/37-Miss-Code-R-SS-1-7501-09001-311) (unofficial mirror of MDOT's "Rules, Regulations and Ordinances Governing Use of State Highways of Mississippi," Subpart 7501 Maintenance, Chapter 09001)

> The use of any fully controlled access facility by pedestrians, bicycles, hitchhikers, ridden or herded animals and animal drawn vehicles is prohibited. The use of any such fully controlled access facility by motor bicycles, non-motorized vehicles or any other vehicle unable to comply with the posted minimum speed limit is also prohibited. It shall be unlawful for any person to fish from any bridge, culvert or other structure on a state highway.

**What it means:** Interstates and other fully controlled access highways are off limits to hitchhikers, by name. This is one of the few rules in the country that uses the word "hitchhikers." Wait at the bottom of the ramp, on the local road.

### Miss. Code Ann. § 63-9-11: Penalties

**Source:** [FindLaw, Mississippi Code § 63-9-11](https://codes.findlaw.com/ms/title-63-motor-vehicles-and-traffic-regulations/ms-code-sect-63-9-11.html) (unofficial mirror, "Current as of January 01, 2025")

> (1) It is a misdemeanor for any person to violate any of the provisions of Chapter 3, 5 or 7 of this title, unless such violation is by such chapters or other law of this state declared to be a felony.
>
> (2) Every person convicted of a misdemeanor for a violation of any of the provisions of such chapters for which another penalty is not provided shall for first conviction thereof be punished by a fine of not more than One Hundred Dollars ($100.00) or by imprisonment for not more than ten (10) days; for a second such conviction within one (1) year thereafter such person shall be punished by a fine of not more than Two Hundred Dollars ($200.00) or by imprisonment for not more than twenty (20) days or by both such fine and imprisonment; upon a third or subsequent conviction within one (1) year after the first conviction such person shall be punished by a fine of not more than Five Hundred Dollars ($500.00) or by imprisonment for not more than six (6) months or by both such fine and imprisonment.

**What it means:** A first offense of soliciting a ride from the roadway (Title 63, Chapter 3) carries up to $100 or 10 days in jail. Repeat offenses within a year cost more.

jurisdictions.title: Tennessee (US-TN)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not stand in a roadway to solicit a ride. Tennessee defines "roadway" to exclude the berm or shoulder. Hitchhiking is banned outright inside Tennessee state parks and natural areas. A 2019 law bars loitering in or near the median of a state highway.

sections.summary:
Tenn. Code Ann. § 55-8-139(a)(1) reads: "No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride or employment from the occupant of any vehicle." Tennessee's definition of "roadway" excludes the berm or shoulder, so standing on the shoulder or curb is outside this rule.

What still applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stay out of medians.** Since 2019, § 55-8-139(c) bans loitering "in, or in proximity to, the median of a state highway." A first offense gets a warning citation.
- **Walk on the left, facing traffic,** on the road or its shoulder where there's no sidewalk (§ 55-8-138). Use sidewalks where they exist.
- **No hitchhiking in state parks and natural areas.** A state parks rule says "Hitchhiking or the soliciting of transportation is prohibited."
- **Interstates:** The Tennessee Department of Transportation (TDOT) says pedestrians may use any road "that is not access controlled (like an interstate)." The statute or rule behind that was not found in this research. Treat interstates as off limits.

A violation of § 55-8-139 is a Class C misdemeanor, punishable by up to 30 days in jail, a fine of up to $50, or both.
sections.laws:
### Tenn. Code Ann. § 55-8-139: Soliciting rides, employment, and median loitering

**Source:** [FindLaw, Tennessee Code § 55-8-139](https://codes.findlaw.com/tn/title-55-motor-and-other-vehicles/tn-code-sect-55-8-139.html) (unofficial mirror, marked "Current as of January 02, 2024"). Tennessee's official code is published by LexisNexis and was not retrieved.

> (a)(1) No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride or employment from the occupant of any vehicle.
>
> (2) It is an offense for an occupant of a vehicle to park, leave standing, or stop the vehicle on a street or highway and to block or impede the normal movement of traffic for the purpose of soliciting, negotiating, or consummating an employment transaction with a person standing on or in proximity to the street or highway.
>
> (b) No person shall stand on or in proximity to a street or highway for the purpose of soliciting the watching or guarding of any vehicle while parked or about to be parked on a street or highway.
>
> (c) No person shall loiter or conduct any commercial activity in, or in proximity to, the median of a state highway.
>
> [...]
>
> (e) A violation of this section is a Class C misdemeanor; except, that:
> (1) A person who violates subsection (c) must receive a warning citation for a first offense; and
> (2) If a vehicle parked, left standing, or stopped on a street or highway in violation of subdivision (a)(2) causes or contributes to a motor vehicle accident, then a violation of this section is a Class B misdemeanor.

**What it means:** Don't stand in the travel lanes to hitch. The shoulder is outside the "roadway." Don't stand in the median of a state highway. Subsection (a)(2) targets drivers who stop in traffic to hire day laborers, not drivers who pick up hitchhikers.

### Tenn. Code Ann. § 55-8-101: Definitions ("roadway," "highway," "controlled-access highway")

**Source:** [FindLaw, Tennessee Code § 55-8-101](https://codes.findlaw.com/tn/title-55-motor-and-other-vehicles/tn-code-sect-55-8-101.html) (unofficial mirror, "Current as of January 02, 2024")

> (15) "Controlled-access highway" means every highway, street or roadway in respect to which owners or occupants of abutting lands and other persons have no legal right of access to or from the same, except at such points only and in such manner as may be determined by the public authority having jurisdiction over the highway, street or roadway;
>
> [...]
>
> (30) "Highway" means the entire width between the boundary lines of every way when any part thereto is open to the use of the public for purposes of vehicular travel;
>
> [...]
>
> (68) "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the berm or shoulder. In the event a highway includes two (2) or more separate roadways, "roadway" refers to any such roadway separately but not to all such roadways collectively;

**What it means:** The shoulder is not part of the "roadway," so the ride-solicitation ban doesn't reach it.

### Tenn. Code Ann. § 55-8-138: Pedestrians on roadways

**Source:** [FindLaw, Tennessee Code § 55-8-138](https://codes.findlaw.com/tn/title-55-motor-and-other-vehicles/tn-code-sect-55-8-138.html) (unofficial mirror, "Current as of January 02, 2024")

> (a) Except as provided in this section, where sidewalks are provided, it is unlawful for any pedestrian to walk or use a wheelchair along and upon an adjacent roadway.
>
> (b) Where sidewalks are not provided or are obstructed, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall, when practicable, walk only on the left side of the roadway or its shoulder facing traffic that may approach from the opposite direction.
>
> [...]
>
> (d) A violation of this section is a Class C misdemeanor.

**What it means:** Use sidewalks where they exist. Otherwise walk on the left, facing oncoming traffic.

### Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 0400-02-02-.04: Begging and soliciting (state parks and natural areas)

**Source:** [Cornell LII, Tenn. Comp. R. & Regs. 0400-02-02-.04](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/tennessee/Tenn-Comp-R-Regs-0400-02-02-.04) (unofficial mirror; Division of State Parks and Division of Natural Areas, Chapter 0400-02-02 "Public Use and Recreation"; amended effective September 12, 2010)

> (1) Begging is prohibited.
> (2) Hitchhiking or the soliciting of transportation is prohibited.

**What it means:** Inside Tennessee state parks and state natural areas, you may not hitchhike at all, even from the shoulder.

### Tenn. Code Ann. § 40-35-111: Penalty for a Class C misdemeanor

**Source:** [FindLaw, Tennessee Code § 40-35-111](https://codes.findlaw.com/tn/title-40-criminal-procedure/tn-code-sect-40-35-111.html) (unofficial mirror, "Current as of January 02, 2024")

> (e)(3) Class C misdemeanor, not greater than thirty (30) days or a fine not to exceed fifty dollars ($50.00), or both [...]

**What it means:** The maximum is 30 days in jail and a $50 fine.
sections.history:
### 2019: median loitering ban (Pub. Ch. 184)

**Source:** [Tennessee General Assembly, HB 0832 (111th General Assembly) bill history](https://wapp.capitol.tn.gov/apps/BillInfo/Default.aspx?BillNumber=HB0832&GA=111)

The bill's summary reads: "As enacted, prohibits persons from loitering or conducting any commercial activity in, or in proximity to, the median of a state highway; creates a Class C misdemeanor offense that requires issuance of a warning citation for a first offense." It became Public Chapter 184, signed May 1, 2019, effective July 1, 2019. Some secondary websites attribute the warning-citation rule to a 2025 public chapter. The bill history shows it dates from 2019.

jurisdictions.title: Illinois (US-IL)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not stand *in a roadway* to solicit a ride (625 ILCS 5/11-1006(a)). Illinois defines the roadway as "exclusive of the berm or shoulder." On the Illinois Tollway, soliciting rides is banned outright. Pedestrians are kept off controlled-access highways where the state has posted signs.

sections.summary:
Illinois uses the Uniform Vehicle Code wording: "No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any vehicle." The Illinois Vehicle Code defines "roadway" as the part of the highway used for vehicle travel, "exclusive of the berm or shoulder." So thumbing from the shoulder, curb or sidewalk of an ordinary road is not covered by § 11-1006(a). The penalty is unusually harsh, though: any violation of § 11-1006 is a **Class A misdemeanor**, which is a criminal offense.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stay out of the travel lanes.** Stand on the shoulder or sidewalk, never in the lane.
- **Don't solicit money or work** from drivers anywhere on the highway (§ 11-1006(b) and (c)). A sign asking for gas money can turn a lawful ride request into a solicitation offense.
- **Don't walk onto a controlled-access highway** (interstate or expressway) where it is signed as closed to pedestrians. The Illinois Department of Transportation (IDOT) may ban pedestrians and must post signs (§ 11-711(b)).
- **Don't hitchhike on the Illinois Tollway** (I-88, I-90, I-94, I-294, I-355 and the other tolled routes, including the oases). Tollway rules ban soliciting rides from drivers "using the Tollway," ban loitering, and bar drivers from stopping on the right-of-way.

### 625 ILCS 5/11-1006: Pedestrians soliciting rides or business

**Source:** [Onecle, 625 ILCS 5/11-1006](https://law.onecle.com/illinois/625ilcs5/11-1006.html) (unofficial mirror, page last modified February 18, 2015; source line "P.A. 88-589, eff. 8-14-94"). Subsections (a) and (e) cross-checked against [FindLaw's mirror](https://codes.findlaw.com/il/chapter-625-vehicles/il-st-sect-625-5-11-1006/) ("current as of January 01, 2025"), which shows the same wording. The official site, ilga.gov, refused automated access.

> (a) No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any vehicle.
>
> (b) No person shall stand on a highway for the purpose of soliciting employment or business from the occupant of any vehicle.
>
> (c) No person shall stand on a highway for the purpose of soliciting contributions from the occupant of any vehicle except within a municipality when expressly permitted by municipal ordinance. [...]
>
> (d) No person shall stand on or in the proximity of a highway for the purpose of soliciting the watching or guarding of any vehicle while parked or about to be parked on a highway.
>
> (e) Every person who is convicted of a violation of this Section shall be guilty of a Class A misdemeanor.

**What it means:** Asking for a ride is illegal only while you stand *in the roadway*, meaning the travel lanes. Standing on the shoulder or sidewalk is not covered (see § 1-179 below). Subsections (b) and (c) are broader. They apply to the whole "highway" right-of-way and cover asking for work, business or money, so keep your sign to a destination. Every violation of this section is a Class A misdemeanor, a criminal charge rather than a traffic ticket.

### 625 ILCS 5/1-179: Roadway

**Source:** [Onecle, 625 ILCS 5/1-179](https://law.onecle.com/illinois/625ilcs5/1-179.html) (unofficial mirror, page last modified February 18, 2015; source line "P.A. 76-1586")

> That portion of a highway improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the berm or shoulder. In the event a highway includes two or more separate roadways the term "roadway" as used herein shall refer to any such roadway separately but not to all such roadways collectively.

**What it means:** The shoulder is expressly *not* part of the roadway. That is why thumbing from the shoulder doesn't violate § 11-1006(a).

### 625 ILCS 5/1-126: Highway

**Source:** [Onecle, 625 ILCS 5/1-126](https://law.onecle.com/illinois/625ilcs5/1-126.html) (unofficial mirror, page last modified February 18, 2015; source line "P.A. 92-780, eff. 8-6-02")

> The entire width between the boundary lines of every way publicly maintained when any part thereof is open to the use of the public for purposes of vehicular travel or located on public school property.

**What it means:** "Highway" is the whole right-of-way, including shoulders, so the bans in § 11-1006(b) to (d) reach further than the ride rule in (a).

### 625 ILCS 5/11-711: Restrictions on use of controlled access highway

**Source:** [Onecle, 625 ILCS 5/11-711](https://law.onecle.com/illinois/625ilcs5/11-711.html) (unofficial mirror, page last modified February 18, 2015; source line "P.A. 76-1586")

> (b) The Department with respect to any controlled access highway under its jurisdiction may prohibit the use of any such highways by pedestrians (except in authorized areas or facilities), bicycles, farm tractors, implements of husbandry, funeral processions, and any vehicle unable to maintain the minimum speed for which the highway is posted, or other non-motorized traffic or by any person operating a motor driven cycle. [...] The Department shall erect and maintain official signs on the controlled access highway on which such prohibitions are applicable and when so erected no person may disobey the restrictions stated on such sign.

**What it means:** Illinois statute doesn't ban pedestrians from every freeway automatically. IDOT may close a controlled-access highway to pedestrians, and when it posts signs, you must obey them. Interstate on-ramps are normally signed "no pedestrians," so wait at the start of the ramp on the surface street.

### 625 ILCS 5/11-1007: Pedestrians walking on highways

**Source:** [Onecle, 625 ILCS 5/11-1007](https://law.onecle.com/illinois/625ilcs5/11-1007.html) (unofficial mirror, page last modified February 18, 2015; source line "P.A. 97-1023, eff. 1-1-13")

> (a) Except as provided in subsection (e), where a sidewalk is provided and its use is practicable, it shall be unlawful for any pedestrian to walk along and upon an adjacent roadway.
>
> (b) Except as provided in subsection (e), where a sidewalk is not available, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall walk only on a shoulder, as far as practicable from the edge of the roadway.
>
> (c) Except as provided in subsection (e), where neither a sidewalk nor a shoulder is available, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall walk as near as practicable to an outside edge of a roadway, and, if on a two-way roadway, shall walk only on the left side of the roadway.

**What it means:** Use the sidewalk if there is one. Otherwise use the shoulder, as far from traffic as you can. With neither, walk on the left facing traffic.

### 92 Ill. Adm. Code 2520.254: Solicitation of Rides (Illinois Tollway)

**Source:** [Cornell LII, Ill. Admin. Code tit. 92, § 2520.254](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/illinois/Ill-Admin-Code-tit-92-SS-2520.254) (unofficial mirror of the Illinois State Toll Highway Authority rules)

> No person shall solicit or attempt to solicit rides from the driver of any vehicle using the Tollway.

**What it means:** On the Illinois Tollway, any attempt to get a ride from a driver is banned. The rule isn't limited to the roadway, so it plausibly covers the shoulders, ramps and oases. Get dropped off before the toll road, or ask at a truck stop off the Tollway.

### 92 Ill. Adm. Code 2520.257, 2520.230 and 2520.320: Loitering, stopping and use of the Tollway

**Source:** Cornell LII mirrors of [§ 2520.257](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/illinois/Ill-Admin-Code-tit-92-SS-2520.257), [§ 2520.230](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/illinois/Ill-Admin-Code-tit-92-SS-2520.230) and [§ 2520.320](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/illinois/Ill-Admin-Code-tit-92-SS-2520.320)

> **2520.257:** No person shall loiter on Tollway property or in any manner interfere with traffic or the control of traffic.

> **2520.230:** Parking, standing or stopping on the right-of-way is prohibited. In emergencies, stopped vehicles shall be immediately driven or moved off the traveled portion of the traffic lane or ramp. [...]

> **2520.320:** a) Any person may use the Tollway only as a transportation facility in accordance with the rules adopted by the Authority pursuant to its powers under Section 10 of the Toll Highway Act and shall not use the Tollway or the right-of-way for any other purposes.
> b) Any person using any part of the Tollway or right-of-way except as provided in this Part is guilty of a trespass.
> c) Any person who fails to immediately depart from Authority property after being directed to leave by the State Police or the Authority is subject to arrest and/or immediate removal from Authority property.

**What it means:** Drivers may not stop on the Tollway right-of-way to pick you up. Hanging around Tollway property can be treated as loitering or trespass. If State Police tell you to leave, leave.

### 92 Ill. Adm. Code 2520.281: Penalty for Violation (Tollway)

**Source:** [Cornell LII, Ill. Admin. Code tit. 92, § 2520.281](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/illinois/Ill-Admin-Code-tit-92-SS-2520.281) (unofficial mirror)

> Except when a different penalty is expressly provided, any person who violates any provision of this Subpart B shall be deemed guilty of a petty offense and, upon conviction, shall be subject to punishment as provided by law for petty offenses.

**What it means:** Soliciting rides on the Tollway is a petty offense, which is fine-only.

jurisdictions.title: Indiana (US-IN)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not stand *in a roadway* to solicit a ride (Ind. Code § 9-21-17-16). A rule from the Indiana Department of Transportation (INDOT) bans pedestrians from every Interstate highway in the state.

sections.summary:
Indiana follows the standard Uniform Vehicle Code pattern: "A person may not stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride." The rule has an emergency exception. The "roadway" is the part of the highway "improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel," so the rule is aimed at people standing in the travel lanes. Unlike many states, the general Indiana definition does not say in so many words that the shoulder is excluded. That express exclusion appears only in a version of the definition used for one bicycle section. Still, a shoulder is not "ordinarily used for vehicular travel."

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stay out of the travel lanes.** Thumb from the shoulder, curb or sidewalk.
- **Never walk on an Interstate** (I-64, I-65, I-69, I-70, I-74, I-80, I-90, I-94, and the I-x64/x65/x69 spurs and loops). This is banned by INDOT rule 105 IAC 9-1-2, and it includes the Indiana Toll Road (I-80/I-90). Wait at the on-ramp entrance on the surface road, or at a truck stop.
- **Don't ask drivers on an Interstate ramp to stop for you.** Stopping or standing a vehicle is banned on Interstates "including ramp connections," except in rest areas (105 IAC 9-1-1).
- **Don't solicit money or work.** Standing on a highway to solicit employment or business is a separate offense (§ 9-21-17-17).

A violation of the pedestrian chapter is a Class C infraction, which is a civil fine and not a crime.
sections.laws:
### Ind. Code § 9-21-17-16: Solicitation of rides; restrictions; emergency

**Source:** [Indiana Code 2021, Title 9, as published by the Indiana Prosecuting Attorneys Council on in.gov (PDF)](https://www.in.gov/ipac/files/Title-9-2021.pdf) (2021 edition, IC 9-21-17-16; history note "As added by P.L.2-1991, SEC.9." with no later amendments). Cross-checked against [FindLaw's mirror of IC 9-21-17-16](https://codes.findlaw.com/in/title-9-motor-vehicles/in-code-sect-9-21-17-16/) (unofficial, "current as of January 01, 2026"), which shows the same operative language.

> Sec. 16. A person may not stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from a person who drives a vehicle unless the person soliciting a ride is faced with an emergency on the roadway, in which case the person may secure a ride to obtain assistance.

**What it means:** Don't stand in the lanes cars drive in while asking for a ride. Standing on the shoulder or sidewalk isn't covered by this section. If you're stranded by an emergency, such as a breakdown, you may flag down a ride to get help.

### Ind. Code § 9-13-2-157: "Roadway"

**Source:** [Indiana Code 2021, Title 9 (in.gov PDF)](https://www.in.gov/ipac/files/Title-9-2021.pdf) (history note "As added by P.L.2-1991, SEC.1. Amended by P.L.42-2011, SEC.22.")

> Sec. 157. (a) Except as provided in subsection (b), "roadway" means that part of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel.
>
> (b) As used in IC 9-21-12-13, "roadway" means the part of a highway that is improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel. The term does not include the sidewalk, berm, or shoulder, even if the sidewalk, berm, or shoulder is used by persons riding bicycles or other human powered vehicles.

**What it means:** Subsection (a) is the definition that applies to the hitchhiking rule. It covers the part of the road "ordinarily used for vehicular travel," which in plain terms means the travel lanes and not the shoulder. The explicit "not the shoulder" sentence in (b) applies only to a bicycle-related section, so Indiana's rule is a little less clear-cut than in states that exclude the shoulder everywhere. Stand well off the pavement to be safe.

### Ind. Code § 9-13-2-73: "Highway or street"

**Source:** [Indiana Code 2021, Title 9 (in.gov PDF)](https://www.in.gov/ipac/files/Title-9-2021.pdf) (amended by P.L.198-2016, SEC.116)

> Sec. 73. "Highway" or "street" means the entire width between the boundary lines of every publicly maintained way when any part of the way is open to the use of the public for purposes of vehicular travel in Indiana. The term includes an alley in a city or town.

**What it means:** A "highway" is the whole public right-of-way, shoulders included. Compare the hitchhiking rule, which uses "roadway," with the solicitation rule below, which uses "highway."

### Ind. Code § 9-21-17-17: Solicitation of employment or business on highway

**Source:** [Indiana Code 2021, Title 9 (in.gov PDF)](https://www.in.gov/ipac/files/Title-9-2021.pdf) ("As added by P.L.2-1991, SEC.9.")

> Sec. 17. A person may not stand on a highway for the purpose of soliciting employment or business from the occupant of a vehicle.

**What it means:** Asking passing drivers for work or business is banned anywhere in the right-of-way. A plain ride request is covered by § 16 instead, but don't add "will work for gas" to your sign.

### Ind. Code § 9-21-17-24: Violations; Class C infraction

**Source:** [Indiana Code 2021, Title 9 (in.gov PDF)](https://www.in.gov/ipac/files/Title-9-2021.pdf) ("As added by P.L.2-1991, SEC.9.")

> Sec. 24. A person who violates this chapter commits a Class C infraction.

**What it means:** Soliciting a ride from the roadway is an infraction, a civil violation that is not a crime. According to IC 34-28-5-4(c), as shown on [FindLaw's mirror](https://codes.findlaw.com/in/title-34-civil-law-and-procedure/in-code-sect-34-28-5-4/) ("current as of January 01, 2026"), a Class C infraction carries a judgment of up to $500.

### 105 Ind. Admin. Code 9-1-2: Pedestrians and certain vehicles prohibited on interstate highways

**Source:** [Cornell LII, 105 IAC 9-1-2](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/indiana/105-IAC-9-1-2) (unofficial mirror; INDOT rule, last readopted filed 10/4/2019, 20191030-IR-105190422RFA)

> Sec. 2. Pedestrians, motorized bicycles, bicycles, and other nonmotorized traffic shall be prohibited from enumerated highways: (1) I-64; (2) I-65; (3) I-69; (4) I-70; (5) I-74; (6) I-80; (7) I-90; (8) I-94; (9) I-164; (10) I-265; (11) I-275; (12) I-465; (13) I-469; and (14) I-865; otherwise known as the "Interstate Highway System".

**What it means:** Walking on any Indiana Interstate is banned, and that includes I-80/I-90, the Indiana Toll Road. The ban comes from an INDOT rule rather than a statute, but it covers every Interstate. Non-Interstate freeways and expressways aren't on this list.

### 105 Ind. Admin. Code 9-1-1: Stopping, standing, or parking prohibited on interstate highways

**Source:** [Cornell LII, 105 IAC 9-1-1](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/indiana/105-IAC-9-1-1) (unofficial mirror; last readopted filed 10/4/2019)

> Sec. 1. Stopping, standing, or parking shall be prohibited on enumerated highways: (1) I-64; (2) I-65; (3) I-69; (4) I-70; (5) I-74; (6) I-80; (7) I-90; (8) I-94; (9) I-164; (10) I-265; (11) I-275; (12) I-465; (13) I-469; and (14) I-865; otherwise known as the "Interstate Highway System", including ramp connections, except in designated rest areas.

**What it means:** Drivers may not stop on an Interstate or its ramps except in rest areas. A driver who pulls over on a ramp to pick you up is breaking this rule, so wait where they can stop legally, before the ramp starts.

jurisdictions.title: Michigan (US-MI)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Legal. The Michigan Vehicle Code has no statewide ban on soliciting rides. However, the state's model Uniform Traffic Code, which most cities, townships and villages adopt as a local ordinance, bans standing *in the roadway* to solicit a ride. Pedestrians are banned from limited-access highways.

sections.summary:
No section of the Michigan Vehicle Code (Act 300 of 1949) prohibits hitchhiking as such. The ride-soliciting rule lives in the **Uniform Traffic Code for Cities, Townships, and Villages** (Mich. Admin. Code R. 28.1001 et seq.), a model code written by the State Police. It applies only where a city, township or village has adopted it by reference under MCL 257.951. Rule 713 of that code says a person "shall not stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride." "Roadway" takes its Vehicle Code meaning: the part of the highway "used for vehicular travel," which does not include the shoulder.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Never walk onto a freeway** (limited-access highway). MCL 257.679a bans pedestrians there.
- **In most towns, stay out of the travel lanes** when you thumb. Standing on the shoulder or sidewalk is not covered by Rule 713.
- **Don't block or impede traffic** with your body (MCL 257.676b).
- **Walk on the sidewalk where there is one.** Otherwise walk on the left, facing traffic (MCL 257.655).

All of these are civil infractions, not crimes. The fine for a Vehicle Code civil infraction is generally up to $100 plus costs (MCL 257.907).
sections.laws:
### Mich. Comp. Laws § 257.679a: Limited access highway; pedestrians and certain vehicles prohibited

**Source:** [Michigan Legislature, MCL 257.679a](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-257-679A.pdf) (Michigan Compiled Laws complete through PA 114 of 2026; last amended 1978 PA 510)

> (1) A person shall not operate a motorcycle with less than a 125 cubic centimeter engine, moped, farm tractor, or other self-propelled farm implement, nor shall a pedestrian, bicycle, except as provided in this section, or other nonmotorized traffic be permitted on a limited access highway in this state. Bicycles shall be permitted on paths constructed separately from the roadway and designated for the exclusive use of bicycles.
>
> (2) A person who violates this section is responsible for a civil infraction.

**What it means:** You may not walk on an interstate or other freeway in Michigan, shoulders included. Hitchhike from the surface road before the on-ramp, or from a gas station or truck stop near the interchange.

### Mich. Comp. Laws § 257.26: "Limited access highway" defined

**Source:** [Michigan Legislature, MCL 257.26](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-257-26.pdf) (unchanged since 1949)

> "Limited access highway" means every highway, street, or roadway in respect to which owners or occupants of abutting lands and other persons have no legal right of access to or from the same except at such points only, and in such manner as may be determined by the public authority having jurisdiction over such highway, street or roadway.

**What it means:** This covers freeways and expressways where you can only get on and off at interchanges.

### Mich. Admin. Code R. 28.1713: Pedestrians; soliciting ride, employment, or business in roadway prohibited (Uniform Traffic Code, Rule 713)

**Source:** [Cornell LII, Mich. Admin. Code R. 28.1713](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-28-1713) (unofficial mirror; history note "1979 AC; 1981 AACS; 2002 AACS")

> (1) A person shall not stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment, or business from the occupant of any vehicle.
>
> (2) A person who violates this rule is responsible for a civil infraction.

**What it means:** Where a city, township or village has adopted the Uniform Traffic Code, don't stand in the travel lanes asking for a ride. The shoulder, curb and sidewalk are not the "roadway" (see MCL 257.55 below), so thumbing from them is not covered by this rule.

### Mich. Admin. Code R. 28.1001: Definitions (Uniform Traffic Code)

**Source:** [Cornell LII, Mich. Admin. Code R. 28.1001](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-28-1001) (unofficial mirror; history note "1979 AC; 1981 AACS; 2002 AACS")

> (2) If any word or phrase used in this code is not defined in this code, but is defined in the Act, PA 300, MCL 257.1 to 257.923, then the definition in the act shall apply to the words and phrases used in this code.

**What it means:** The Uniform Traffic Code borrows the Vehicle Code's definition of "roadway."

### Mich. Comp. Laws § 257.55: "Roadway" defined

**Source:** [Michigan Legislature, MCL 257.55](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-257-55.pdf) (unchanged since 1949)

> "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel. In the event a highway includes 2 or more separate roadways, the term "roadway", as used herein, shall refer to any such roadway separately, but not to all such roadways collectively.

**What it means:** The roadway is the part cars drive on. The definition doesn't name the shoulder, but a shoulder isn't "ordinarily used for vehicular travel," so standing on it is generally treated as outside the roadway.

### Mich. Comp. Laws § 257.951: Uniform traffic code; adoption by reference

**Source:** [Michigan Legislature, MCL 257.951](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-257-951.pdf) (Michigan Compiled Laws complete through PA 114 of 2026)

> (1) A city, township, or village may adopt by reference a code or ordinance for the regulation of traffic within cities, townships, and villages that has been promulgated by the director of the department of state police. [...]

**What it means:** Rule 713 is not automatically statewide. It applies inside a city, township or village that has adopted the Uniform Traffic Code, and most have. Assume it applies in town.

### Mich. Comp. Laws § 257.676b: Interference with normal flow of traffic prohibited

**Source:** [Michigan Legislature, MCL 257.676b](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-257-676B.pdf) (last amended 2021 PA 43)

> (1) Subject to subsection (2), a person, without authority, shall not block, obstruct, impede, or otherwise interfere with the normal flow of vehicular, streetcar, or pedestrian traffic upon a public street or highway in this state, by means of a barricade, object, or device, or with his or her person. [...]
>
> (2) Subsection (1) and any provision of the Michigan Administrative Code that prohibits a person from standing in a roadway other than a limited access highway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment, or business from the occupant of any vehicle do not apply to a person who is soliciting contributions on behalf of a charitable or civic organization during daylight hours, if all of the following are satisfied: [...]
>
> (4) A person who violates this section is responsible for a civil infraction.

**What it means:** Don't step out to slow or stop cars. Subsection (2) confirms that the Legislature knows about the Administrative Code ban on standing in a roadway to solicit a ride, and it carves out only charity collectors.

### Mich. Comp. Laws § 257.655: Pedestrians on highways

**Source:** [Michigan Legislature, MCL 257.655](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-257-655.pdf) (last amended 1978 PA 510)

> (1) Where sidewalks are provided, a pedestrian shall not walk upon the main traveled portion of the highway. Where sidewalks are not provided, pedestrians shall, when practicable, walk on the left side of the highway facing traffic which passes nearest.
>
> (2) A person who violates this section is responsible for a civil infraction.

**What it means:** Use the sidewalk. With no sidewalk, walk on the left side facing oncoming traffic.

### Mich. Comp. Laws § 257.907: Civil infraction fines

**Source:** [Michigan Legislature, MCL 257.907](https://legislature.mi.gov/documents/mcl/pdf/MCL-257-907.pdf) (Michigan Compiled Laws complete through PA 114 of 2026)

> (a) Except as otherwise provided, for a civil infraction under this act or a local ordinance that substantially corresponds to a provision of this act, the person must be ordered to pay a civil fine of not more than $100.00.

**What it means:** Walking on a freeway or blocking traffic gets you a ticket of up to $100 plus court costs, not a criminal record.
sections.unverified-open-questions:
- Rule 713 was quoted from Cornell LII, an unofficial mirror. The official Michigan Administrative Code text (Office of Administrative Hearings and Rules) was not retrieved in this session.
- Which municipalities have adopted the Uniform Traffic Code, and whether any have changed Rule 713 locally, was not checked. Detroit, for example, has its own traffic ordinance.
- Whether MCL 257.679a's ban covers on- and off-ramps isn't stated in the text. Ramps are normally part of the limited-access facility, so treat them as off-limits.

jurisdictions.title: Minnesota (US-MN)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not stand *in a roadway* to solicit a ride from the driver of a private vehicle (Minn. Stat. § 169.22). Minnesota defines the roadway as "exclusive of the sidewalk or shoulder." Pedestrians may be banned from controlled-access highways by order of the transportation commissioner or by local ordinance, and the ban is enforced through posted signs.

sections.summary:
Minnesota's statute is literally titled "Hitchhiking; solicitation of business." It bans standing *in the roadway* to ask a private driver for a ride. Because "roadway" excludes the sidewalk and shoulder, hitchhiking from the shoulder or sidewalk is not covered. The one exception: where the state runs "dynamic shoulder lanes" (shoulders opened to traffic at peak times), the shoulder counts as roadway while it is open to traffic.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stand on the shoulder or sidewalk, not in a lane.** Avoid shoulders that are signed as part-time travel lanes, mostly on Twin Cities freeways.
- **Obey "no pedestrians" signs** on freeways and other controlled-access highways (§ 169.305). Wait at the ramp entrance on the surface street.
- **Don't solicit money, work or business** from the roadway (§ 169.22, subd. 2).

A violation is normally a petty misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of up to $300 with no jail. It can become a misdemeanor if you endanger people or property, or after two or more petty misdemeanor convictions in the past 12 months.
sections.laws:
### Minn. Stat. § 169.22: Hitchhiking; solicitation of business

**Source:** [Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes, Minn. Stat. § 169.22](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/169.22) (2026 Minnesota Statutes; history: 1937 c 464 s 56; 1974 c 379 s 3)

> Subdivision 1. Soliciting ride.
> No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any private vehicle.
>
> Subd. 2. Soliciting employment, business, or contributions.
> No person shall stand on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting employment, business, or contributions from the occupant of any vehicle.

**What it means:** Don't stand in the travel lanes asking for a ride. Thumbing from the shoulder or sidewalk is not covered by this section. Subdivision 2 also uses "roadway," so asking for money or work is likewise limited only in the lanes, though it's still smart to keep money requests off your sign.

### Minn. Stat. § 169.011: Definitions

**Source:** [Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes, Minn. Stat. § 169.011](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/169.011) (2026 Minnesota Statutes)

> Subd. 68. Roadway.
> "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the sidewalk or shoulder. During periods when the commissioner allows the use of dynamic shoulder lanes as defined in subdivision 25, roadway includes that shoulder. In the event a highway includes two or more separate roadways, the term "roadway" as used herein shall refer to any such roadway separately but not to all such roadways collectively.
>
> Subd. 74. Shoulder.
> "Shoulder" means that part of a highway which is contiguous to the regularly traveled portion of the highway and is on the same level as the highway. The shoulder may be pavement, gravel, or earth.
>
> Subd. 19. Controlled-access highway.
> "Controlled-access highway" means, in this chapter, every highway, street, or roadway in respect to which the right of access of the owners or occupants of abutting lands and other persons has been acquired and to which the owners or occupants of abutting lands and other persons have no legal right of access to or from the same except at such points only and in such manner as may be determined by the public authority having jurisdiction over such highway, street or roadway.

**What it means:** The shoulder is not part of the roadway, so standing there to hitchhike doesn't violate § 169.22. The exception is a shoulder that is open as a "dynamic shoulder lane." While it carries traffic, it is roadway.

### Minn. Stat. § 169.305: Controlled-access rules and penalties

**Source:** [Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes, Minn. Stat. § 169.305](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/169.305) (2026 Minnesota Statutes; last amended 2022 c 55 art 1 s 63)

> (c) The commissioner of transportation may by order, and any public authority may by ordinance, with respect to any controlled-access highway under their jurisdictions prohibit or regulate the use of any such highway by pedestrians, bicycles, or other nonmotorized traffic, or by motorized bicycles, or by any class or kind of traffic which is found to be incompatible with the normal and safe flow of traffic.
>
> (d) The commissioner of transportation or the public authority adopting any such prohibitory rules shall erect and maintain official signs on the controlled-access highway on which such rules are applicable and when so erected no person shall disobey the restrictions stated on such signs.
>
> [...]
>
> Subd. 3. Petty misdemeanor.
> Any person who violates the provisions of this section or any order or ordinance promulgated or enacted by the commissioner of transportation or a public authority pursuant thereto is guilty of a petty misdemeanor.

**What it means:** No statute bans pedestrians from every freeway automatically. The ban applies where the state or a local authority has prohibited pedestrians and posted signs. Interstate ramps are normally signed, so don't walk past the "no pedestrians" sign. Breaking a posted ban is a petty misdemeanor.

### Minn. Stat. § 169.89: Penalties

**Source:** [Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes, Minn. Stat. § 169.89](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/169.89) (2026 Minnesota Statutes)

> Subdivision 1. Violation; when petty misdemeanor enhanced to misdemeanor.
> Unless otherwise declared in this chapter with respect to particular offenses, it is a petty misdemeanor for any person to do any act forbidden or fail to perform any act required by this chapter; except that:
> (1) a violation which is committed in a manner or under circumstances so as to endanger or be likely to endanger any person or property; or
> (2) exclusive of violations relating to the standing or parking of an unattended vehicle, a violation of any of the provisions of this chapter, classified therein as a petty misdemeanor, when preceded by two or more petty misdemeanor convictions within the immediate preceding 12-month period;
> is a misdemeanor to which the provisions of subdivision 2 shall not apply.
>
> Subd. 2. Petty misdemeanor penalty; no jury trial.
> A person charged with a petty misdemeanor is not entitled to a jury trial but shall be tried by a judge without a jury. If convicted, the person is not subject to imprisonment but shall be punished by a fine of not more than $300.

**What it means:** Hitchhiking from the roadway is a petty misdemeanor with a fine of up to $300 and no jail. If you do it in a way that endangers people, such as stepping into fast traffic, or if you have two or more recent petty misdemeanor convictions, it becomes a misdemeanor.

- Local ordinances (for example Minneapolis or St. Paul) were not checked.

jurisdictions.title: Ohio (US-OH)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not solicit a ride while on the roadway (the travel and parking lanes), but Ohio's definition of "roadway" excludes the berm and shoulder. Pedestrians are banned from freeways, and hitchhiking is banned outright on the Ohio Turnpike.

sections.summary:
Ohio Revised Code § 4511.51(A) says no person "while on a roadway outside a safety zone shall solicit a ride from the driver of any vehicle." Section 4511.01(EE) defines "roadway" as the part of a highway used for vehicle travel and parking lanes, "not including the berm, sidewalk, or shoulder." So thumbing from the sidewalk, curb or shoulder of an ordinary road is not covered by § 4511.51(A).

What still applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stay out of the travel lanes** when you ask for a ride.
- **Don't go onto a freeway at all.** Section 4511.051 bars pedestrians from anywhere within the right-of-way of a freeway, which includes the shoulders, except in a rest area, on a marked pedestrian path, or in an emergency such as a breakdown.
- **The Ohio Turnpike is stricter.** Turnpike Commission rules ban hitchhiking, ban drivers from stopping to pick up or drop off hitchhikers, ban loitering at toll plazas and service plazas, and bar pedestrians from the turnpike.
- **Panhandling-style solicitation is separate.** Section 4511.51(B) bars standing on a highway to solicit "employment, business, or contributions" from vehicle occupants. That division is not about rides.

A first violation of § 4511.51(A) or § 4511.051 is a minor misdemeanor (fine of up to $150). Prior traffic convictions within a year raise it to a fourth- or third-degree misdemeanor.
sections.laws:
### Ohio Rev. Code § 4511.51: Hitchhiking - soliciting employment, business, or contributions from occupant of vehicle

**Source:** [Ohio Laws (Legislative Service Commission), R.C. 4511.51](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-4511.51) (effective January 1, 2004; latest legislation S.B. 123, 124th General Assembly)

> (A) No person while on a roadway outside a safety zone shall solicit a ride from the driver of any vehicle.

**What it means:** Don't stand in the travel lanes (or parking lanes) asking for a ride. Because "roadway" excludes the shoulder and sidewalk (see § 4511.01 below), standing on the shoulder or sidewalk with your thumb out is not covered by this division. A "safety zone" is an officially marked pedestrian island within the roadway.

> (B)(1) Except as provided in division (B)(2) of this section, no person shall stand on a highway for the purpose of soliciting employment, business, or contributions from the occupant of any vehicle.

**What it means:** This bans standing anywhere on a "highway" (which includes the whole right-of-way) to ask drivers for money, work or business. It doesn't mention rides, so it is not a hitchhiking rule. Don't combine a ride request with asking for gas money or donations on a sign.

> (C) No person shall hang onto or ride on the outside of any motor vehicle, streetcar, or trackless trolley while it is moving upon a roadway, [...]
>
> (D) No operator shall knowingly permit any person to hang onto, or ride on the outside of, any motor vehicle, streetcar, or trackless trolley while it is moving upon a roadway, [...]

**What it means:** Ride inside the vehicle. Riding on the outside is illegal for you and for the driver.

> (G)(1) Except as otherwise provided in this division, whoever violates any provision of divisions (A) to (D) of this section is guilty of a minor misdemeanor. If, within one year of the offense, the offender previously has been convicted of or pleaded guilty to one predicate motor vehicle or traffic offense, whoever violates any provision of divisions (A) to (D) of this section is guilty of a misdemeanor of the fourth degree. If, within one year of the offense, the offender previously has been convicted of two or more predicate motor vehicle or traffic offenses, whoever violates any provision of divisions (A) to (D) of this section is guilty of a misdemeanor of the third degree.

**What it means:** A first offense is a minor misdemeanor, the lowest level of offense in Ohio, which carries no jail. Repeat traffic offenses within a year make it a more serious misdemeanor.

### Ohio Rev. Code § 4511.01: Definitions

**Source:** [Ohio Laws (Legislative Service Commission), R.C. 4511.01](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-4511.01) (effective September 30, 2025; latest legislation H.B. 96, 136th General Assembly)

> (BB) "Street" or "highway" means a general term for denoting a public way for purposes of travel by vehicles, streetcars, trackless trolleys, and vulnerable road users, including the entire area within the right-of-way.
>
> [...]
>
> (EE) "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel and parking lanes, not including the berm, sidewalk, or shoulder, even if the berm, sidewalk, or shoulder is used by a person operating a bicycle or other human-powered vehicle. If a highway includes two or more separate roadways the term "roadway" means any such roadway separately but not all such roadways collectively.
>
> [...]
>
> (MM) "Safety zone" means the area or space officially set apart within a roadway for the exclusive use of pedestrians and protected or marked or indicated by adequate signs as to be plainly visible at all times.
>
> [...]
>
> (YY) "Freeway" means a divided multi-lane highway for through traffic with all crossroads separated in grade and with full control of access.

**What it means:** The "roadway" is only the lanes cars drive and park in. The shoulder, berm and sidewalk are not part of it, so the hitchhiking ban in § 4511.51(A) does not reach them. A "highway" is the whole right-of-way, which matters for the freeway ban below.

### Ohio Rev. Code § 4511.051: Freeways - prohibited acts

**Source:** [Ohio Laws (Legislative Service Commission), R.C. 4511.051](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-4511.051) (effective October 29, 2018; latest legislation H.B. 250 and H.B. 95, 132nd General Assembly)

> (A) No person, unless otherwise directed by a police officer, shall:
> (1) As a pedestrian, occupy any space within the limits of the right-of-way of a freeway, except: in a rest area; on a facility that is separated from the roadway and shoulders of the freeway and is designed and appropriately marked for pedestrian use; in the performance of public works or official duties; as a result of an emergency caused by an accident or breakdown of a motor vehicle; or to obtain assistance;
>
> [...]
>
> (B) Except as otherwise provided in this division, whoever violates this section is guilty of a minor misdemeanor. If, within one year of the offense, the offender previously has been convicted of or pleaded guilty to one predicate motor vehicle or traffic offense, whoever violates this section is guilty of a misdemeanor of the fourth degree. If, within one year of the offense, the offender previously has been convicted of two or more predicate motor vehicle or traffic offenses, whoever violates this section is guilty of a misdemeanor of the third degree. [...]

**What it means:** As a pedestrian you may not be anywhere inside a freeway's right-of-way. That covers the shoulders, and ramps are generally inside the freeway right-of-way too (the statute doesn't name ramps, so where the right-of-way begins is a local fact). Rest areas are an exception. Hitchhike from the surface street before the on-ramp, or from a gas station or truck stop near the interchange.

### Ohio Admin. Code 5537-3-02: Hitchhiking and loitering prohibited (Ohio Turnpike)

**Source:** [Ohio Laws, Ohio Administrative Code rule 5537-3-02](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-5537-3-02) (effective March 3, 2001; Ohio Turnpike and Infrastructure Commission)

> The solicitation of a ride, commonly known as "hitchhiking," or stopping for the purpose of picking up or discharging a hitchhiker, is hereby prohibited on the turnpike. Loitering in or about the toll plazas, service plazas or any other portion of the turnpike is prohibited.

**What it means:** On the Ohio Turnpike (I-80/I-90 across northern Ohio), hitchhiking is banned everywhere, including service plazas and toll plazas. Drivers are also forbidden to stop to pick you up or drop you off. Asking for rides at turnpike service plazas can get you cited.

### Ohio Admin. Code 5537-3-01: Prohibited users (Ohio Turnpike)

**Source:** [Ohio Laws, Ohio Administrative Code rule 5537-3-01](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-administrative-code/rule-5537-3-01) (effective September 1, 2023)

> The following shall not be permitted to travel on the turnpike: (A) Pedestrians. (B) Bicycles. [...]

**What it means:** You may not walk on the turnpike.

### Ohio Rev. Code §§ 5537.16(C) and 5537.99: Penalty for violating turnpike rules

**Source:** [R.C. 5537.16](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-5537.16) (effective March 23, 2022) and [R.C. 5537.99](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-5537.99) (effective July 1, 2009), Ohio Laws

> (C) No person shall violate any such bylaws or rules of the commission.

> (A) Except as provided in division (B) of this section, whoever violates division (C) of section 5537.16 of the Revised Code is guilty of a minor misdemeanor on a first offense; on each subsequent offense such person is guilty of a misdemeanor of the fourth degree.

**What it means:** Breaking the turnpike hitchhiking rule is a minor misdemeanor the first time, and a fourth-degree misdemeanor after that. This applies to drivers who stop for you, too.

### Ohio Rev. Code § 2929.28: Financial sanctions for misdemeanors

**Source:** [Ohio Laws, R.C. 2929.28](https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-2929.28) (effective October 3, 2023)

> (iv) For a misdemeanor of the fourth degree, not more than two hundred fifty dollars;
> (v) For a minor misdemeanor, not more than one hundred fifty dollars.

**What it means:** The maximum fine for a minor misdemeanor is $150, and $250 for a fourth-degree misdemeanor, plus court costs.

jurisdictions.title: Wisconsin (US-WI)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not be *on a roadway* to solicit a ride (Wis. Stat. § 346.29(1)). Wisconsin's definition of "roadway" excludes the berm and shoulder. Pedestrians are barred from expressways and freeways where official signs prohibit them.

sections.summary:
Wisconsin bans soliciting a ride while you are on the roadway, meaning the travel lanes. The statute defines "roadway" as the area "between the regularly established curb lines" or the part "ordinarily used for vehicular travel, excluding the berm or shoulder." So thumbing from the shoulder or from behind the curb is not covered by § 346.29(1). The ban has a built-in exception for "public passenger vehicles," such as buses and taxis.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stay off the travel lanes and behind the curb** when you ask for a ride.
- **Don't stand or loiter in the roadway** in a way that interferes with traffic (§ 346.29(2)).
- **Stay off expressways and freeways** where "no pedestrians" signs are posted (§ 346.16(2)(a)). Interstate on-ramps are typically signed, so wait at the start of the ramp.
- **Walk on the left side, facing traffic,** when there's no sidewalk (§ 346.28).

The penalties are small civil forfeitures. A first violation of § 346.29 costs $2 to $20. Walking on a signed freeway costs $30 to $300.
sections.laws:
### Wis. Stat. § 346.29: When standing or loitering in roadway or highway prohibited

**Source:** [LawServer, Wisconsin Statutes 346.29](https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/wisconsin/wi-laws/wisconsin_laws_346-29) (unofficial mirror, "Current as of: 2024"). Subsection (1) is cross-checked against [Wisconsin Civil Jury Instruction 1250 (Wisconsin Court System, 2022, Release No. 53)](https://wilawlibrary.gov/jury/files/civil/1250.pdf), which quotes the same words and cites "Wis. Stat. § 346.29(1)." The official site, docs.legis.wisconsin.gov, could not be reached from this environment.

> (1) No person shall be on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the operator of any vehicle other than a public passenger vehicle.
>
> (2) No person shall stand or loiter on any roadway other than in a safety zone if such act interferes with the lawful movement of traffic.

**What it means:** You can't stand in the travel lanes to ask a private driver for a ride. The shoulder and the area behind the curb are not "roadway" (see § 340.01(54) below), so thumbing from there is not covered by this section. Hailing a bus or taxi from the roadway is expressly allowed.

### Wis. Stat. § 340.01(54): "Roadway" defined

**Source:** [LawServer, Wisconsin Statutes 340.01](https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/wisconsin/wi-laws/wisconsin_laws_340-01) (unofficial mirror, "Current as of: 2024")

> (54) "Roadway" means that portion of a highway between the regularly established curb lines or that portion which is improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, excluding the berm or shoulder. In a divided highway the term "roadway" refers to each roadway separately but not to all such roadways collectively.

**What it means:** The shoulder and berm are expressly excluded. In town, everything between the curbs counts as roadway, so stand on the sidewalk side of the curb.

### Wis. Stat. § 340.01(22): "Highway" defined

**Source:** [LawServer, Wisconsin Statutes 340.01](https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/wisconsin/wi-laws/wisconsin_laws_340-01) (unofficial mirror, "Current as of: 2024")

> (22) "Highway" means all public ways and thoroughfares and bridges on the same. It includes the entire width between the boundary lines of every way open to the use of the public as a matter of right for the purposes of vehicular travel. [...]

**What it means:** "Highway" is the whole right-of-way. The freeway rule below uses "go upon any expressway or freeway," which reaches beyond just the lanes.

### Wis. Stat. § 346.16: Use of controlled-access highways, expressways and freeways

**Source:** [LawServer, Wisconsin Statutes 346.16](https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/wisconsin/wi-laws/wisconsin_laws_346-16) (unofficial mirror, "Current as of: 2024")

> (2) (a) Except as provided in par. (b), no pedestrian or person riding a bicycle or other nonmotorized vehicle and no person operating a moped or motor bicycle may go upon any expressway or freeway when official signs have been erected prohibiting such person from using the expressway or freeway.
>
> [...]
>
> (b) A pedestrian or other person under par. (a) or (am) may go upon a portion of a hiking trail, cross-country ski trail, bridle trail or bicycle trail incorporated into the highway right-of-way and crossing the highway if the portion of the trail is constructed under s. 84.06 (11).

**What it means:** The pedestrian ban applies only where official signs prohibit pedestrians. Those signs are standard at interstate and freeway on-ramps, so in practice don't walk past them. Hitchhike from the surface street before the sign.

### Wis. Stat. § 346.28: Pedestrians on highways

**Source:** [LawServer, Wisconsin Statutes 346.28](https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/wisconsin/wi-laws/wisconsin_laws_346-28) (unofficial mirror, "Current as of: 2024")

> (1) Any pedestrian traveling along and upon a highway other than upon a sidewalk shall travel on and along the left side of the highway and upon meeting a vehicle shall, if practicable, move to the extreme outer limit of the traveled portion of the highway.

**What it means:** When there's no sidewalk, walk on the left facing traffic, and step to the edge when cars come.

### Wis. Stat. § 346.30: Penalty for violating sections 346.23 to 346.29

**Source:** [LawServer, Wisconsin Statutes 346.30](https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/wisconsin/wi-laws/wisconsin_laws_346-30) (unofficial mirror, "Current as of: 2024")

> (1) (a) Any pedestrian violating s. 346.23, 346.24 (2), 346.25, 346.28 or 346.29 and any personal delivery device operator violating s. 346.23 or 346.24 (2) may be required to forfeit not less than $2 nor more than $20 for the first offense and not less than $10 nor more than $50 for the 2nd or subsequent conviction within a year.

**What it means:** Soliciting a ride from the roadway is a civil forfeiture of $2 to $20 the first time, and $10 to $50 for a repeat within a year. It is not a crime.

### Wis. Stat. § 346.17: Penalty for violating sections 346.04 to 346.16

**Source:** [LawServer, Wisconsin Statutes 346.17](https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/wisconsin/wi-laws/wisconsin_laws_346-17) (unofficial mirror, "Current as of: 2024")

> (2) Except as provided in sub. (6), any person violating ss. 346.05, 346.07 (2) or (3), 346.072, 346.08, 346.09, 346.10 (2) to (4), 346.11, 346.13 (2) or 346.14 to 346.16 may be required to forfeit not less than $30 nor more than $300.

**What it means:** Walking onto a signed freeway carries a much bigger forfeiture, $30 to $300, than hitchhiking from the roadway.
