jurisdictions.title: Colorado (US-CO)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not stand in the roadway (the part used by moving traffic) to solicit a ride. On interstates you may solicit a ride only at an entrance or exit, or at places the Colorado Department of Transportation (CDOT) designates. The statute itself refers to "an individual lawfully soliciting a ride", and it tells drivers to pick up pedestrians only where there is room to pull off safely.

sections.summary:
Colorado's C.R.S. § 42-4-805 accommodates hitchhikers more than most states' laws do:

- **(1)(a)** lets "an individual lawfully soliciting a ride" stand on either side of a two-way road where there's a view of traffic from both directions. The usual left-side rule doesn't apply to them.
- **(2)** bans standing *in the roadway* to solicit a ride from a private vehicle. For this subsection, roadway means "that portion of the road normally used by moving motor vehicle traffic", so the shoulder is outside it.
- **(6)** bans soliciting a ride *on an interstate*, **except at an entrance to or exit from** the interstate or at CDOT-designated places. A driver or passenger of a disabled vehicle may solicit a ride anywhere.
- **(7)** says pedestrians shall be picked up only where vehicles have room to pull off without endangering or impeding traffic.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stand on the shoulder, not in the lane.** Pick a spot where a car can pull fully off the road.
- **Interstates:** hitch at the on-ramp (an "entrance"), not along the interstate itself.
- **Penalty:** a class B traffic infraction. This is a civil matter, not a crime. The scheduled penalty for § 42-4-805 is $15 plus a $6 surcharge.
sections.laws:
### C.R.S. § 42-4-805: Pedestrians walking or traveling in a wheelchair on highways

**Source:** [Colorado Office of Legislative Legal Services, 2026 C.R.S. Title 42](https://olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-42.htm) (current through the 2026 Regular Session; subsection (1) last amended by SB 25-149, effective August 6, 2025)

> (1) Pedestrians walking or traveling in a wheelchair along and upon highways where sidewalks are not provided shall walk or travel only on a road shoulder as far as practicable from the edge of the roadway. Where neither a sidewalk nor road shoulder is available, any pedestrian walking or traveling in a wheelchair along and upon a highway shall walk or travel as near as practicable to an outside edge of the roadway and, in the case of a two-way roadway, shall walk or travel only on the left side of the roadway facing traffic that may approach from the opposite direction; except that:
> (a) An individual lawfully soliciting a ride may stand on either side of a two-way roadway where there is a view of traffic approaching from both directions; [...]

**What it means:** Walk on the shoulder. When you stop to hitch, you may stand on whichever side of the road your traffic is on, as long as drivers coming both ways can see you.

> (2) No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any private vehicle. For the purposes of this subsection (2), "roadway" means that portion of the road normally used by moving motor vehicle traffic.

**What it means:** Stay out of the travel lanes. The section defines its own "roadway" as the part used by moving traffic, so the shoulder doesn't count.

> (6) No person shall solicit a ride on any highway included in the interstate system, as defined in section 43-2-101 (2), C.R.S., except at an entrance to or exit from such highway or at places specifically designated by the department of transportation; or, in an emergency affecting a vehicle or its operation, a driver or passenger of a disabled vehicle may solicit a ride on any highway.
>
> (7) Pedestrians shall only be picked up where there is adequate road space for vehicles to pull off and not endanger and impede the flow of traffic.

**What it means:** On interstates, hitch from the on-ramp or off-ramp, not from the interstate shoulder. Subsection (7) is aimed at drivers. A driver who stops in a lane to pick you up is breaking it, so choose spots with room to pull over.

> (5) Any city or town may, by ordinance, regulate the use by pedestrians of streets and highways under its jurisdiction to the extent authorized under subsection (6) of this section and sections 42-4-110 and 42-4-111, but no ordinance regulating such use of streets and highways in a manner differing from this section shall be effective until official signs or devices giving notice thereof have been placed as required by section 42-4-111 (2).
>
> (9) Any person who violates any provision of this section commits a class B traffic infraction.

**What it means:** Cities and towns can add pedestrian rules, but a rule that differs from the state law takes effect only once it is signed.

### C.R.S. § 42-1-102(85): "Roadway" defined

**Source:** [Colorado Office of Legislative Legal Services, 2026 C.R.S. Title 42](https://olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-42.htm)

> (85) "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the sidewalk, berm, or shoulder even though such sidewalk, berm, or shoulder is used by persons riding bicycles or other human-powered vehicles [...].

**What it means:** The general definition agrees with § 42-4-805(2): the shoulder isn't roadway.

### C.R.S. § 42-4-1010(3): Restrictions on controlled-access highways

**Source:** [Colorado Office of Legislative Legal Services, 2026 C.R.S. Title 42](https://olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-42.htm)

> (3) The department of transportation may by resolution or order entered in its minutes and local authorities may by ordinance consistent with the provisions of section 43-2-135 (1)(g), C.R.S., with respect to any controlled-access highway under their respective jurisdictions, prohibit the use of any such highway by any class or kind of traffic which is found to be incompatible with the normal and safe movement of traffic. The department of transportation or the local authority adopting such prohibitory regulations shall install official traffic control devices [...] at entrance points or along the highway on which such regulations are applicable. When such devices are so in place, giving notice thereof, no person shall disobey the restrictions made known by such devices. This subsection (3) shall not be construed to give the department authority to regulate pedestrian use of highways in a manner contrary to the provisions of section 42-4-805.

**What it means:** CDOT can post signs closing a controlled-access highway to a class of traffic, and you must obey them. The statute adds that CDOT may not regulate pedestrians in a way that contradicts § 42-4-805, which expressly allows soliciting rides at interstate entrances and exits.

### C.R.S. § 42-4-1701: Penalty

**Source:** [Colorado Office of Legislative Legal Services, 2026 C.R.S. Title 42](https://olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-42.htm)

> (1) It is a traffic infraction for any person to violate any of the provisions of articles 1 to 3 of this title 42 and parts 1 to 3 and 5 to 19 of this article 4 unless such violation is [...] declared to be a felony, misdemeanor, petty offense, civil infraction, or misdemeanor traffic offense. Such a traffic infraction constitutes a civil matter.

The penalty and surcharge schedule in § 42-4-1701(4)(a)(I), under "Pedestrian violations", lists:

> 42-4-805 | $15.00 | $6.00

**What it means:** A ticket under § 42-4-805 is a civil traffic infraction with a $15 penalty and a $6 surcharge. No points are assessed for class B infractions (§ 42-4-1701(3)(c)).
sections.history:
### 2025 SB 25-149: subsection (1) restructured

**Source:** [2024 C.R.S. Title 42](https://olls.info/crs/crs2024-title-42.htm) compared with [2026 C.R.S. Title 42](https://olls.info/crs/crs2026-title-42.htm) (official OLLS publications)

The 2024 text of § 42-4-805(1) ended: "except that any person lawfully soliciting a ride may stand on either side of such two-way roadway where there is a view of traffic approaching from both directions." SB 25-149 (effective August 6, 2025) moved this into a lettered paragraph (1)(a), "An individual lawfully soliciting a ride may stand on either side of a two-way roadway [...]", and added (1)(b) for horse riders. The hitchhiking rules in subsections (2), (6) and (7) did not change.

jurisdictions.title: Idaho (US-ID)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Illegal. Idaho Code § 49-709 says "No person shall stand on a highway for the purpose of soliciting a ride". Idaho's definition of "highway" expressly includes sidewalks, shoulders, berms and rights-of-way. Violation is an infraction.

sections.summary:
Idaho's hitchhiking rule uses the word *highway*, not *roadway*. Idaho's definition of highway goes further than most states. It spells out that the highway extends to the adjacent property line, "including sidewalks, shoulders, berms and rights-of-way". Standing on the shoulder, or even the sidewalk, to solicit a ride is therefore covered.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Don't stand anywhere on the highway right-of-way to solicit a ride**, shoulder and sidewalk included. Practical options are private property such as gas stations, truck stops and parking lots, with the owner's permission, or asking drivers directly.
- **Walking** along a highway is allowed. Use the sidewalk if there is one, otherwise the shoulder. With neither, walk on the left side of a two-way road.
- **Interstates and other controlled-access highways:** the Idaho Transportation Department must regulate or prohibit traffic that is incompatible with normal, safe traffic flow, and must sign any prohibitions. Obey "pedestrians prohibited" signs.
- **Penalty:** an infraction. The maximum is $300, with no jail.
sections.laws:
### Idaho Code § 49-709: Pedestrians soliciting rides or business

**Source:** [Idaho Legislature, Idaho Code § 49-709](https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/Title49/T49CH7/SECT49-709/) (history: added 1988, ch. 265, sec. 200; am. 2001, ch. 392, sec. 1)

> (1) No person shall stand on a highway for the purpose of soliciting a ride.
>
> (2) No person shall stand on a highway for the purpose of soliciting employment, business or contributions from the occupant of any vehicle, provided however, that a person may stand on a highway other than a state or federal highway to solicit contributions if authorized to do so in writing by the local authority having jurisdiction over the highway, and provided further, that any such authorization shall not be valid for more than one (1) year from the date of issuance.

**What it means:** The ban covers the whole highway, not just the travel lanes. Read literally, a sign held up from the shoulder is a violation. Hitching in Idaho is safest, legally, from private property off the highway, such as fuel stations, where you aren't "on a highway". Highway rest areas may be within the highway right-of-way, so they are not a safe bet.

### Idaho Code § 49-109(4): "Highway" defined

**Source:** [Idaho Legislature, Idaho Code § 49-109](https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/Title49/T49CH1/SECT49-109/) (history: added 1988; last am. 2019, ch. 213, sec. 6)

> (4) "Highway" means the entire width between the boundary lines of every way publicly maintained when any part is open to the use of the public for vehicular travel, with jurisdiction extending to the adjacent property line, including sidewalks, shoulders, berms and rights-of-way not intended for motorized traffic. The term "street" is interchangeable with highway.

**What it means:** Shoulders and sidewalks are part of the "highway" in Idaho. That is why the hitchhiking ban reaches the shoulder.

### Idaho Code § 49-119(19): "Roadway" defined

**Source:** [Idaho Legislature, Idaho Code § 49-119](https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/Title49/T49CH1/SECT49-119/) (history: added 1988; last am. 2024, ch. 234, sec. 1)

> (19) "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of sidewalks, shoulders, berms and rights-of-way.

**What it means:** It's included for contrast. Had the legislature written "roadway" in § 49-709, the shoulder would be fine. It wrote "highway".

### Idaho Code § 49-708: Pedestrians on highways

**Source:** [Idaho Legislature, Idaho Code § 49-708](https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/Title49/T49CH7/SECT49-708/) (added 1988, ch. 265, sec. 199)

> (1) Where a sidewalk is provided and its use is practicable, it shall be unlawful for any pedestrian to walk along and upon an adjacent roadway.
>
> (2) Where a sidewalk is not available, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall walk only on a shoulder, as far as practicable from the edge of the roadway.
>
> (3) Where neither a sidewalk nor a shoulder is available, any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall walk as near as practicable to an outside edge of the roadway, and, if on a two-way highway, shall walk only on the left side of the highway.

**What it means:** Walking along a highway is lawful if you keep to the sidewalk or shoulder. Soliciting a ride while you're there is what § 49-709 prohibits.

### Idaho Code §§ 49-202(23)-(24) and 49-208(1)(k): Controlled-access highways

**Source:** [Idaho Legislature, Idaho Code § 49-202](https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/Title49/T49CH2/SECT49-202/) and [§ 49-208](https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/Title49/T49CH2/SECT49-208/)

§ 49-202:

> (23) The department shall regulate or prohibit the use of any controlled-access highway by any class or kind of traffic which is found to be incompatible with the normal and safe movement of traffic.
>
> (24) The department shall erect and maintain traffic-control devices on controlled-access highways on which any prohibitions are applicable.

§ 49-208:

> (1) The provisions of this title shall not be deemed to prevent local authorities with respect to highways under their jurisdiction and within the reasonable exercise of the police power from: [...]
> (k) Prohibiting or regulating the use of controlled-access highways by any class or kind of traffic;

**What it means:** No statute bans pedestrians on Idaho interstates outright. Restrictions come from the Transportation Department or local authorities and are shown by signs. Hitching on any part of an interstate, ramps included, is in any case already covered by § 49-709, because ramps are part of the highway.

### Idaho Code §§ 49-236 and 18-113A: Penalty

**Source:** [Idaho Legislature, Idaho Code § 49-236](https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/Title49/T49CH2/SECT49-236/) and [§ 18-113A](https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/Title18/T18CH1/SECT18-113A/)

§ 49-236:

> (2) It is an infraction for any person to violate any of the provisions of chapters 3, 4 and 6 through 9 of this title unless otherwise specifically provided.

§ 18-113A:

> Every offense declared to be an infraction is punishable only by a penalty not exceeding three hundred dollars ($300) as provided in this section and no imprisonment. The penalty for an infraction shall be:
> (1) The amount set by statute;
> (2) Subject to subsection (1) of this section, the amount set as a fixed penalty for that infraction as of January 1, 2014, by the Idaho supreme court infraction rule 9 [...];
> (3) The amount set by city or county ordinance [...]; or
> (4) Fifteen dollars and fifty cents ($15.50) for an infraction without a specific penalty set under subsection (1), (2) or (3) of this section.

**What it means:** Section 49-709 is in chapter 7, so a violation is an infraction: a ticket, no jail, and at most $300. The exact amount comes from the Idaho Supreme Court's infraction rule schedule, which I didn't retrieve.

jurisdictions.title: Montana (US-MT)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. "A person may not stand on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride." Montana defines the roadway as excluding the berm or shoulder, so hitchhiking from the shoulder is not prohibited by state law. Restrictions on pedestrians on interstates and other controlled-access highways come from the Montana Department of Transportation and are shown by signs.

sections.summary:
Montana follows the standard Uniform Vehicle Code pattern. You can't stand in the travel lanes to solicit a ride, but the shoulder isn't part of the roadway.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stand on the shoulder, not in the lane.**
- **Walking:** use the sidewalk where one is provided. Otherwise walk on the shoulder, as far from the roadway edge as practicable.
- **Interstates and other controlled-access highways:** the Montana Department of Transportation (by rule) and local authorities (by ordinance) may prohibit any class of traffic that is incompatible with normal, safe traffic flow, and must post signs. Obey any "pedestrians prohibited" signs.
- **Penalty:** a misdemeanor punished only by a fine. It is $10 to $100 for a first offense, rising for repeat offenses within a year.
sections.laws:
### Mont. Code Ann. § 61-8-507: Pedestrian soliciting rides, business, or contributions

**Source:** [Montana Legislature, MCA 61-8-507](https://leg.mt.gov/bills/mca/title_0610/chapter_0080/part_0050/section_0070/0610-0080-0050-0070.html) (Montana Code Annotated 2025; history: En. Sec. 79, Ch. 263, L. 1955; amd. Sec. 6, Ch. 374, L. 2003)

> (1) A person may not stand on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride.
>
> (2) A person may not stand on a highway for the purpose of soliciting employment, business, or contributions from the occupant of a vehicle unless the solicitation is authorized by the proper jurisdictional authority.

**What it means:** Subsection (1), about rides, uses "roadway", the travel lanes. Subsection (2), about business and contributions, uses the broader "highway". Because (1) says "roadway", a hitchhiker on the shoulder is not covered by it.

### Mont. Code Ann. § 61-1-101: "Roadway" and "Highway" defined

**Source:** [Montana Legislature, MCA 61-1-101](https://leg.mt.gov/bills/mca/title_0610/chapter_0010/part_0010/section_0010/0610-0010-0010-0010.html) (Montana Code Annotated 2025)

> (26) "Highway" or "public highway" means the entire width between the boundary lines of every publicly maintained way when any part of the publicly maintained way is open to the use of the public for purposes of vehicular travel.

> (66) "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the berm or shoulder. In the event that a highway includes two or more separate roadways, the term refers to any roadway separately but not to all roadways collectively.

**What it means:** The shoulder is part of the highway but not the roadway. You may hitch from the shoulder. Stay out of the lanes.

### Mont. Code Ann. § 61-8-506: Pedestrians on roadways and highways

**Source:** [Montana Legislature, MCA 61-8-506](https://leg.mt.gov/bills/mca/title_0610/chapter_0080/part_0050/section_0060/0610-0080-0050-0060.html) (Montana Code Annotated 2025; history: En. Sec. 78, Ch. 263, L. 1955; amd. 2003, 2005)

> (1) Where sidewalks are provided and their use is practicable, a pedestrian may not walk along and upon an adjacent roadway.
>
> (2) Where sidewalks are not provided, a pedestrian, other than an intoxicated pedestrian referred to in 61-8-508, who is walking along and upon a highway may walk only on the shoulder, as far as practicable from the edge of the roadway.

**What it means:** Use the sidewalk if there is one. Otherwise stay on the shoulder, as far from the traffic lane as you reasonably can.

### Mont. Code Ann. § 61-8-332: Restrictions on use of controlled-access roadway

**Source:** [Montana Legislature, MCA 61-8-332](https://leg.mt.gov/bills/mca/title_0610/chapter_0080/part_0030/section_0320/0610-0080-0030-0320.html) (Montana Code Annotated 2025; history: En. Sec. 60, Ch. 263, L. 1955; amd. 1974, 1991; amd. Sec. 16, Ch. 352, L. 2003)

> (1) The department of transportation may by rule and local authorities may by ordinance regulate or prohibit the use of a controlled-access highway under their respective jurisdictions by any class or kind of traffic that is found to be incompatible with the normal and safe movement of traffic or by any vehicle.
>
> (2) The department or the local authority that adopts the prohibitory regulation shall erect and maintain official traffic control devices on the controlled-access highway on which these regulations are applicable. A person may not violate the restrictions stated on the official traffic control devices.

**What it means:** No statute bans pedestrians from all interstates. Any ban comes from a Transportation Department rule or local ordinance and is posted on signs. If the on-ramp says pedestrians are prohibited, wait before the sign.

### Mont. Code Ann. § 61-8-711: Penalty

**Source:** [Montana Legislature, MCA 61-8-711](https://leg.mt.gov/bills/mca/title_0610/chapter_0080/part_0070/section_0110/0610-0080-0070-0110.html) (Montana Code Annotated 2025)

> (1) It is a misdemeanor for a person to violate any of the provisions of this chapter unless the violation is declared to be a felony.
>
> (2) Each person convicted of a misdemeanor for a violation of any of the provisions of this chapter for which another penalty is not provided shall for a first conviction be punished by a fine of not less than $10 or more than $100. For a second conviction within 1 year after the first conviction, the person shall be punished by a fine of not less than $25 or more than $200. Upon a third or subsequent conviction within 1 year after the first conviction, the person shall be punished by a fine of not less than $50 or more than $500.

**What it means:** Standing in the lane to hitch is technically a misdemeanor, but the penalty is a fine only: $10 to $100 the first time.
sections.history:
### 2003: hitchhiking split from business solicitation; freeway pedestrian language generalized

**Source:** [Montana Code Annotated 2001, § 61-8-507](https://archive.legmt.gov/bills/2001/mca/61/8/61-8-507.htm) and [MCA 1997, § 61-8-332](https://archive.legmt.gov/bills/1997/mca/61/8/61-8-332.htm) (official Montana Legislature archive)

Before the 2003 amendment (Ch. 374, L. 2003), § 61-8-507 read: "(1) No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment, or business from the occupant of any vehicle." The 2003 rewrite kept the roadway-only rule for rides. Business and contributions moved into a separate subsection that applies to the whole highway.

Before 2003, § 61-8-332(1) said the department "may by rule and local authorities may by ordinance prohibit the use of a controlled-access highway under their respective jurisdictions by pedestrians, bicycles, or other nonmotorized traffic or by a person operating a motor-driven cycle." The current text refers to "any class or kind of traffic" instead.

**What it means:** The rule for hitchhikers has been essentially the same since 1955: stay out of the roadway.

jurisdictions.title: Utah (US-UT)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Legal. No Utah statute currently prohibits soliciting a ride. Walking on no-access freeways is prohibited, and you may not impede or block traffic on interstates, freeways, state highways, or fast roads.

sections.summary:
Utah no longer has a statewide ban on hitchhiking. Before 2017, Utah Code § 41-6a-1009(4) listed "soliciting rides, contributions, or other business" as conduct that may impede or block traffic. The 2017 General Session (H.B. 161, "Pedestrian Safety Amendments") struck that wording. The section now targets handing money or property between pedestrians and occupants of moving traffic.

What still applies to hitchhikers:

- **Don't walk on no-access freeways** (interstates and other limited-access highways) unless there is an emergency. Stand at the on-ramp, before the freeway begins.
- **Don't impede or block traffic** on interstates, freeways, state highways or routes, or highways that are paved with a speed limit of 35 mph or more, that have a median, or that share the right-of-way with a railway. This includes shoulders, on-ramps, off-ramps and medians.
- **Walk on the sidewalk** if there is one. Otherwise walk on the shoulder, or on the left edge facing traffic.
- **Cities and counties may add their own rules** for the locations listed in subsection (4).

A violation is an infraction. A third violation of subsection (4) within one year is a class C misdemeanor.
sections.laws:
### Utah Code § 41-6a-1009: Use of roadway by pedestrians -- Prohibited activities

**Source:** [Utah Legislature, Utah Code § 41-6a-1009](https://le.utah.gov/xcode/Title41/Chapter6A/41-6a-S1009.html) (version effective 5/8/2018, amended by Chapter 122, 2018 General Session)

> (1) Where there is a sidewalk provided and its use is practicable, a pedestrian may not walk along or on an adjacent roadway.
>
> (2) Where a sidewalk is not provided, a pedestrian walking along or on a highway shall walk only on the shoulder, as far as practicable from the edge of the roadway.
>
> (3) Where a sidewalk or a shoulder is not available, a pedestrian walking along or on a highway shall:
> (a) walk as near as practicable to the outside edge of the roadway; and
> (b) if on a two-way roadway, walk only on the left side of the roadway facing traffic.

**What it means:** If there is a sidewalk, walk on it. If there isn't one, walk on the shoulder. If there's no shoulder, walk on the left side of the road facing traffic.

> (4)(a) An individual may not impede or block traffic within any of the following:
> (i) an interstate system, as defined in Section 72-1-102;
> (ii) a freeway, as defined in Section 41-6a-102;
> (iii) a state highway, as defined in Title 72, Chapter 4, Designation of State Highways Act;
> (iv) a state route, or "SR," as defined in Section 72-1-102; or
> (v) a highway, as defined in Section 72-1-102, that:
> (A) is paved and has a speed limit of 35 miles per hour or higher;
> (B) has a median, whether elevated or flat; or
> (C) has a fixed guideway as defined in Section 59-12-102 or any other railway that shares the highway right-of-way.
>
> (b) The locations described in Subsection (4)(a) include:
> (i) shoulder areas, as defined in Section 41-6a-102;
> (ii) on-ramps;
> (iii) off-ramps; and
> (iv) an area between the roadways of a divided highway, as defined in Section 41-6a-102.
>
> (c) The locations described in Subsection (4)(a) do not include sidewalks, as defined in Section 41-6a-102.
>
> (d) Conduct that may impede or block traffic includes:
> (i) while a pedestrian, accepting, transacting, exchanging, or otherwise taking possession or control of money or property from a person within a motor vehicle while that motor vehicle is within an area described in Subsection (4)(a); [...]
>
> (f) A county or municipality may adopt a resolution, ordinance, or regulation prohibiting conduct in locations described in Subsections (4)(a) and (b) within any of the roadways under its jurisdiction.

**What it means:** Standing on a shoulder or ramp with your thumb out is not listed as prohibited conduct. Stepping into traffic or making cars stop in a travel lane is. Pick a spot where a driver can pull completely off the road. Local ordinances can be stricter (see (4)(f)), so check city rules in places like Salt Lake City.

> (7) A pedestrian may not walk along or on a no-access freeway facility except during an emergency.

**What it means:** Don't walk on interstates or other limited-access freeways. Hitchhike from the on-ramp entrance or a nearby gas station, not from the freeway shoulder.

> (9)(a) Except as provided in Subsection (9)(b), a violation of this section is an infraction.
> (b) A third or subsequent violation of Subsection (4) in a one-year period is a class C misdemeanor.

**What it means:** A first or second violation is an infraction, which carries a fine and no jail. Repeat violations of the traffic-blocking rule within a year become a class C misdemeanor.
sections.history:
### 2017 H.B. 161: "soliciting rides" removed

**Source:** [Utah Legislature, 2017 H.B. 161 (enrolled), Pedestrian Safety Amendments](https://le.utah.gov/~2017/bills/hbillenr/HB0161.htm)

Before this bill, § 41-6a-1009(4)(d) read: "Conduct that impedes or blocks traffic may include: (i) loitering; (ii) demonstrating or picketing; (iii) distributing materials; (iv) gathering signatures; (v) holding signs; or (vi) soliciting rides, contributions, or other business." The bill struck that whole list and replaced it with the money and property exchange language quoted above.

**What it means:** Older guides that say "Utah bans soliciting rides on highways" describe the pre-2017 law.

jurisdictions.title: Wyoming (US-WY)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Legal. Wyoming repealed its ban on soliciting rides on highways in 2013. Ordinary pedestrian rules still apply. The Wyoming Department of Transportation (WYDOT) and local authorities may restrict pedestrians on controlled-access highways (interstates) where signs are posted.

sections.summary:
Until 2013, Wyo. Stat. § 31-5-606(a) said "No person shall be on a highway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment, business or contributions from the occupant of any vehicle." That ban covered the whole highway, shoulders included. Senate File 29 (2013), titled simply "Hitchhiking", struck the words "a ride," along with the disabled-vehicle exception. The act took effect July 1, 2013. The section now covers only employment, business and contributions.

What still applies to hitchhikers:

- **Hitchhiking itself is not a statutory offense** in Wyoming.
- **Walk on the sidewalk** where one exists. Otherwise walk on the left side of the road or its shoulder, facing traffic.
- **Yield to vehicles** when you're on the roadway, and don't step into traffic to stop a car.
- **Interstates and other controlled-access highways:** WYDOT (by rule) and local authorities (by ordinance) may prohibit or regulate any class of traffic that is incompatible with safe traffic flow, and must post signs. Obey "pedestrians prohibited" signs.
- **Penalty** for breaking a pedestrian rule: a misdemeanor, with a fine of up to $200 for a first conviction.
sections.laws:
### Wyo. Stat. § 31-5-606: Soliciting on streets and highways

**Source:** [Wyoming Legislature, Wyoming Statutes Title 31 (PDF)](https://wyoleg.gov/statutes/compress/title31.pdf) (file generated May 8, 2026)

> (a) No person shall be on a highway for the purpose of soliciting employment, business or contributions from the occupant of any vehicle.
>
> (b) No person shall stand on or in proximity to a street or highway for the purpose of soliciting the watching or guarding of any vehicle while parked or about to be parked on a street or highway.

**What it means:** Soliciting a ride is no longer listed. Don't offer to work or ask for money from drivers, because that is still prohibited on any part of the highway. A sign asking for a ride to a destination is fine. A sign asking for cash is not.

### Wyo. Stat. § 31-5-605: Walking along roadways or highways

**Source:** [Wyoming Legislature, Wyoming Statutes Title 31 (PDF)](https://wyoleg.gov/statutes/compress/title31.pdf)

> (a) Where a sidewalk is provided and its use is practicable it is unlawful for any pedestrian to walk along and upon an adjacent roadway.
>
> (b) Where sidewalks are not provided any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall, when practicable, walk only on the left side of the roadway or its shoulder facing traffic which may approach from the opposite direction as far as practicable from the edge of the roadway.
>
> (c) Except as otherwise provided in this act, any pedestrian upon a roadway shall yield the right-of-way to all vehicles upon the roadway.

**What it means:** When walking between spots, use the left shoulder facing traffic. When you stop to hitch, pick a place where drivers can pull fully off the road.

### Wyo. Stat. § 31-5-102(a)(xl): "Roadway" defined

**Source:** [Wyoming Legislature, Wyoming Statutes Title 31 (PDF)](https://wyoleg.gov/statutes/compress/title31.pdf)

> (xl) "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the sidewalk, berm or shoulder. In the event a highway includes two (2) or more separate roadways the term "roadway" as used herein shall refer to any such roadway separately but not to all such roadways collectively;

**What it means:** The shoulder is not part of the roadway. Standing on the shoulder doesn't count as being "upon a roadway" for § 31-5-605(c).

### Wyo. Stat. § 31-5-213: Restrictions on use of controlled-access highways

**Source:** [Wyoming Legislature, Wyoming Statutes Title 31 (PDF)](https://wyoleg.gov/statutes/compress/title31.pdf)

> (a) The department may by rule or regulation, and local authorities may by ordinance, with respect to any controlled-access highway under their respective jurisdictions prohibit or regulate the use of the highway by any class or kind of traffic which is found to be incompatible with the normal and safe movement of traffic.
>
> (b) The department or the local authority adopting any prohibitory regulation under subsection (a) of this section shall erect and maintain official traffic-control devices on the controlled-access highway on which the regulations are applicable and when so erected no person shall disobey the restrictions stated on the devices.

**What it means:** No statute bans pedestrians on Wyoming interstates. Any ban comes from a WYDOT rule or local ordinance and must be signed. Where an on-ramp is signed against pedestrians, hitch from before the sign.

### Wyo. Stat. § 31-5-1201: Penalty

**Source:** [Wyoming Legislature, Wyoming Statutes Title 31 (PDF)](https://wyoleg.gov/statutes/compress/title31.pdf)

> (a) It is a misdemeanor for any person to violate any of the provisions of this act or rules and regulations authorized under this act unless the violation is by this act or other law of this state declared to be a felony.
>
> (b) Every person convicted of a misdemeanor for a violation of any of the provisions of this act or rules and regulations authorized under this act for which another penalty is not provided shall:
> (i) For a first conviction be punished by a fine of not more than two hundred dollars ($200.00);
> (ii) For a second conviction of the same offense within one (1) year thereafter, be punished by a fine of not more than three hundred dollars ($300.00);
> (iii) For a third or subsequent conviction of the same offense within one (1) year after the first conviction, be punished by a fine of not more than five hundred dollars ($500.00) or by imprisonment for not more than six (6) months, or both.

**What it means:** Breaking a pedestrian rule, such as walking on a posted interstate, is a misdemeanor. The first offense carries a fine of up to $200.
sections.history:
### 2013 SF0029 (Enrolled Act 58): hitchhiking ban repealed

**Source:** [Wyoming Legislature, 2013 SF0029 enrolled act](https://wyoleg.gov/2013/Enroll/SF0029.pdf) and [bill summary](https://www.wyoleg.gov/2013/Summaries/SF0029.htm)

The enrolled act amends § 31-5-606(a). The bill text shows the pre-2013 wording, with the deleted words struck through in the original. In plain text (strike-through formatting not reproduced) that wording reads:

> (a) No person shall be on a highway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment, business or contributions from the occupant of any vehicle. This subsection does not apply to persons attempting to obtain assistance for disabled vehicles.

The Legislative Service Office summary describes the bill this way: "This act repeals the state statutory prohibition on soliciting rides on highways (hitchhiking)." Effective date: July 1, 2013. Prime sponsor: Senator Christensen.

**What it means:** Older guides that list Wyoming as a no-hitchhiking state describe the law before July 1, 2013.

- National parks in Wyoming (Yellowstone, Grand Teton) are under federal regulations, which were not researched here.

jurisdictions.title: Alaska (US-AK)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. Alaska does not ban hitchhiking outright, but you may not solicit a ride "in a manner which distracts a driver's attention" (13 AAC 02.180). Walking on controlled-access highways is prohibited except in an emergency.

sections.summary:
Alaska's rules of the road are mostly in the Alaska Administrative Code (13 AAC 02), not the statutes. The hitchhiking rule is 13 AAC 02.180. Unlike the common "no standing in the roadway" model, it doesn't say where you may stand. It bans soliciting a ride in a way that distracts a driver.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Don't distract drivers.** Thumbing from a safe spot is not banned. Running at cars, waving in the lane, or anything that pulls a driver's attention off the road is.
- **No walking on controlled-access highways** except in an emergency (13 AAC 02.175(b)). Wait at the on-ramp entrance or a pull-out on an ordinary highway.
- **Use the shoulder.** Where there's no sidewalk, walk on the shoulder, away from the roadway. "Roadway" excludes the shoulder.
- **Don't loiter on the highway.** 13 AAC 02.175(e) bans sleeping or loitering "upon a highway", and "highway" covers the entire width between the boundary lines, shoulders included.
- **Don't interfere with traffic** or put yourself at unreasonable risk on a roadway (13 AAC 02.175(d)).

Breaking a traffic regulation is an infraction with a fine of up to $300, unless another law sets a different penalty (AS 28.90.010(c)).
sections.laws:
### 13 AAC 02.180: Pedestrians soliciting rides or business

**Source:** [Alaska Legislature, Alaska Administrative Code, 13 AAC 02.180](https://www.akleg.gov/basis/aac.asp#13.02.180) (official AAC database, retrieved 2026-11-02)

> No person may solicit a ride in a manner which distracts a driver's attention, nor may a pedestrian upon a highway solicit employment, business, or contributions from the occupant of a vehicle.

**What it means:** Hitchhiking itself is not banned. The offence is soliciting a ride in a way that distracts a driver. Stand well off the travel lane, somewhere drivers can see you early and pull over safely, and don't step toward moving cars. The second half of the rule bans asking drivers for work, business or donations from a highway. It does not mention rides.

### 13 AAC 02.175: Pedestrians on highways

**Source:** [Alaska Legislature, Alaska Administrative Code, 13 AAC 02.175](https://www.akleg.gov/basis/aac.asp#13.02.175) (official AAC database, retrieved 2026-11-02)

> (a) Where a sidewalk is provided and its use is practicable, a pedestrian may not walk upon an adjacent roadway except when crossing the roadway.
>
> (b) Where a sidewalk is not available, a pedestrian walking upon a highway shall walk on a shoulder as far as practicable from the edge of the roadway. Where neither a sidewalk nor a shoulder is available, a pedestrian walking on a highway shall walk as near as practicable to the outside edge of the highway and, if walking along a two-way roadway, shall walk only on the left side of the roadway. No pedestrian may walk on a controlled-access highway except in an emergency.
>
> [...]
>
> (d) No pedestrian may be upon or along a roadway in such a manner as to create an unreasonable risk of danger to himself or interfere with the normal flow of traffic.
>
> (e) No pedestrian may sleep or loiter upon a highway or, without lawful permit, obstruct free passage upon a highway.

**What it means:** Walk on the sidewalk if there is one, otherwise on the shoulder, as far from traffic as you can. Never walk on a controlled-access highway (a road you can only enter at ramps or designated entrances) except in an emergency. Subsection (e) is the one to watch. An officer could treat standing around on a highway shoulder as "loitering", so look like you are actively getting a ride, and use pull-outs, gas stations or wide shoulders where cars can stop.

### 13 AAC 40.010: Definition of "controlled-access highway"

**Source:** [Alaska Legislature, Alaska Administrative Code, 13 AAC 40.010](https://www.akleg.gov/basis/aac.asp#13.40.010) (official AAC database, retrieved 2026-11-02)

> (9) "controlled-access highway" means every highway, street, or roadway where access to or from the highway is determined by the public authority having jurisdiction over the highway, street or roadway;

**What it means:** This covers freeways and expressways where you can only get on and off at ramps. On those, the walking ban in 13 AAC 02.175(b) applies.

### AS 28.90.990: Definitions of "highway" and "roadway"

**Source:** [Alaska Legislature, Alaska Statutes, AS 28.90.990](https://www.akleg.gov/basis/statutes.asp#28.90.990) (official statutes database, retrieved 2026-11-02)

> (17) "highway" means the entire width between the boundary lines of every way that is publicly maintained when a part of it is open to the public for purposes of vehicular travel, including but not limited to every street and the Alaska state marine highway system but not vehicular ways or areas;
>
> [...]
>
> (27) "roadway" means that portion of a highway designed or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the sidewalk, berm, or shoulder, even though the sidewalk, berm, or shoulder is used by persons riding bicycles or other human powered vehicles; and in the event that a highway includes two or more separate roadways, the term refers to each roadway separately but not to all such roadways collectively;

**What it means:** The **roadway** is the travel lanes only. The shoulder is not part of it, so rules that refer to the "roadway" do not reach you on the shoulder. The **highway** is the whole public right-of-way, shoulders included. Rules that say "upon a highway" (loitering, the walking ban on controlled-access highways) apply on the shoulder too.

### AS 28.90.010: Penalties

**Source:** [Alaska Legislature, Alaska Statutes, AS 28.90.010](https://www.akleg.gov/basis/statutes.asp#28.90.010) (official statutes database, retrieved 2026-11-02)

> (c) Unless otherwise specified by law a person convicted of a violation of a regulation adopted under this title, or a municipal ordinance regulating vehicles or traffic when the municipal ordinance does not correspond to a provision of this title, is guilty of an infraction and is punishable by a fine not to exceed $300.
>
> (d) An infraction, as provided for in (c) of this section, is not considered a criminal offense and may not result in imprisonment, [...]

**What it means:** Breaking 13 AAC 02.175 or 02.180 is an infraction, not a crime. The fine is capped at $300 and there is no jail.

- **Rulemaking authority and history of 13 AAC 02.180.** The official AAC page shows no history note for this section. I could not confirm when it was adopted or last amended, or which statute it was adopted under. (A secondary mirror lists AS 28.05.011.)
- **Scheduled fine amount.** I did not retrieve the court bail/fine schedule, so the actual ticket amount for 13 AAC 02.180 is unknown. The $300 figure is the statutory maximum.
- **Anchorage.** Anchorage Municipal Code 9.20.060 reportedly deals with soliciting from vehicle occupants on a roadway. I did not retrieve its current text, so check it before relying on it.
- **Statutes.** I did not search all of Alaska Statutes Title 28 for any separate hitchhiking statute. The hitchhiking rule found is the regulation above.

jurisdictions.title: California (US-CA)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not stand in the roadway to solicit a ride. The shoulder and sidewalk are not part of the "roadway", so hitchhiking from the curb or shoulder is not banned by state law. Pedestrians are kept off freeways and expressways wherever Caltrans or a local authority has posted signs prohibiting them.

sections.summary:
California's hitchhiking rule is one sentence long and has not changed since the Vehicle Code was enacted in 1959: "No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any vehicle." The Vehicle Code defines "roadway" as the part of the highway used for vehicle travel, so the rule targets standing in the travel lanes.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stay out of the travel lanes.** Stand on the shoulder, curb or sidewalk and let drivers pull over to you.
- **Freeways and expressways:** Caltrans and local authorities can prohibit pedestrians by order, and the ban takes effect once signs are posted. Check the ramp entrance for a prohibition sign and stand before it.
- **Walking along a road outside towns:** walk close to the left edge, facing traffic.
- **Penalty:** a pedestrian infraction, with a fine of up to $50.
sections.laws:
### Cal. Veh. Code § 21957: Hitchhiking

**Source:** [California Legislative Information, Vehicle Code § 21957](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=VEH&sectionNum=21957) (text retrieved from the Legislative Counsel's official bulk database, pubinfo_2025, file dated 2026-11-01; enacted by Stats. 1959, Ch. 3)

> No person shall stand in a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride from the driver of any vehicle.

**What it means:** Thumbing a ride is not banned in California. Standing in the travel lanes to do it is. Stand on the shoulder or curb, where a driver can pull out of traffic to pick you up.

### Cal. Veh. Code § 530: "Roadway" defined

**Source:** [California Legislative Information, Vehicle Code § 530](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=VEH&sectionNum=530) (text retrieved from the Legislative Counsel's official bulk database, pubinfo_2025; enacted by Stats. 1959, Ch. 3)

> A "roadway" is that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel.

**What it means:** The roadway is the part cars drive on. California's definition doesn't mention the shoulder, unlike states that explicitly exclude the shoulder. A paved shoulder isn't "ordinarily used for vehicular travel", though, so the usual reading is that the shoulder isn't roadway. Stay well to the outside edge.

### Cal. Veh. Code § 21960: Freeways and expressways

**Source:** [California Legislative Information, Vehicle Code § 21960](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=VEH&sectionNum=21960) (text retrieved from the Legislative Counsel's official bulk database, pubinfo_2025; amended by Stats. 2015, Ch. 777, Sec. 4, AB 604)

> (a) The Department of Transportation and local authorities, by order, ordinance, or resolution, with respect to freeways, expressways, or designated portions thereof under their respective jurisdictions, to which vehicle access is completely or partially controlled, may prohibit or restrict the use of the freeways, expressways, or any portion thereof by pedestrians, bicycles or other nonmotorized traffic [...]. Notwithstanding any order, ordinance, or resolution to the contrary, the driver or passengers of a disabled vehicle stopped on a freeway or expressway may walk to the nearest exit, in either direction, on that side of the freeway or expressway upon which the vehicle is disabled, from which telephone or motor vehicle repair services are available.
>
> (b) The prohibitory regulation authorized by subdivision (a) shall be effective when appropriate signs giving notice thereof are erected upon any freeway or expressway and the approaches thereto. [...]

**What it means:** No statute bans pedestrians on every freeway. Caltrans or the local authority does it road by road, and a ban takes effect once its signs are posted on the freeway and its approaches. If a ramp is signed "pedestrians prohibited", wait before the sign. If your car breaks down, you may walk to the nearest exit.

### Cal. Veh. Code § 21956: Walking along a roadway

**Source:** [California Legislative Information, Vehicle Code § 21956](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=VEH&sectionNum=21956) (text retrieved from the Legislative Counsel's official bulk database, pubinfo_2025; amended by Stats. 2022, Ch. 957, Sec. 12, AB 2147)

> (a) A pedestrian shall not walk upon a roadway outside of a business or residence district otherwise than close to the pedestrian's left-hand edge of the roadway.
>
> (b) A pedestrian may walk close to their right-hand edge of the roadway if a crosswalk or other means of safely crossing the roadway is not available or if existing traffic or other conditions would compromise the safety of a pedestrian attempting to cross the road.
>
> (c) (1) A peace officer [...] shall not stop a pedestrian for a violation of this section unless a reasonably careful person would realize there is an immediate danger of a collision with a moving vehicle or other device moving exclusively by human power.

**What it means:** Out of town, if you have to walk on the road itself, keep to the left edge, facing oncoming traffic. Since 2023, police may stop you for this only if there is an immediate danger of a collision.

### Cal. Veh. Code §§ 40000.1 and 42001: Penalty

**Source:** [California Legislative Information, Vehicle Code § 40000.1](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=VEH&sectionNum=40000.1) and [§ 42001](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=VEH&sectionNum=42001) (text retrieved from the Legislative Counsel's official bulk database, pubinfo_2025; § 42001 amended by Stats. 2006, Ch. 900, Sec. 3)

§ 40000.1:

> Except as otherwise provided in this article, it is unlawful and constitutes an infraction for any person to violate, or fail to comply with any provision of this code, or any local ordinance adopted pursuant to this code.

§ 42001:

> (b) A pedestrian convicted of an infraction for a violation of this code or any local ordinance adopted pursuant to this code shall be punished by a fine not exceeding fifty dollars ($50).

**What it means:** Standing in the roadway to hitch, or walking on a posted freeway, is an infraction. It is not a crime. The fine set by § 42001(b) for a pedestrian is up to $50. Other court fees and assessments may apply; they are not covered here.
sections.history:
### 2022 AB 2147 ("Freedom to Walk Act")

**Source:** History notes on [Vehicle Code § 21956](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=VEH&sectionNum=21956) and § 21955, § 21961 and § 21966 in the Legislative Counsel's database ("Amended by Stats. 2022, Ch. 957 ... (AB 2147) Effective January 1, 2023")

AB 2147 did not touch the hitchhiking section (§ 21957, unchanged since 1959). It did limit when officers may stop pedestrians for walking-in-the-road and jaywalking offenses, which is why § 21956(c) now requires an immediate danger of collision before a stop.

jurisdictions.title: Hawaii (US-HI)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Illegal statewide, unless a county ordinance allows it. HRS § 291C-77(a) bans standing in, walking along, or otherwise occupying any part of a highway to solicit a ride. Because "highway" covers the whole public right-of-way, that includes the shoulder. Counties can carve out exceptions.

sections.summary:
Hawaii has one of the broader hitchhiking bans in the US. The state statute doesn't stop at the travel lanes. It covers "a portion of a highway", which is the entire width between the boundary lines of the public way. The statute opens with "Except as otherwise provided by county ordinance", so a county can allow hitchhiking in some places. Honolulu (Oʻahu) is reported to do so, but I have not verified its ordinance text (see open questions).

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Statewide default: no soliciting rides from any part of a highway**, shoulders included.
- **County ordinances can override the state ban.** Check the rules for the island you are on.
- **Freeways:** the state and counties can ban classes of traffic from controlled-access highways by posting signs, and you must obey them (HRS § 291C-53 and § 291C-71).
- **Walk on the sidewalk** where one exists. Otherwise walk on the left side of the roadway or its shoulder, facing traffic.

A violation is a traffic violation (not a crime), with a fine of up to $250 for a first offence.
sections.laws:
### HRS § 291C-77: Pedestrians soliciting rides, business, or attention of motorist

**Source:** [Hawaii State Legislature, HRS § 291C-77](https://data.capitol.hawaii.gov/hrscurrent/Vol05_Ch0261-0319/HRS0291C/HRS_0291C-0077.htm) (official current HRS, history note through L 2015, c 35)

> (a) Except as otherwise provided by county ordinance, no person shall stand in, walk along, or otherwise occupy a portion of a highway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment, business, or contributions from the occupant of any vehicle.
>
> (b) No person shall stand on or in proximity to a street or highway for the purpose of soliciting the watching or guarding of any vehicle while parked or about to be parked on a street or highway. [L 1971, c 150, pt of §1; am L 1973, c 216, §2; am L 2015, c 35, §5]

**What it means:** Unless a county ordinance says otherwise, you can't stand anywhere on a public road, shoulder included, to thumb a ride. The statute's annotations note that a 1975 Attorney General opinion (Att. Gen. Op. 75-17) found subsection (a) "is not unconstitutionally vague." To stay within the state law, solicit rides from private property next to the road, such as a parking lot or gas station, or from a spot a county ordinance expressly allows.

### HRS § 291C-1: Definitions of "highway", "roadway" and "controlled-access highway"

**Source:** [Hawaii State Legislature, HRS § 291C-1](https://data.capitol.hawaii.gov/hrscurrent/Vol05_Ch0261-0319/HRS0291C/HRS_0291C-0001.htm) (official current HRS)

> "Controlled-access highway" means every highway, street, or roadway in respect to which owners or occupants of abutting lands and other persons have no legal right of access to or from the same except at such points only and in such manner as may be determined by the public authority having jurisdiction over such highway, street, or roadway.
>
> [...]
>
> "Highway" means the entire width between the boundary lines of every way publicly maintained and those private streets, as defined in section 46-16, over which the application of this chapter has been extended by ordinance, when any part thereof is open to the use of the public for purposes of vehicular travel.
>
> [...]
>
> "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the berm or shoulder. In the event a highway includes two or more separate roadways the term "roadway" as used herein refers to any such roadway separately but not to all such roadways collectively.

**What it means:** The shoulder is not part of the "roadway", but it is part of the "highway". § 291C-77 uses "highway", so the shoulder gives you no safe harbour in Hawaii.

### HRS § 291C-76: Pedestrians on roadways

**Source:** [Hawaii State Legislature, HRS § 291C-76](https://data.capitol.hawaii.gov/hrscurrent/Vol05_Ch0261-0319/HRS0291C/HRS_0291C-0076.htm) (official current HRS)

> (a) Where sidewalks are provided it shall be unlawful for any pedestrian to walk along and upon an adjacent roadway, bicycle lane, or bicycle path.
>
> (b) Where sidewalks are not provided any pedestrian walking along and upon a highway shall, when practicable, walk only on the left side of the roadway or its shoulder facing traffic which may approach from the opposite direction.

**What it means:** Use the sidewalk if there is one. Otherwise walk on the left side, facing oncoming traffic.

### HRS § 291C-53 and § 291C-71: Controlled-access highways and obeying signs

**Source:** [Hawaii State Legislature, HRS § 291C-53](https://data.capitol.hawaii.gov/hrscurrent/Vol05_Ch0261-0319/HRS0291C/HRS_0291C-0053.htm) and [HRS § 291C-71](https://data.capitol.hawaii.gov/hrscurrent/Vol05_Ch0261-0319/HRS0291C/HRS_0291C-0071.htm) (official current HRS)

> **§ 291C-53** (a) The director of transportation by rules adopted in accordance with chapter 91, and the counties by ordinance, may regulate or prohibit the use of any controlled-access roadway or highway within their respective jurisdictions by any class or kind of traffic which is found to be incompatible with the normal and safe movement of traffic. [...]
>
> (b) The director of transportation or a county adopting any such prohibition shall erect and maintain official traffic-control devices on the controlled-access roadway or highway on which such prohibitions are applicable and when in place no person shall disobey the restrictions stated on such devices.

> **§ 291C-71** (a) A pedestrian shall obey the instructions of any official traffic-control device specifically applicable to the pedestrian, unless otherwise directed by a police officer.

**What it means:** No statute bans pedestrians from freeways by name. Instead, the state or a county can ban them, and the ban takes effect through posted signs. Where a sign bans pedestrians, you may not walk there. Wait on the surface street before the on-ramp.

### HRS § 291C-161: Penalties

**Source:** [Hawaii State Legislature, HRS § 291C-161](https://data.capitol.hawaii.gov/hrscurrent/Vol05_Ch0261-0319/HRS0291C/HRS_0291C-0161.htm) (official current HRS)

> (a) It shall be a violation for any person to violate any of the provisions of this chapter, except as otherwise specified in subsections (c) and (d) and unless the violation is by other law of this State declared to be a felony, misdemeanor, or petty misdemeanor.
>
> (b) Except as provided in subsections (c) and (d), every person who is determined to have violated any provision of this chapter for which another penalty is not provided shall be fined not more than:
> (1) $250 for a first violation thereof;
> (2) $300 for a second violation committed within one year after the date of the first violation; and
> (3) $500 for a third or subsequent violation committed within one year after the date of the first violation.

**What it means:** Hitchhiking against § 291C-77 is a "violation", the lowest level of offence, not a crime. The fine is up to $250 the first time and climbs for repeat violations within a year.

The official code host (codelibrary.amlegal.com) blocked automated retrieval, so I could not confirm the text. jurisdictions.title: Oregon (US-OR)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. Being on the roadway to solicit a ride is "unlawful hitchhiking". Oregon defines the roadway as excluding the shoulder, and its pedestrian law expressly lets a hitchhiker stand on the right shoulder facing traffic. Pedestrians are banned only on specific, signed freeway segments around Portland and Medford.

sections.summary:
Oregon is one of the few states whose statutes openly accommodate hitchhikers:

- **ORS 814.080** makes it an offense to be *on a roadway* to solicit a ride.
- **ORS 801.450** defines "roadway" as excluding the shoulder.
- **ORS 814.070** normally requires pedestrians on two-way highways to use the left shoulder. It makes an exception for **a hitchhiker on the right shoulder, as long as the hitchhiker faces the traffic in the adjacent lane**.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stand on the shoulder, not in the lane.** The right shoulder is fine if you face oncoming traffic in that lane.
- **Freeways:** an Oregon Department of Transportation rule bans pedestrians only on listed freeway segments: parts of I-84, US 26 (Sunset Highway), I-5, I-205, all of I-405 and US 30 in the Portland area, plus I-5 through Medford. The ban applies once signs are up. No statute bans pedestrians from all freeways.
- **Penalty:** unlawful hitchhiking is a Class D traffic violation. The maximum fine is $250 and the presumptive fine is $115. There is no jail.
sections.laws:
### ORS 814.080: Unlawful hitchhiking

**Source:** [Oregon State Legislature, ORS chapter 814](https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors814.html) (2025 Edition; history: 1983 c.338 §559; 1995 c.383 §87. Not on the 2026 session's list of amended or repealed sections)

> (1) A person commits the offense of unlawful hitchhiking if the person is on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride.
>
> (2) The offense described in this section, unlawful hitchhiking, is a Class D traffic violation.

**What it means:** The offense is being *on the roadway*, the travel lanes. Stand on the shoulder and you aren't committing it.

### ORS 801.450 and 801.480: "Roadway" and "Shoulder" defined

**Source:** [Oregon State Legislature, ORS chapter 801](https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors801.html) (2025 Edition; both 1983 c.338)

> 801.450 Roadway. "Roadway" means the portion of a highway that is improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the shoulder. In the event a highway includes two or more separate roadways the term "roadway" shall refer to any such roadway separately, but not to all such roadways collectively.

> 801.480 Shoulder. "Shoulder" means the portion of a highway, whether paved or unpaved, contiguous to the roadway that is primarily for use by pedestrians, for the accommodation of stopped vehicles, for emergency use and for lateral support of base and surface courses.

**What it means:** By law the shoulder is not roadway, and it is "primarily for use by pedestrians". The shoulder is where a hitchhiker belongs.

### ORS 814.070: Pedestrian position on a highway (hitchhiker exception)

**Source:** [Oregon State Legislature, ORS chapter 814](https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors814.html) (2025 Edition; history ends 2013 c.474 §1)

> (1) A pedestrian commits the offense of pedestrian with improper position upon or improperly proceeding along a highway if the pedestrian does any of the following:
> (a) Takes a position upon or proceeds along and upon the roadway where there is an adjacent usable sidewalk or shoulder.
> (b) Does not take a position upon or proceed along and upon the shoulder, as far as practicable from the roadway edge, on a highway that has an adjacent shoulder area on one or both sides.
> (c) Except in the case of the divided highway, does not take a position upon or proceed along and upon the left shoulder and as far as practicable from the roadway edge on a two-way highway that has no sidewalk and that does have an adjacent shoulder area. This paragraph does not apply to:
> (A) A hitchhiker who takes a position upon or proceeds along and upon the right shoulder so long as the hitchhiker does so facing the vehicles using the adjacent lane of the roadway; [...]
> (d) Does not take a position upon or proceed along and upon the right highway shoulder, as far as practicable from the roadway edge, on a divided highway that has no sidewalk and does have a shoulder area. [...]
> (e) Fails to take a position upon or proceed along and upon a highway that has neither sidewalk nor shoulder available, as near as practicable to an outside edge of the roadway, and, if the roadway is a two-way roadway, only on the left side of it.
> [...]
> (5) The offense described in this section, pedestrian with improper position upon or improperly proceeding along a highway, is a Class D traffic violation.

**What it means:** Pedestrians normally use the left shoulder on two-way roads. Hitchhikers get an explicit exception: you may stand on the right shoulder, on the side where the cars you want are traveling, as long as you face them. Stay as far from the lane edge as practicable. Use a sidewalk if there is one.

### OAR 734-020-0045: Prohibition of bicycles and pedestrians on freeways

**Source:** [Oregon Secretary of State, Oregon Administrative Rules, Chapter 734, Division 20](https://secure.sos.state.or.us/oard/displayDivisionRules.action?selectedDivision=3305) (last amended HWD 13-2010, f. & cert. ef. 10-25-10)

> (1) Bicycles and pedestrians as defined in ORS 801.150 and 801.385, are prohibited upon the following segments of freeways within the State of Oregon:
> (a) Portland area:
> (A) The Columbia River Highway No. 2 (Banfield/I-84) from its intersection with I-5, M.P. 0.00, to 238th Drive, M.P. 15.96;
> (B) The Sunset Highway No. 47 easterly of the Jefferson Street Interchange, M.P. 73.35;
> (C) Interstate 5 (Hwy. No. 1) northerly of the Beaverton-Tigard Highway Interchange, M.P. 292.20;
> (D) Interstate 205 (Hwy. No. 64) northerly of the Overcrossing of the Oswego Highway No. 3, M.P. 8.82;
> (E) Interstate 405 (Hwy. No. 61) in its entirety; and
> (F) Lower Columbia Highway No. 2W from its intersection with I-405, M.P. 0.00, to 23rd Street, M.P. 1.99.
> (b) Medford area: Interstate 5 (Pacific Highway No. 1) from the South Medford Interchange, M.P. 27.16, to the North Medford Interchange, M.P. 30.29 (in Medford).
>
> (2) The closure of the above sections to bicycles and pedestrians shall become effective following the erection of adequate signing.
>
> (3) The prohibition of pedestrians from the above segments of freeways does not prohibit the driver and passengers of a disabled vehicle from walking to the nearest freeway exit in accordance with ORS 814.100.

**What it means:** Outside these urban segments, no Oregon rule bans pedestrians from freeways. Even so, a hitchhiker in a freeway travel lane is breaking ORS 814.080, and a freeway shoulder is a dangerous place to stand. The freeway on-ramp is the usual spot. Inside Portland and Medford, stay off the listed freeways entirely.

### ORS 810.020 and 811.445: Signed restrictions on throughways

**Source:** [Oregon State Legislature, ORS chapter 810](https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors810.html) and [ORS chapter 811](https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors811.html) (2025 Edition)

> 810.020 (1) Each road authority may prohibit or restrict the use of a throughway in its jurisdiction by any of the following: [...] (b) Bicycles or other nonmotorized traffic. [...] (2) Regulation under this section becomes effective when appropriate signs giving notice of the regulation are erected upon a throughway and the approaches to the throughway.

> 811.445 (1) A person commits the offense of use of a throughway when prohibited if any use restrictions or prohibitions are posted by appropriate signs giving notice thereof and the person violates any restriction or prohibition so posted. [...] (3) The offense described in this section, use of a throughway when prohibited, is a Class D traffic violation.

**What it means:** Each road authority can post signs closing a throughway to pedestrians. Ignoring such a sign is also a Class D violation.

### ORS 153.018 and 153.019: Fines for a Class D violation

**Source:** [Oregon State Legislature, ORS chapter 153](https://www.oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/ors/ors153.html) (2025 Edition)

> 153.018 (1) The penalty for committing a violation is a fine. The law creating a violation may impose other penalties in addition to a fine but may not impose a term of imprisonment.
> (2) Except as otherwise provided by law, the maximum fine for a violation committed by an individual is: [...] (d) $250 for a Class D violation.

> 153.019 (1) Except as provided in ORS 153.020, the presumptive fines for violations are: [...] (d) $115 for a Class D violation.

**What it means:** A hitchhiking ticket is a violation, not a crime. The maximum is $250, the usual (presumptive) fine is $115, and you can't be jailed for it.

jurisdictions.title: Washington (US-WA)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. Hitchhiking is legal where a car can safely pull off the main traveled lanes to pick you up. It is illegal anywhere inside the right-of-way of a limited access highway (freeway), unless the highway authority has posted permission.

sections.summary:
Washington's rule (RCW 46.61.255) bans soliciting a ride in two situations:

1. Standing in or beside a public roadway **at a place where a vehicle cannot safely stop off the main traveled portion**.
2. Soliciting a ride **from within the right-of-way of any limited access facility**, unless the state, county or city has given and posted permission at that spot.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Ordinary roads:** pick a spot with a wide shoulder or pull-out where a driver can get completely out of the travel lanes.
- **Freeways (limited access highways), including their ramps:** soliciting a ride inside the right-of-way is prohibited unless permission is posted. WSDOT rules also ban all nonmotorized traffic, including pedestrians, on fully controlled limited access state highways. Stand on the local street before the freeway right-of-way begins.
- **Emergencies:** the rule doesn't stop you from asking for, or a driver from giving, a ride in a real emergency.
- **Statewide rule:** the state preempts local hitchhiking laws, except that a city or county may ban hitchhiking in an area where it has found that prostitution is occurring.
- **Penalty:** a traffic infraction, not a crime.
sections.laws:
### RCW 46.61.255: Pedestrians soliciting rides or business

**Source:** [Washington State Legislature, RCW 46.61.255](https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=46.61.255) (history: 2010 c 8 s 9068; 1989 c 288 s 1; 1972 ex.s. c 38 s 1; 1965 ex.s. c 155 s 38)

> (1) No person shall stand in or on a public roadway or alongside thereof at any place where a motor vehicle cannot safely stop off the main traveled portion thereof for the purpose of soliciting a ride for himself or herself or for another from the occupant of any vehicle.
>
> (2) It shall be unlawful for any person to solicit a ride for himself or herself or another from within the right-of-way of any limited access facility except in such areas where permission to do so is given and posted by the highway authority of the state, county, city, or town having jurisdiction over the highway.
>
> (3) The provisions of subsections (1) and (2) above shall not be construed to prevent a person upon a public highway from soliciting, or a driver of a vehicle from giving a ride where an emergency actually exists, nor to prevent a person from signaling or requesting transportation from a passenger carrier for the purpose of becoming a passenger thereon for hire.

**What it means:** On ordinary roads the test is practical: could a car stop safely off the travel lanes where you're standing? If yes, you're fine. If you're on a narrow road with no shoulder, on a blind curve, or anywhere a driver would have to stop in the lane, you're breaking the law. On freeways the rule is stricter. The whole right-of-way is off-limits for hitching, including the shoulder and, in practice, the ramps. The only exception is a spot where the highway authority has posted permission.

> (6)(a) Except as provided in (b) of this subsection, the state preempts the field of the regulation of hitchhiking in any form, and no county, city, or town shall take any action in conflict with the provisions of this section.
>
> (b) A county, city, or town may regulate or prohibit hitchhiking in an area in which it has determined that prostitution is occurring and that regulating or prohibiting hitchhiking will help to reduce prostitution in the area.

**What it means:** Cities and counties generally can't add their own hitchhiking bans. The one exception lets them ban hitchhiking in specific areas tied to prostitution enforcement, so watch for local signs.

### RCW 46.04.500: "Roadway" defined

**Source:** [Washington State Legislature, RCW 46.04.500](https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=46.04.500) (history: 1977 c 24 s 1; 1961 c 12 s 46.04.500)

> "Roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the sidewalk or shoulder even though such sidewalk or shoulder is used by persons riding bicycles. [...]

**What it means:** The shoulder isn't part of the roadway. Subsection (1) of the hitchhiking rule still reaches people "alongside" the roadway, though, so a shoulder spot is lawful only if a car can safely stop there.

### RCW 47.52.010: "Limited access facility" defined

**Source:** [Washington State Legislature, RCW 47.52.010](https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=47.52.010) (history: 1967 c 108 s 10; 1961 c 13 s 47.52.010)

> For the purposes of this chapter, a "limited access facility" is defined as a highway or street especially designed or designated for through traffic, and over, from, or to which owners or occupants of abutting land, or other persons, have no right or easement, or only a limited right or easement of access, light, air, or view by reason of the fact that their property abuts upon such limited access facility, or for any other reason to accomplish the purpose of a limited access facility. Such highways or streets may be parkways, [...] or they may be freeways open to use by all customary forms of street and highway traffic [...].

**What it means:** Interstates and other freeways are limited access facilities. Some divided highways with only partial access control can be too.

### RCW 46.61.160 and WAC 468-58-050: Pedestrians on limited access highways

**Source:** [Washington State Legislature, RCW 46.61.160](https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=46.61.160) (history: 1982 c 55 s 5; 1975 c 62 s 25; 1965 ex.s. c 155 s 27) and [WAC 468-58-050](https://app.leg.wa.gov/WAC/default.aspx?cite=468-58-050) (WSR 82-01-029, filed 12/14/81; "No agency filings affecting this section since 2003")

RCW 46.61.160:

> The department of transportation may by order, and local authorities may by ordinance or resolution, with respect to any limited access highway under their respective jurisdictions prohibit the use of any such highway by funeral processions, or by parades, pedestrians, bicycles or other nonmotorized traffic, or by any person operating a motor-driven cycle. [...]
>
> The department of transportation or the local authority adopting any such prohibitory regulation shall erect and maintain official traffic control devices on the limited access roadway on which such regulations are applicable, and when so erected no person may disobey the restrictions stated on such devices.

WAC 468-58-050:

> (1) All nonmotorized traffic shall be prohibited on state highways which have been established and constructed as fully controlled limited access facilities, and signs giving notice of such prohibition shall be posted upon all such highways.
>
> (2) This prohibition of nonmotorized traffic on fully controlled limited access highways shall not apply to:
> (a) Pedestrian overcrossings and undercrossings or other facilities provided specifically for the use of such traffic.
> (b) Bicycles utilizing the right-hand shoulders; except where the secretary of transportation or his designee has prohibited such use. [...]

**What it means:** WSDOT's rule keeps pedestrians off every fully controlled limited access state highway, i.e. the freeways. Bicycles may use the shoulder unless signed otherwise, but pedestrians may not. Don't walk along the interstate.

### RCW 46.63.020: Penalty

**Source:** [Washington State Legislature, RCW 46.63.020](https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=46.63.020)

> Failure to perform any act required or the performance of any act prohibited by this title or an equivalent administrative regulation or local law, ordinance, regulation, or resolution relating to traffic including parking, standing, stopping, and pedestrian offenses, is designated as a traffic infraction and may not be classified as a criminal offense, except for an offense contained in the following provisions of this title [...]

**What it means:** Hitchhiking violations are traffic infractions (a ticket and a fine), not crimes. RCW 46.61.255 is not on the list of exceptions. The RCW page notes that the fine amount comes from the court rules' monetary penalty schedule (IRLJ 6.2), which I did not retrieve.
