jurisdictions.title: New Brunswick (CA-NB)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. No one may be on a roadway to solicit a ride (s. 174(3)). New Brunswick's "roadway" excludes the shoulder *unless the shoulder is paved*. That makes an unpaved (gravel) shoulder the safe legal spot. Pedestrians can be barred from controlled-access roadways by order or by-law, with signs posted at each entrance.

sections.summary:
The Motor Vehicle Act follows the Uniform Vehicle Code pattern: "No person shall be on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment or business from an occupant of a vehicle." The New Brunswick twist is in the definition of "roadway". It excludes the shoulder "unless the shoulder is paved". On a highway with a paved shoulder, the shoulder counts as roadway, so standing on it to thumb a ride falls within s. 174(3).

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Don't solicit rides from the roadway**, which includes paved shoulders. Stand off the pavement: on a gravel shoulder, the verge, a sidewalk, or a pull-off or parking area.
- **Controlled-access highways** (for example, the four-lane Trans-Canada, Route 2) can be closed to pedestrians. The closure must be ordered by the authority in charge and signed at each entrance. If you see a "no pedestrians" sign at the ramp, stay off.
- **Use the sidewalk** where there is one. Otherwise walk on the far left of the roadway or shoulder, facing traffic (s. 174(1) and (2)).

Penalty: s. 174(3) is a category B offence under the Provincial Offences Procedure Act. A judge must impose a fine of $140 to $640.
sections.laws:
### Motor Vehicle Act s. 174: Sidewalks; soliciting rides

**Source:** [Government of New Brunswick, Motor Vehicle Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. M-17](https://laws.gnb.ca/en/document/cs/M-17) (page shows "Current to 1 January 2024")

> 174 (1) Where sidewalks are provided it is unlawful for any pedestrian to travel along or upon an adjacent roadway.
>
> 174 (2) Where sidewalks are not provided any pedestrians travelling along or upon a highway shall, when practicable, travel only on the extreme left side of the roadway or its shoulder, not more than two abreast, facing traffic which may approach from the opposite direction and shall give way to the left to traffic approaching on the roadway.
>
> 174 (3) No person shall be on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment or business from an occupant of a vehicle.

**What it means:** Thumbing from the roadway is an offence. Because of the roadway definition below, that includes a paved shoulder. When you walk, stay on the left facing traffic.

### Motor Vehicle Act s. 1: Definitions of "roadway", "highway" and "controlled-access highway"

**Source:** [Government of New Brunswick, Motor Vehicle Act, s. 1](https://laws.gnb.ca/en/document/cs/M-17)

> "roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the shoulder unless the shoulder is paved and in the event a highway includes two or more separate roadways the term "roadway" refers to any such roadway separately but not to all such roadways collectively;
>
> "highway" means the entire width between the boundary lines of every street, road, lane, alley, park, parking lot, drive-in theatre, school yard, picnic site, beach, winter road across ice or place when any part thereof is used by the general public for the passage or parking of vehicles [...]
>
> "controlled-access highway" means a highway
> (a) on to which persons have a right to enter from abutting land, and
> (b) from which persons have a right to enter on to abutting land,
> only at fixed locations;

**What it means:** A paved shoulder is part of the "roadway" in New Brunswick. A gravel or grass shoulder is not. Parking lots count as "highway" here, but s. 174(3) only bites on the roadway.

### Motor Vehicle Act s. 160: Controlled-access roadway, pedestrians

**Source:** [Government of New Brunswick, Motor Vehicle Act, s. 160](https://laws.gnb.ca/en/document/cs/M-17)

> 160 (1) The use of any controlled-access roadway by pedestrians, bicycles, or other non-motorized traffic or by any person operating a motor-driven cycle may be prohibited as follows:
> (a) by local authorities by by-law, with respect to any controlled-access roadway under their jurisdictions;
> (b) by the New Brunswick Highway Corporation by order, with respect to any controlled-access roadway under its administration and control; and
> (c) by the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure by order, with respect to all other roadways, including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, those under the administration and control of a project company.
>
> 160 (2) Notice of such prohibition shall be given by the erection of a traffic control device at each entrance to the controlled-access roadway and no person shall walk or drive on the roadway in disobedience to a prohibition indicated by the traffic control device.
>
> 160 (3) On a prosecution for an offence under subsection (2), evidence that a traffic control device giving notice of the prohibition was at the time of the alleged offence erected at any entrance to the controlled-access roadway is prima facie proof
> (a) of the existence and validity of the order or by-law creating the prohibition, and
> (b) that such a traffic control device was erected at each entrance to such roadway.

**What it means:** Pedestrians are not automatically banned from divided highways. The ban applies where the authority has prohibited them *and* posted signs at the entrances. Look for the sign at the bottom of the ramp. If it is there, hitchhike from before the sign. Section 160(2) is a category C offence (Schedule A), with a fine of $140 to $1,100.

### Motor Vehicle Act s. 347 and Schedule A: Offence categories

**Source:** [Government of New Brunswick, Motor Vehicle Act, s. 347 and Schedule A](https://laws.gnb.ca/en/document/cs/M-17)

> 347 (1) A person who violates or fails to comply with a provision of this Act that is listed in Column I of Schedule A commits an offence.
>
> 347 (2) For the purposes of Part II of the Provincial Offences Procedure Act, each offence listed in Column I of Schedule A is punishable as an offence of the category listed beside it in Column II of Schedule A.
>
> SCHEDULE A [...]
> 160(2) .............. C
> [...]
> 174(1) .............. B
> 174(2) .............. B
> 174(3) .............. B

### Provincial Offences Procedure Act s. 56(2): Category B fine

**Source:** [Government of New Brunswick, Provincial Offences Procedure Act, S.N.B. 1987, c. P-22.1](https://laws.gnb.ca/en/document/cs/P-22.1) (chapter P-22.1, assented to June 27, 1987)

> 56 (2) Where an Act makes an offence punishable as a category B offence, a judge shall impose a fine of not less than $140 and not more than $640.
>
> 56 (3) Where an Act makes an offence punishable as a category C offence, a judge shall impose a fine of not less than $140 and not more than $1,100.

**What it means:** Soliciting a ride from the roadway, or walking on the roadway beside a sidewalk, carries a fine of $140 to $640 on conviction. Walking past a posted "no pedestrians" sign onto a controlled-access roadway (s. 160(2), category C) carries $140 to $1,100.

jurisdictions.title: Newfoundland and Labrador (CA-NL)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. "A person shall not be on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride" (s. 128(3)). The Act's "roadway" excludes the shoulder *unless the shoulder is paved*. An unpaved shoulder or the verge is the lawful place to stand. No provincial statute bans pedestrians from controlled-access highways.

sections.summary:
Newfoundland and Labrador uses the Uniform Vehicle Code-style rule: you may not be on a roadway to solicit a ride, employment or business from a vehicle's occupant. As in New Brunswick and PEI, the definition of "roadway" excludes the shoulder only if the shoulder is unpaved. On stretches of the Trans-Canada with paved shoulders, standing on the shoulder to thumb a ride falls within the rule.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stand off the roadway.** Use a gravel shoulder, the verge, a sidewalk or a pull-off. Do not stand on a paved shoulder or in a lane.
- **Use the sidewalk** if there is a reasonably passable one (s. 128(1)).
- **No sidewalk:** walk on the left side of the roadway or shoulder, facing traffic, no more than 2 abreast (s. 128(2)).
- **Obey traffic-control devices**, including any "no pedestrians" sign (s. 106(1)).

Penalty: a fine of $25 to $180 for soliciting rides on the roadway. In default of payment, the Schedule lists imprisonment of 1 to 6 days.
sections.laws:
### Highway Traffic Act s. 128: Pedestrians to use sidewalks; soliciting rides

**Source:** [House of Assembly of Newfoundland and Labrador, Highway Traffic Act, R.S.N.L. 1990, c. H-3](https://www.assembly.nl.ca/Legislation/sr/statutes/h03.htm) (consolidated statute; amendment list ends "2024 c17; 2024 cN-5.1 s59")

> 128. (1) Where there is a sidewalk that is reasonably passable on either or both sides of a highway, a pedestrian shall not walk on a roadway.
>
> (2) Where there is no sidewalk, a pedestrian walking along or upon a roadway or the shoulder of a highway shall, where practicable walk only on the left side of the roadway or the shoulder of the highway facing traffic approaching from the opposite direction and no more than 2 persons shall walk abreast on the roadway.
>
> (3) A person shall not be on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment or business from the occupant of a vehicle.

**What it means:** Thumbing from the roadway, including a paved shoulder, is an offence. Thumbing from beyond the pavement, or from an unpaved shoulder, is not covered.

### Highway Traffic Act s. 2: Definitions

**Source:** [House of Assembly of Newfoundland and Labrador, Highway Traffic Act, s. 2](https://www.assembly.nl.ca/Legislation/sr/statutes/h03.htm)

> (k) "controlled-access highway" means a highway
> (i) on to which persons have a right to enter from abutting land, and
> (ii) from which persons have a right to enter on to abutting land, only at fixed locations;
>
> (aa) "highway" means a place or way, including a structure forming part of the place or way, designed and intended for, or used by, the public for the passage of traffic or the parking of vehicles and includes all the space between the boundary lines of the place or way;
>
> (jjj) "roadway" means the portion of a highway that is improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular traffic, but does not include the shoulder unless the shoulder is paved, and where a highway includes 2 or more separate roadways the term "roadway" refers to any 1 roadway separately and not to all of the roadways collectively;

**What it means:** A paved shoulder counts as roadway. A gravel shoulder does not.

### Highway Traffic Act ss. 105 and 106: Controlled-access highways; traffic control devices

**Source:** [House of Assembly of Newfoundland and Labrador, Highway Traffic Act, ss. 105 to 106](https://www.assembly.nl.ca/Legislation/sr/statutes/h03.htm)

> 105. (1) Where on a controlled-access highway there is a sign indicating a location at which vehicles are permitted to enter, a driver shall not drive a vehicle onto the highway except at that location.
> (2) Where on a controlled-access highway there is a sign indicating a location at which vehicles are permitted to leave, a driver shall not drive a vehicle from the highway except at that location.
>
> 106. (1) Except when a traffic officer directs otherwise, drivers and pedestrians shall obey the instructions of a traffic-control signal or traffic-control device prescribed by the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure in accordance with this Part.

**What it means:** The controlled-access rule in s. 105 is about where drivers enter and exit. No section of the Act bans pedestrians from those highways. If a sign prohibits pedestrians somewhere, s. 106(1) makes it binding on you.

### Highway Traffic Act s. 208 and Schedule: Penalties

**Source:** [House of Assembly of Newfoundland and Labrador, Highway Traffic Act, s. 208 and Schedule](https://www.assembly.nl.ca/Legislation/sr/statutes/h03.htm)

> 208. (1) Notwithstanding the Provincial Offences Act, unless otherwise provided by this Act or the regulations or regulations made under section 189, a person who has been convicted of an offence under this Act or the regulations or regulations made under section 189 is liable to a fine of not more than the maximum and not less than the minimum amount prescribed for the offence in the Schedule [...] and in default of payment of the fine or, where no fine is prescribed, to imprisonment for a term not exceeding the maximum and not less than the minimum period prescribed for that offence in that Schedule [...]
>
> Schedule, Penalties [fine Max. / Min.; default imprisonment Max. / Min.]
> 128(1) Walking on roadway when sidewalks provided | 180 | 25 | 6 days | 1 day
> 128(2) Walking on wrong side of highway | 180 | 25 | 6 days | 1 day
> 128(3) Standing on roadway to solicit rides, etc. | 180 | 25 | 6 days | 1 day

**What it means:** Soliciting a ride from the roadway carries a fine of $25 to $180. Jail time applies only if you don't pay.

jurisdictions.title: Nova Scotia (CA-NS)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. Under the new Traffic Safety Act (in effect October 19, 2026), "No person shall stand on a main travelled way for the purpose of soliciting a ride." The "main travelled way" excludes paved shoulders, parking areas and bike lanes, so standing on any shoulder to thumb a ride is not covered. A traffic authority can ban pedestrians from a highway by posting a sign.

sections.summary:
Nova Scotia replaced its old Motor Vehicle Act with the Traffic Safety Act (TSA), Chapter 20 of the Acts of 2025, effective October 19, 2026. The hitchhiking rule is now s. 208(3). It applies only to the "main travelled way", a term the Act defines to exclude "a paved shoulder, paved area provided for parking or bicycle lane". This is more hitchhiker-friendly than New Brunswick, PEI or Newfoundland, where a paved shoulder counts as roadway.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stand on the shoulder, never in the travel lanes.** The shoulder (paved or unpaved) is outside the "main travelled way".
- **Don't approach cars on the roadway** to solicit people in them (s. 208(1)). Note the wider word "roadway" there, which *includes* paved shoulders. Stay put and let drivers come to you rather than walking up to stopped cars.
- **Obey "no pedestrians" signs.** Any traffic authority can ban pedestrians from a highway by posting a sign (s. 26). Ignoring the sign is an offence under s. 160. Check the ramps of 100-series highways for such signs.
- **When walking,** use the sidewalk, or if none, the shoulder on the left facing traffic (Using the Road Regulations s. 20(5)).

Penalty: soliciting a ride on the main travelled way (s. 208(3)) is a category A offence with a maximum fine of $100. Being on a highway against a sign or the regulations (s. 160) is category B, maximum $200.
sections.laws:
### Traffic Safety Act s. 208: Selling or soliciting on highway

**Source:** [Nova Scotia Legislature, Traffic Safety Act, Chapter 20 of the Acts of 2025](https://nslegislature.ca/sites/default/files/legc/statutes%20HTML/traffic%20safety.htm) (consolidated electronic version, "amended 2026, c. 3, Sch., ss. 36-39", page created October 19, 2026)

> 208 (1) No person shall stop, attempt to stop or approach a motor vehicle on a roadway for the purpose of offering, selling or providing any good or service to, or soliciting a person in, the motor vehicle.
>
> (2) Subsection (1) does not apply to
> (a) the offer, sale or provision of towing, vehicle removal or repair services or another commodity or service in an emergency situation; or
> (b) a fund-raising activity that is
> (i) permitted by a bylaw of the municipality in which the activity is being conducted, and
> (ii) approved by the traffic authority.
>
> (3) No person shall stand on a main travelled way for the purpose of soliciting a ride.

**What it means:** You may not stand in the lanes that cars drive in to ask for a ride. Standing on the shoulder is outside (3). Subsection (1) is broader: it bans stopping or approaching a car "on a roadway" to solicit the people in it. Don't walk up to cars stopped at lights or in traffic.

### Traffic Safety Act s. 2: Definitions

**Source:** [Nova Scotia Legislature, Traffic Safety Act, s. 2](https://nslegislature.ca/sites/default/files/legc/statutes%20HTML/traffic%20safety.htm)

> "main travelled way" means the part of a roadway that is improved and ordinarily used for vehicular travel and, for greater certainty, does not include a paved shoulder, paved area provided for parking or bicycle lane;
>
> "roadway" means
> (a) the part of a highway between the curbs or, in the absence of curbs, the part of a highway that is improved and ordinarily used by vehicles or bicycles, including any paved shoulder or paved area provided for parking and any bicycle lane; and
> (b) with respect to a highway that is a divided highway and includes two or more separate roadways, any one roadway separately and not all of the roadways collectively;
>
> "shoulder" means the paved or unpaved portion of a highway that is adjacent to, but does not form part of, the main travelled way;

**What it means:** There are two different terms. The "roadway" includes a paved shoulder, but the "main travelled way" does not. The hitchhiking rule in s. 208(3) uses the narrower "main travelled way", so a paved shoulder is fine for thumbing.

### Traffic Safety Act ss. 26, 155 and 160: Prohibiting pedestrians on a highway

**Source:** [Nova Scotia Legislature, Traffic Safety Act](https://nslegislature.ca/sites/default/files/legc/statutes%20HTML/traffic%20safety.htm)

> 26 A traffic authority with jurisdiction over a highway may prohibit the use of the highway by a type of traffic specified by the traffic authority, including pedestrians, individuals driving bicycles and individuals driving slow-moving vehicles or other conveyances, by placing an official traffic sign on the highway that indicates the type of traffic that is prohibited.
>
> 155 Every driver of a vehicle or other conveyance, and every pedestrian, travelling on or otherwise using a highway shall comply with Sections 156 to 214 and the regulations, except when directed to do otherwise by a traffic control device, traffic control person or peace officer.
>
> 160 No pedestrian shall walk on or use a highway or a portion of the highway contrary to the regulations or the direction of a traffic control device, a traffic control person or a peace officer.

**What it means:** No statute bans pedestrians from every controlled-access highway. Instead, a highway is closed to pedestrians where an official sign says so. If you pass a "no pedestrians" sign at a ramp, you are committing an offence under s. 160.

### Using the Road Regulations s. 20(5): Where pedestrians travel

**Source:** [Nova Scotia Royal Gazette Part II, Using the Road Regulations, N.S. Reg. 230/2026 (Schedule "D" of O.I.C. 2026-346), PDF](https://novascotia.ca/just/regulations/regs/2026-230.pdf) (effective on and after October 19, 2026)

> 20 [...]
> (5) Unless it is impracticable, a pedestrian travelling on a highway must travel
> (a) if a sidewalk is present, on the sidewalk;
> (b) if no sidewalk is present, on the shoulder on the left side of the highway facing oncoming traffic; or
> (c) if no sidewalk is present and there is no shoulder on the left side of the highway, on the outside edge of the left side of the roadway facing oncoming traffic.

**What it means:** When walking between spots, use the sidewalk, or else the left shoulder facing traffic. The rule speaks of pedestrians "travelling". It is not clear that it stops you from standing still on the right-hand shoulder to face traffic heading your way.

### Offences, Penalties and Mandatory Suspension Periods Regulations, Schedule B

**Source:** [Nova Scotia Royal Gazette Part II, N.S. Reg. 223/2026 (Schedule "C" of O.I.C. 2026-343), PDF](https://novascotia.ca/just/regulations/regs/2026-223.pdf) (effective on and after October 19, 2026)

> Offence | Section | Offence Category | Maximum Fine
> Pedestrian walking on or using highway contrary to regulations | 160 | B | $200.00
> [...]
> Stopping, attempting to stop or approaching motor vehicle to offer, sell or provide commodity or service to or solicit person in motor vehicle | 208(1) | B | $200.00
> Soliciting ride while on main travelled way | 208(3) | A | $100.00
> [...]
> Pedestrian failing to walk on sidewalk | 20(5)(a) | A | $100.00
> Pedestrian failing to walk on shoulder on [...] | 20(5)(b) | A | $100.00

**What it means:** Thumbing from the travel lane is the lowest class of offence (category A), with a maximum fine of $100. Ignoring a "no pedestrians" sign is category B, with a maximum of $200. The "maximum fine" in these tables is the third-offence amount under the Summary Proceedings Act (Schedule B, s. 1(1)), so a first ticket is usually lower.

### Traffic Safety Act s. 317: General offence

**Source:** [Nova Scotia Legislature, Traffic Safety Act, s. 317](https://nslegislature.ca/sites/default/files/legc/statutes%20HTML/traffic%20safety.htm)

> 317 A person who contravenes a provision of this Act, the regulations or a bylaw made under this Act is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to the penalties prescribed for that offence by the regulations.
sections.history:
### Motor Vehicle Act replaced on October 19, 2026

**Source:** [Province of Nova Scotia, "Traffic Safety Act: legislative changes"](https://novascotia.ca/tsa); [Nova Scotia Legislature, Consolidated Public Statutes](https://nslegislature.ca/legislative-business/bills-statutes/consolidated-public-statutes)

The province states: "The Traffic Safety Act (TSA) passed in the Nova Scotia Legislature in October 2025 and will come into effect on 19 October 2026. [...] The Act will replace the Motor Vehicle Act (MVA), in place since the early 1900s." The Legislature's statute list is "Consolidated to October 19, 2026" and no longer lists the Motor Vehicle Act. The TSA regulations quoted above are each made "effective on and after October 19, 2026". An earlier Traffic Safety Act (S.N.S. 2018, c. 29) was passed but is listed as "not proclaimed in force". The TSA defines "former Act" as "Chapter 293 of the Revised Statutes, 1989, the Motor Vehicle Act".

jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. "No person shall be on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride" (s. 193(3), headed "Soliciting & hitch hiking prohibited"). PEI's "roadway" excludes the shoulder *unless the shoulder is paved*. An unpaved shoulder or the verge is the lawful place to stand. No provincial statute bans pedestrians from any class of highway.

sections.summary:
PEI's Highway Traffic Act has an explicit hitchhiking section, headed "Soliciting & hitch hiking prohibited". It only applies "on a roadway", and the Act defines roadway to exclude the shoulder "unless the shoulder is paved". On highways with paved shoulders, the paved shoulder counts as roadway.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stand off the roadway.** Use a gravel shoulder, the grass verge, a sidewalk or a pull-off. Do not stand on a paved shoulder or in a lane.
- **Use the sidewalk** where one is reasonably passable (s. 193(1)).
- **No sidewalk:** walk on the left side of the roadway or shoulder, facing traffic, no more than two abreast (s. 193(2)).
- **No freeway ban.** The Act has a driver rule for entering and leaving controlled-access highways (s. 165), but no pedestrian prohibition. Traffic authorities may still make by-laws on "pedestrian traffic" (s. 310(1)(c)).

Penalty: a fine of $100 to $500 for soliciting rides on the roadway (Schedule, item 193(3)).

### Highway Traffic Act s. 193: Pedestrians to use sidewalks; soliciting and hitch hiking

**Source:** [Government of Prince Edward Island, Highway Traffic Act, R.S.P.E.I. 1988, c. H-5 (office consolidation, PDF)](https://www.princeedwardisland.ca/sites/default/files/legislation/h-05-highway_traffic_act.pdf) (current to May 29, 2026)

> 193. Pedestrians to use sidewalks
> (1) Where there is a sidewalk that is reasonably passable on either or both sides of a highway, a pedestrian shall not walk on a roadway.
>
> Pedestrians on roadway, general rules
> (2) Where there is no sidewalk, a pedestrian walking along or upon a roadway or the shoulder thereof shall when practicable walk only on the left side of the roadway or the shoulder of the highway facing traffic approaching from the opposite direction and no more than two persons shall walk abreast on the roadway.
>
> Soliciting & hitch hiking prohibited
> (3) No person shall be on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting a ride, employment or business from the occupant of a vehicle. R.S.P.E.I. 1974, Cap. H-6, s.178.

**What it means:** Thumbing while standing on the roadway is an offence. The roadway definition below decides whether the shoulder counts. When walking, keep left and face traffic.

### Highway Traffic Act s. 1: Definitions

**Source:** [Government of Prince Edward Island, Highway Traffic Act, s. 1](https://www.princeedwardisland.ca/sites/default/files/legislation/h-05-highway_traffic_act.pdf)

> (c) "controlled access highway" means a highway
> (i) on to which persons have a right to enter from abutting land, and
> (ii) from which persons have a right to enter onto abutting land,
> only at fixed locations;
>
> (h.1) "highway" means the entire width between the boundary lines of every road, street, lane, alley, or right-of-way designed or intended for or used by the general public for the passage of vehicles, and includes any bridges over which every such road, street, lane, alley, or right-of-way is laid, and every private place or passage way to which the public, for the purpose of the parking or servicing of vehicles, has access or is invited;
>
> (q.3) "roadway" means that portion of a highway improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular travel, exclusive of the shoulder unless the shoulder is paved, and where a highway includes two or more separate roadways the term "roadway" refers to any one roadway separately and not to all of the roadways collectively;

**What it means:** On PEI a paved shoulder is part of the roadway, so s. 193(3) applies there. A gravel shoulder is not. Gas-station forecourts and parking areas open to the public count as "highway", but not as "roadway".

### Highway Traffic Act s. 310: Traffic authority by-laws

**Source:** [Government of Prince Edward Island, Highway Traffic Act, s. 310](https://www.princeedwardisland.ca/sites/default/files/legislation/h-05-highway_traffic_act.pdf)

> 310. Traffic authority may make certain bylaws
> (1) A traffic authority may make bylaws or regulations not inconsistent with this Act respecting
> (a) parking of vehicles;
> (b) one way streets;
> (c) pedestrian traffic;
> [...]

**What it means:** Charlottetown, Summerside and other traffic authorities can add pedestrian rules, which were not reviewed here.

### Highway Traffic Act s. 300 and Schedule: Penalties

**Source:** [Government of Prince Edward Island, Highway Traffic Act, s. 300 and Schedule](https://www.princeedwardisland.ca/sites/default/files/legislation/h-05-highway_traffic_act.pdf)

> 300. Application of penalties in Schedule
> (1) Unless otherwise provided by this Act, any person convicted of an offence against this Act shall be adjudged to pay a fine of an amount not more than the maximum nor less than the minimum amount prescribed for that offence in the Schedule and in the Schedule appearing opposite the number or letter or both of the section, subsection or clause and the statement of the offence.
>
> SCHEDULE [...] PENALTIES
> H T ACT Reference | OFFENCE | Minimum | Maximum
> 193(1) | Walking on roadway when sidewalk provided | 100 | 500
> 193(2) | Walking on wrong side of road | 100 | 500
> 193(3) | Standing on roadway to solicit rides, etc. | 100 | 500

**What it means:** Hitchhiking from the roadway carries a fine of $100 to $500.

jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not solicit a ride while standing on the roadway. Ontario's definition of "roadway" excludes the shoulder, so thumbing from the shoulder or curb is not covered by s. 177(1). sections.summary:
Ontario has a specific hitchhiking rule. Highway Traffic Act (HTA) s. 177(1) says no person "while on the roadway" shall solicit a ride from a driver, except from a public passenger vehicle such as a bus or taxi. The HTA defines "roadway" as the part of the highway used for vehicles, and the definition expressly says it "does not include the shoulder".

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stay off the roadway.** Stand on the shoulder, the curb or the sidewalk, never in a travel lane.
- **Stay off the controlled-access highways listed in R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 627.** These include all of Highways 400 (except one short stretch in Barrie), 401, 402, 403, 404, 405, 406, 407, 407 East, 409, 410, 412, 416, 417, 418 and 427, the QEW, and listed sections of other King's Highways. Hitchhike from the on-ramp approach on the local road, before the controlled-access section begins.
- **Walk facing traffic** on the left side when there is no sidewalk (s. 179).
- **Municipalities can ban pedestrians** on highways under their jurisdiction by by-law (s. 185(2)).

Penalty: s. 177(1) has no penalty of its own, so the general penalty in s. 214(1) applies: a fine of $60 to $1,000. Using a controlled-access highway contrary to Reg. 627 falls under the same general penalty.
sections.laws:
### Highway Traffic Act s. 177: Soliciting rides or business from drivers

**Source:** [Ontario e-Laws, Highway Traffic Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.8, s. 177](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h08) (consolidation period from July 1, 2026; last amendment 2026, c. 7, Sched. 5)

> 177 (1) No person, while on the roadway, shall solicit a ride from the driver of a motor vehicle other than a public passenger conveyance.
>
> (2) No person, while on the roadway, shall stop, attempt to stop or approach a motor vehicle for the purpose of offering, selling or providing any commodity or service to the driver or any other person in the motor vehicle.
>
> [...]
>
> (4) Every person who contravenes subsection (2) is guilty of an offence and is liable,
> (a) on a first conviction, to a fine of not more than $500; and
> (b) on each subsequent conviction, to a fine of not more than $1,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than six months, or to both.

**What it means:** Asking for a ride while you stand in the roadway is an offence. Asking from the shoulder or the sidewalk is not covered by this subsection. The tougher penalty in (4) applies only to selling or offering services to drivers under (2), not to soliciting a ride under (1).

### Highway Traffic Act s. 1(1): Definitions of "highway" and "roadway"

**Source:** [Ontario e-Laws, Highway Traffic Act, s. 1(1)](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h08)

> "highway" includes a common and public highway, street, avenue, parkway, driveway, square, place, bridge, viaduct or trestle, any part of which is intended for or used by the general public for the passage of vehicles and includes the area between the lateral property lines thereof;
>
> "roadway" means the part of the highway that is improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular traffic, but does not include the shoulder, and, where a highway includes two or more separate roadways, the term "roadway" refers to any one roadway separately and not to all of the roadways collectively;

**What it means:** The shoulder is part of the "highway" but not part of the "roadway". Section 177(1) only applies on the roadway, so the shoulder is the legal place to stand, as long as the highway itself is not closed to pedestrians.

### Highway Traffic Act s. 179: Duties of pedestrian when walking along highway

**Source:** [Ontario e-Laws, Highway Traffic Act, s. 179](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h08)

> 179 (1) Where sidewalks are not provided on a highway, a pedestrian walking along the highway shall walk on the left side thereof facing oncoming traffic and, when walking along the roadway, shall walk as close to the left edge thereof as possible.

**What it means:** When you walk between spots and there is no sidewalk, walk on the left, facing oncoming cars.

### Highway Traffic Act s. 185: Regulating or prohibiting use of highway by pedestrians

**Source:** [Ontario e-Laws, Highway Traffic Act, s. 185](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h08)

> 185 (1) The Minister may make regulations prohibiting or regulating the use of any highway or part thereof by pedestrians or animals or any class or classes of vehicles.
>
> (2) The council of a municipality may by by-law prohibit pedestrians or the use of motor assisted bicycles, bicycles, wheelchairs or animals on any highway or portion of a highway under its jurisdiction.
>
> (3) Where a pedestrian is on a highway in contravention of a regulation made or by-law passed under this section, a police officer may require the pedestrian to accompany him or her to the nearest intersecting highway on which pedestrians are not prohibited and the pedestrian shall comply with the request.

**What it means:** The province bans pedestrians from specific highways by regulation (Reg. 627, below), and cities can ban them from their own roads by by-law. If you are on one of those roads, police can walk you to the nearest road where pedestrians are allowed.

### R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 627: Use of Controlled-Access Highways by Pedestrians

**Source:** [Ontario e-Laws, R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 627](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900627) (consolidation period from December 15, 2021; last amendment O. Reg. 827/21)

> 1. (1) Subject to subsection (2), pedestrians are prohibited from using those parts of the controlled-access highways described in Schedule 1.
>
> (2) Subsection (1) does not apply to pedestrians,
> (a) engaged in police, highway maintenance, highway construction or vehicle inspection duties;
> (b) within commuter parking lots established and maintained by the Ministry or proceeding directly between such lots and adjacent intersecting highways;
> (c) within truck inspection stations or pulp load check areas established and maintained by the Ministry;
> (d) making use of a controlled-access highway where the use is necessary because of an emergency; or
> (e) crossing at a traffic control signal or a crosswalk.
>
> [...]
>
> SCHEDULE 1
> 1. All of the King's Highways known as Nos. 401, 402, 403, 404, 405, 406, 409, 410, 412, 416, 417, 418 and 427 and the Queen Elizabeth Way.
> 1.1 All of the King's Highway known as Highway 407 East.
> 1.2 All of the private toll highway known as Highway 407.
> 2. All of the King's Highway known as No. 400, except for that part of King's Highway No. 400 known as Rose Street in the City of Barrie [...]
> [...]

**What it means:** No walking or standing on the 400-series highways, the QEW, the 407 or the other listed sections, including their shoulders. Schedule 1 also lists sections of Highways 3, 6, 7, 8, 11, 17, 26, 35, 58, 61, 69, 85, 115, 137 and others, so check the full schedule for your route. There is a useful exception in (2)(b): you may be inside a Ministry commuter parking lot (carpool lot) and walk directly between it and the crossroad. Carpool lots near interchanges are lawful places to look for rides.

### Highway Traffic Act s. 214: General penalty

**Source:** [Ontario e-Laws, Highway Traffic Act, s. 214](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h08)

> 214 (1) Every person who contravenes this Act or any regulation is guilty of an offence and on conviction, where a penalty for the contravention is not otherwise provided for herein, is liable to a fine of not less than $60 and not more than $1,000.

**What it means:** Soliciting a ride from the roadway, or walking on a highway listed in Reg. 627, can bring a fine of $60 to $1,000. It is a provincial offence, not a criminal one.
sections.notable-local-rules:
### Safe Streets Act, 1999, s. 3(2): Solicitation of captive audience

**Source:** [Ontario e-Laws, Safe Streets Act, 1999, S.O. 1999, c. 8](https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/99s08) (consolidation period from December 15, 2005)

> "solicit" means to request, in person, the immediate provision of money or another thing of value, regardless of whether consideration is offered or provided in return, using the spoken, written or printed word, a gesture or other means.
>
> 3 (2) No person shall,
> [...]
> (e) solicit a person who is in the process of getting in, out of, on or off a vehicle or who is in a parking lot; or
> (f) while on a roadway, solicit a person who is in or on a stopped, standing or parked vehicle.

**What it means:** This province-wide Act is aimed at panhandling. It is not a local by-law, but it matters most in cities. It bans asking people for money "or another thing of value" in parking lots or at stopped cars. Whether a free ride counts as a "thing of value" has not been confirmed here (see below). Avoid going car to car in parking lots or at red lights. Fines are up to $500 for a first conviction (s. 5(1)).

sections.summary:
Quebec's rules of the road are in the *Code de la sécurité routière* (official English title: *Highway Safety Code*, CQLR c. C-24.2). Both the official LégisQuébec site and CanLII refused connections from this research environment (HTTP 403), so no article of the Code is quoted here. The rules below come from the Société de l'assurance automobile du Québec (SAAQ). The SAAQ is the provincial government agency that administers the Code, and its summary is official guidance, not the law itself.

What applies to hitchhikers, per the SAAQ:

- **Don't hitchhike on the roadway.** Standing off the roadway (on the shoulder or sidewalk) is not covered by the rule the SAAQ describes.
- **Don't hitchhike where passing is prohibited**, for example where there is a solid centre line or a no-passing sign. This is a Quebec-specific rule. It applies even if you are off the roadway, so pick a spot where passing is allowed.
- **Don't walk on autoroutes or their access ramps.** Hitchhike from the local road before the ramp begins, or from a service area or park-and-ride lot.
- **Use the sidewalk.** Where there isn't one, walk along the side of the roadway or on the shoulder, against traffic, unless walking with traffic is safer.

Penalty (per the SAAQ): "Pedestrians who don't obey the rules laid out in the Highway Safety Code face a fine of $15 to $30."
sections.laws:
### SAAQ summary of the Highway Safety Code for pedestrians (official guidance, not statute text)

**Source:** [Société de l'assurance automobile du Québec, "As a pedestrian: What the law says"](https://saaq.gouv.qc.ca/en/road-safety/modes-transportation/as-pedestrian/what-the-law-says) (retrieved 2026-11-02)

> According to the Highway Safety Code, pedestrians must: use the sidewalk bordering the roadway. If there is no sidewalk, pedestrians can walk along the side of the roadway or on the shoulder, against traffic. However, they may walk with the flow of traffic if that option is safer (for example, if the road is better lit or the shoulder is wider) [...]
>
> According to the Highway Safety Code, pedestrians must not: [...] hitchhike on the roadway or in an area where passing is prohibited [...] walk on highways or access ramps
>
> [...]
>
> Pedestrians who don't obey the rules laid out in the Highway Safety Code face a fine of $15 to $30.

**What it means:** Hitchhiking is legal in Quebec if you stand off the roadway, at a place where passing is allowed, and not on an autoroute or its ramps. A shoulder on an ordinary two-lane highway, at a stretch with a broken centre line, fits the SAAQ's description of a lawful spot. The fine for breaking these pedestrian rules is small: $15 to $30, according to the SAAQ.

sections.summary:
I searched the current consolidations of the Traffic Safety Act and its Rules of the Road regulation for "solicit", "hitch" and "ride" and found no provincial hitchhiking rule. Hitchhiking is governed only by the general pedestrian rules in Part 3 of the regulation.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Where there's a sidewalk or path beside the road**, you must use it and must not "proceed along or remain on the roadway" (s. 90(1)).
- **Where there isn't one**, walk on the left side of the roadway or the shoulder, facing traffic (s. 90(2)).
- **Crossing:** don't stop or loiter while crossing, and don't step into the path of a close vehicle (s. 91).
- **Freeways:** I found no provincial statute or regulation that bans pedestrians from freeways. Posted traffic control devices and local bylaws may do so, so obey any "no pedestrians" signs.
- **Municipal and park rules can be stricter.** Check local bylaws in cities and towns, including the townsite of Jasper.

A violation of the regulation carries the fine set under the Provincial Offences Procedure Act (TSA s. 158).
sections.laws:
### Use of Highway and Rules of the Road Regulation s. 90: Pedestrians on roadway

**Source:** [Alberta King's Printer, Alta. Reg. 304/2002](https://kings-printer.alberta.ca/documents/Regs/2002_304.pdf) (office consolidation with amendments up to Alta. Reg. 167/2025, current as of August 8, 2025)

> 90(1) When a sidewalk or path is located beside a roadway, a pedestrian
> (a) shall at all times when it is reasonable and practicable to do so use the sidewalk or path, and
> (b) shall not proceed along or remain on the roadway.
>
> (2) If there is no sidewalk or path, a pedestrian who is proceeding along or on a highway shall at all times when reasonable and practicable to do so, proceed only on the left side of the roadway or the shoulder of the highway facing traffic approaching from the opposite direction.

**What it means:** In town, where there's a sidewalk, don't stand in the street to thumb. Use the sidewalk or a pull-out. On rural highways without a sidewalk, the shoulder is fine. No rule says which side of the road you must stand on while waiting for a ride, but walk facing traffic.

### Use of Highway and Rules of the Road Regulation s. 91: Pedestrians crossing roadway

**Source:** [Alberta King's Printer, Alta. Reg. 304/2002](https://kings-printer.alberta.ca/documents/Regs/2002_304.pdf) (consolidation current as of August 8, 2025)

> 91(1) A pedestrian who is crossing a roadway
> (a) shall cross as quickly as is reasonable, and
> (b) shall not stop or loiter while crossing the highway or otherwise impede the free movement of vehicles on the highway.
>
> (2) A pedestrian shall not proceed onto a roadway or proceed along a roadway into the path of any vehicle that is so close that it is impracticable for the driver of the vehicle to yield the right of way.

**What it means:** Don't stand in the lane or step out toward a car to flag it down.

### Traffic Safety Act s. 1(1): Definitions of "highway" and "roadway"

**Source:** [Alberta King's Printer, Traffic Safety Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. T-6](https://kings-printer.alberta.ca/documents/Acts/T06.pdf) (office consolidation current as of July 2, 2026)

> (p) "highway" means any thoroughfare, street, road, trail, avenue, parkway, driveway, viaduct, lane, alley, square, bridge, causeway, trestleway or other place or any part of any of them, whether publicly or privately owned, that the public is ordinarily entitled or permitted to use for the passage or parking of vehicles and includes
> (i) a sidewalk, including a boulevard adjacent to the sidewalk,
> (ii) if a ditch lies adjacent to and parallel with the roadway, the ditch, and
> (iii) if a highway right of way is contained between fences or between a fence and one side of the roadway, all the land between the fences, or all the land between the fence and the edge of the roadway, as the case may be,
> but does not include a place declared by regulation not to be a highway;
>
> [...]
>
> (nn) "roadway" means that part of a highway intended for use by vehicular traffic;

**What it means:** The "roadway" is the part used by vehicles. The "highway" takes in the sidewalk, the ditch and everything up to the fence line. Since Alberta has no ban on soliciting rides, these definitions matter mainly for s. 90: keep off the roadway where a sidewalk or path exists.

### Traffic Safety Act s. 111: Observance of Rules of the Road

**Source:** [Alberta King's Printer, Traffic Safety Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. T-6](https://kings-printer.alberta.ca/documents/Acts/T06.pdf) (consolidation current as of July 2, 2026)

> 111 A driver of a vehicle and any other person using a highway shall, insofar as applicable, obey the Rules of the Road, except when otherwise
> (a) instructed by any applicable traffic control device, or
> (b) directed by a peace officer.

**What it means:** The pedestrian rules bind you as "any other person using a highway". If a peace officer tells you to move, do it.

### Traffic Safety Act s. 158: Punishment

**Source:** [Alberta King's Printer, Traffic Safety Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. T-6](https://kings-printer.alberta.ca/documents/Acts/T06.pdf) (consolidation current as of July 2, 2026)

> 158(1) Except as otherwise provided in this Act, a person who is guilty of an offence under this Act for which a penalty is not otherwise provided is liable to a fine or other punishment as provided for under the Provincial Offences Procedure Act.

**What it means:** A pedestrian-rule ticket is a provincial offence fine, not a criminal matter.

jurisdictions.title: Manitoba (CA-MB)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Legal. The current Highway Traffic Act contains no provision on soliciting rides or hitchhiking. The ordinary pedestrian rules apply: use the sidewalk where one is reasonably passable, otherwise keep to the left edge of the roadway or shoulder.

sections.summary:
A search of the full current consolidation of The Highway Traffic Act (current as of October 28, 2026) found no section on soliciting rides, hitchhiking, or soliciting from vehicle occupants. The Act has no statewide ban on pedestrians on limited-access highways either. Section 194 only governs where *drivers* enter and leave them. The province's transportation department says on its website that walking on provincial highways is legal, though not recommended.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Use the sidewalk** if there is a reasonably passable one (s. 143(1)).
- **No sidewalk:** walk as close as practicable to the left-hand edge of the roadway or shoulder, no more than two abreast (s. 143(2)).
- **Obey signs.** Every person must obey traffic control devices (s. 85). Traffic authorities (the minister for provincial highways, municipalities for local roads) can make rules on pedestrian traffic (s. 90(1)(e)). A posted "no pedestrians" sign is binding.
- **Use caution** entering or walking along any highway (s. 75).

Penalty: there is no specific hitchhiking offence. A breach of the pedestrian rules is an offence under the general penalty in s. 239(1), with a fine of up to $2,000.
sections.laws:
### The Highway Traffic Act s. 143: Use of sidewalks required; keeping left

**Source:** [Manitoba Laws, The Highway Traffic Act, C.C.S.M. c. H60](https://web2.gov.mb.ca/laws/statutes/ccsm/h060.php) (unofficial version, current as of October 28, 2026, in effect since June 1, 2026)

> 143(1) Where there is a sidewalk that is reasonably passable on either or both sides of a highway, a pedestrian shall not walk on a roadway.
>
> 143(2) Any pedestrian proceeding along a highway where no sidewalk is provided or where the sidewalk is not passable, shall walk as closely as is practicable to
> (a) the left-hand edge of the roadway or of the shoulder, as the case may be; or
> (b) any person who may be walking on the pedestrian's left side;
> but persons walking on a roadway shall not walk more than two abreast.

**What it means:** When you are walking, stay on the left facing traffic. The Act does not forbid standing still on a shoulder to thumb a ride.

### The Highway Traffic Act s. 1(1): Definitions of "highway" and "roadway"

**Source:** [Manitoba Laws, The Highway Traffic Act, s. 1(1)](https://web2.gov.mb.ca/laws/statutes/ccsm/h060.php)

> "highway" means any place or way, including any structure forming part thereof, which or any part of which the public is ordinarily entitled or permitted to use for the passage of vehicles, with or without fee or charge therefor, and includes all the space between the boundary lines thereof; but does not include any area designed or intended, and primarily used, for the parking of vehicles and the necessary passageways thereon;
>
> "roadway" means the portion of a highway that is improved, designed, or ordinarily used for vehicular traffic, and includes that portion thereof that, but for the presence of a safety zone, would be ordinarily so used, but does not include the shoulder; [...]

**What it means:** The shoulder is not part of the roadway. Standing on the shoulder keeps you out of vehicle traffic.

### The Highway Traffic Act ss. 75 and 85: Due care; obey traffic control devices

**Source:** [Manitoba Laws, The Highway Traffic Act](https://web2.gov.mb.ca/laws/statutes/ccsm/h060.php)

> 75 A pedestrian or the operator of a bicycle or power-assisted bicycle who is entering, crossing or proceeding along a highway shall, at all times, do so with due caution, care and attention, taking into account the traffic on the highway at the time.
>
> 85 Except when otherwise directed by a peace officer, every person shall obey the instructions or directions on, or conveyed by means of, an applicable traffic control device.

**What it means:** Use common sense near traffic. If a sign bans pedestrians on a stretch of road, it applies to you.

### The Highway Traffic Act s. 90(1): Traffic authority rules

**Source:** [Manitoba Laws, The Highway Traffic Act](https://web2.gov.mb.ca/laws/statutes/ccsm/h060.php)

> 90(1) A traffic authority may classify vehicles [...] and may make rules or by-laws supplementary to, or in addition to, but not contrary to, any provision of this Act, The Drivers and Vehicles Act or the regulations under either Act and applicable on highways over which the traffic authority has jurisdiction or within any area over which the traffic authority has jurisdiction, with respect to
> [...]
> (d) prescribing routes of travel, including prohibiting certain traffic from travelling on certain routes of travel or requiring certain traffic to travel only on certain routes of travel;
> (e) pedestrian traffic including pedestrian corridors;

**What it means:** The province (on provincial highways) and municipalities (on city streets) can add local pedestrian rules. "Traffic" includes pedestrians under s. 1(1). No such rule banning pedestrians or hitchhikers was found, but check signs and city by-laws, for example in Winnipeg.

### The Highway Traffic Act s. 239(1): General offences and penalties

**Source:** [Manitoba Laws, The Highway Traffic Act](https://web2.gov.mb.ca/laws/statutes/ccsm/h060.php)

> 239(1) A person who contravenes or fails to comply with or obey
> (a) a provision of this Act or the regulations;
> (b) a municipal by-law passed under the authority of this Act or the regulations; or
> (c) an order, direction or requirement of a peace officer, a traffic authority or another authority or person
> (i) given under the authority of this Act or the regulations, or
> (ii) indicated or conveyed by a traffic control device;
> is guilty of an offence and, except where another penalty is provided in this Act, is liable on summary conviction to a fine of not more than $2,000.

**What it means:** Breaking a pedestrian rule (such as walking on the roadway beside a usable sidewalk) is a provincial offence with a maximum $2,000 fine. Ticket amounts are usually far lower.

jurisdictions.title: Saskatchewan (CA-SK)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Legal. The Traffic Safety Act contains no rule on soliciting rides or hitchhiking, and no provincial ban on pedestrians on controlled-access highways. When walking along the travelled part of a highway, keep close to the left edge.

sections.summary:
A full-text search of the consolidated Traffic Safety Act (amended through S.S. 2024, c. 4) found no section on soliciting rides, hitchhiking, or soliciting from vehicle occupants. The only controlled-access rule (s. 226) tells *drivers* where they may enter and leave. Pedestrian rules in the Act cover right of way at crosswalks and stepping into traffic (s. 223), plus the duty to walk near the left edge of the travelled portion (s. 223(5)).

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Walk near the left edge** of the part of the highway used by vehicles, facing traffic (s. 223(5)).
- **Don't step into the path of a vehicle** that is too close to yield (s. 223(3)).
- **Pick a spot where cars can pull fully off the road.** The Act does not forbid standing on a shoulder or at an on-ramp to ask for a ride.
- **Check city by-laws.** Regina, Saskatoon and other municipalities have their own traffic by-laws, which were not reviewed here.

Penalty: there is no hitchhiking offence. A breach of the pedestrian rules falls under the general penalty in s. 275, with a fine of up to $1,000 for an individual.
sections.laws:
### The Traffic Safety Act s. 223: Rules re pedestrians

**Source:** [Publications Saskatchewan, The Traffic Safety Act, S.S. 2004, c. T-18.1 (consolidated PDF)](https://publications.saskatchewan.ca/api/v1/products/12208/formats/18166/download) (unofficial consolidation, amended through S.S. 2024, c. 4)

> 223(1) A driver of a vehicle on a highway within a hamlet or any municipality other than a rural municipality or the prescribed part of a municipal district shall stop the vehicle and yield the right of way to the pedestrian if:
> (a) the driver of the vehicle approaches an intersection or clearly marked pedestrian crosswalk where a peace officer is not on duty and traffic lights are not in operation; and
> (b) the pedestrian is crossing the highway.
>
> [...]
>
> (3) No pedestrian shall leave a curb or other place of safety and proceed into the path of a vehicle on a highway that is so close that it is impracticable for the driver to yield the right of way.
>
> (4) Nothing in this section relieves the driver of a vehicle from the duty to exercise due care for the safety of pedestrians.
>
> (5) No person, other than a pedestrian in charge of an animal, shall walk along that portion of a highway used for vehicular traffic, except close to the edge on his or her left.

**What it means:** If you are walking on the road surface itself, stay close to the left edge, facing oncoming cars. Never step out in front of a car that can't stop. The section does not regulate standing on the shoulder.

### The Traffic Safety Act s. 2: Definitions of "highway" and "pedestrian"

**Source:** [Publications Saskatchewan, The Traffic Safety Act, s. 2](https://publications.saskatchewan.ca/api/v1/products/12208/formats/18166/download)

> (k) "highway" means a road, parkway, driveway, square or place designed and intended for or used by the general public for the passage of vehicles, but does not include any area, whether privately or publicly owned, that is primarily intended to be used for the parking of vehicles and the necessary passageways on that area;
>
> (aa) "pedestrian" means:
> (i) a person on foot; or
> (ii) a person in or on a mobility aid;

**What it means:** The Act does not define "roadway" or "shoulder". Section 223(5) instead speaks of "that portion of a highway used for vehicular traffic". A gravel or paved shoulder that is not used for traffic is arguably outside that phrase.

### The Traffic Safety Act s. 226: Rules re controlled access highways

**Source:** [Publications Saskatchewan, The Traffic Safety Act, s. 226](https://publications.saskatchewan.ca/api/v1/products/12208/formats/18166/download)

> 226 No driver of a vehicle shall enter or leave a controlled access highway except at a place where signs indicate that vehicles may do so.

**What it means:** This applies to drivers only. No provincial statute found here bans pedestrians from controlled-access highways. Stopping on a high-speed highway is still dangerous, so stand where a driver can pull over safely, such as an on-ramp approach, a service road or a gas station.

### The Traffic Safety Act s. 275: General offence and penalty

**Source:** [Publications Saskatchewan, The Traffic Safety Act, s. 275](https://publications.saskatchewan.ca/api/v1/products/12208/formats/18166/download)

> 275 Any person who contravenes any provision of this Act or the regulations for which no other penalty is specifically provided, or who disobeys an order of the board, is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction:
> (a) in the case of an individual, to a fine of not more than $1,000; and
> (b) in the case of a corporation, to a fine of not more than $2,000.

**What it means:** Walking the wrong way along the road, or stepping into traffic, can bring a fine of up to $1,000.

jurisdictions.title: British Columbia (CA-BC)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Restricted. You may not be on the **roadway** to solicit a ride (Motor Vehicle Act s. 182(3)). The roadway excludes the shoulder, so thumbing from the shoulder is lawful under this section. Pedestrians are banned outright on the "Schedule 1" freeways, such as parts of Highway 1, the Coquihalla and Highway 99.

sections.summary:
BC follows the common "not in the roadway" model. The Motor Vehicle Act defines "roadway" as the part of the highway used for vehicles, "but does not include the shoulder". So hitchhiking from the shoulder or curb is not an offence under s. 182, and soliciting a ride in an emergency is expressly exempt.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Stay off the roadway** while thumbing. Stand on the shoulder, or on the sidewalk where there is one.
- **Schedule 1 highways are off-limits to pedestrians** except at intersection crossings or when attending a disabled vehicle (B.C. Reg. 26/58 s. 19.07). The listed sections include Highway 1 from Horseshoe Bay to the Second Narrows Bridge and from Rupert Street to Hope, Coquihalla Highway 5, Highway 99 from 1st Avenue in Surrey to the Oak Street Bridge, Highway 97C, and the Inland Island Highway. On those, wait before the on-ramp.
- **Where there's no sidewalk**, walk on the extreme left side of the roadway or the shoulder, facing traffic.
- **Municipalities have their own bylaws.** Check local rules in cities.

The Act sets no specific penalty for s. 182. The general penalty in the Offence Act is a fine of up to $2,000 or up to 6 months in jail, or both. I found no fixed ticket fine for s. 182 in the fines schedule (see open questions).

### Motor Vehicle Act s. 182: Pedestrians using highways

**Source:** [BC Laws, Motor Vehicle Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 318, Part 3](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96318_05) (official consolidation, current to October 27, 2026)

> (1) If there is a sidewalk that is reasonably passable on either or both sides of a highway, a pedestrian must not use a roadway.
>
> (2) If there is no sidewalk, a pedestrian using a highway must use only the extreme left side of the roadway or the shoulder of the highway, facing traffic approaching from the opposite direction.
>
> (3) A person must not be on a roadway to solicit a ride, employment or business from an occupant of a vehicle.
>
> (4) Except for a person who solicits a ride in an emergency situation, a person who contravenes this section commits an offence.

**What it means:** It is an offence to be in the travel lanes while asking for a ride. Standing on the shoulder or the sidewalk is not covered by s. 182(3). Subsection (4) means a genuine emergency, such as a breakdown or an injury, is a defence to soliciting a ride.

### Motor Vehicle Act s. 119 and s. 1: Definitions of "roadway" and "highway"

**Source:** [BC Laws, Motor Vehicle Act, s. 119 (Part 3 definitions)](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96318_05) and [s. 1 (general definitions)](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96318_01) (official consolidation)

> **s. 119:** "roadway" means the portion of the highway that is improved, designed or ordinarily used for vehicular traffic, but does not include the shoulder, and if a highway includes 2 or more separate roadways, the term "roadway" refers to any one roadway separately and not to all of them collectively;
>
> **s. 1:** "highway" includes (a) every highway within the meaning of the Transportation Act, (b) every road, street, lane or right of way designed or intended for or used by the general public for the passage of vehicles, and (c) every private place or passageway to which the public, for the purpose of the parking or servicing of vehicles, has access or is invited, but does not include an industrial road;

**What it means:** The shoulder is expressly excluded from the "roadway", so the s. 182(3) ban stops at the white line. The "highway" is broader, but s. 182(3) doesn't use that word.

### Motor Vehicle Act Regulations s. 19.07: Schedule 1 highways restrictions

**Source:** [BC Laws, Motor Vehicle Act Regulations, B.C. Reg. 26/58, Division 19](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/26_58_06) (official consolidation)

> (1) Except as authorized by a permit issued by the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure, and except for crossing a highway at an intersection, use of any highway named in Schedule 1 by the following is prohibited at all times:
> [...]
> (d) pedestrians, unless attending a disabled vehicle;
> [...]
>
> (2) Subsection (1) does not apply to pedestrians and to operators of pedal cycles and limited speed motorcycles using footpaths constructed adjacent to the travel portion of the highway or the shoulder on the travel portion of the highway where the minister causes signs to be erected designating the footpath or shoulder for such permitted use.

> **Schedule 1 — Highways**
> (1) Trans-Canada Highway #1 — from the ferry terminal at Horseshoe Bay to the north approach to the Ironworkers Memorial Second Narrows Bridge; from its intersection with Rupert Street to its junction with Route #3 in Hope; from its junction with the Coquihalla Highway (Afton Interchange) on the west approach to Kamloops to its junction with the Yellowhead Highway on the east approach to Kamloops.
> (2) Hope-Princeton Highway #3 — from its junction with the Trans-Canada Highway in Hope to its junction with the Coquihalla Highway, 7.7 km east.
> (3) Coquihalla Highway #5 — from its junction with the Hope-Princeton Highway, 7.7 km east of Hope to its junction with the Trans-Canada Highway (Afton Interchange) on the west approach to Kamloops.
> (4) Annacis Highway #91 — [...]
> (5) Annacis Highway #91A — from the Richmond Connector to the south approach to the Queensborough Bridge.
> (6) Vancouver-Blaine Highway #99 — from 1st Avenue in Surrey to the south approach of the Oak Street Bridge.
> (7) Okanagan Connector Highway #97C — from its junction with Highway 5A to its junction with Okanagan Highway 97, a total distance of approximately 84 kilometres.
> (8) The Inland Island Highway 19 from Craig's Crossing south of Parksville to its intersection with Highway 19A at Willow/Tamarac in Campbell River.
> (9) Highway 19 from its North Cedar Road intersection with Trans-Canada Highway 1, south of Nanaimo, to its intersection with Highway 19A north of Nanaimo.

**What it means:** On these highway sections you may not be on foot at all, not even on the shoulder, unless you are with a broken-down vehicle or crossing at an intersection. Hitchhike from the on-ramp approach on the local road, or from a rest area or gas station before the restricted section. Highways not listed in Schedule 1 are not covered by this ban. There, s. 182 and the shoulder rule apply, along with any posted signs.

### Offence Act s. 4: General penalty

**Source:** [BC Laws, Offence Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 338](https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96338_01) (official consolidation)

> Unless otherwise specifically provided in an enactment, a person who is convicted of an offence is liable to a fine of not more than $2 000 or to imprisonment for not more than 6 months, or to both.

**What it means:** This is the maximum for an offence with no specific penalty, which appears to include s. 182. It is a ceiling, not a typical fine.

jurisdictions.title: Northwest Territories (CA-NT)
jurisdictions.statusLine: Legal. The Motor Vehicles Act bans pedestrians from being on the roadway to solicit **employment or business** (s. 257), but it does not mention rides. Ordinary pedestrian rules apply.

sections.summary:
The NWT Motor Vehicles Act has a solicitation section, but it covers only "employment or business". Unlike the BC and US model rules, the word "ride" is not in it. I searched the current office consolidation for "solicit" and found only s. 257. The Act has no controlled-access or freeway provisions, and I found no pedestrian ban on any class of highway.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Walk on the sidewalk** where one is usable. Otherwise walk on the left-hand side of the roadway or the shoulder (s. 255).
- **Stay off the roadway** when asking anyone for anything. Standing on the shoulder keeps you clear of s. 257 under any reading.
- **Don't hold onto vehicles** to be towed (s. 256), a winter-road warning.

Offences under the Act carry a maximum fine of $5,000 or up to six months in jail (s. 338). That is a ceiling, not a typical ticket.
sections.laws:
### Motor Vehicles Act s. 255 to 257: Pedestrians

**Source:** [Government of the Northwest Territories, Motor Vehicles Act, R.S.N.W.T. 1988, c. M-16 (office consolidation PDF)](https://gnwt.ca/sites/default/files/legacy_justice/files/legislation/motor-vehicles/motor-vehicles.a.pdf) (consolidation includes amendments through S.N.W.T. 2025, c. 3, in force March 21, 2025. The consolidation states it "is not an official statement of the law.")

> 255. (1) A pedestrian shall not walk or run on a roadway if there is a sidewalk that is usable on either side of the roadway.
>
> (2) Where there is no sidewalk that is usable on either side of a roadway, a pedestrian shall, unless it is impracticable, walk or run on the left-hand side of the roadway or the shoulder of the highway.
>
> 256. (1) No person who is outside of a vehicle shall
> (a) hold onto a vehicle that is in motion, or
> (b) hold onto a vehicle that is stationary,
> for the purpose of being towed.
>
> (2) No driver shall knowingly tow a person that is holding onto the vehicle he or she is driving.
>
> 257. No pedestrian shall be on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting employment or business with an occupant of a vehicle using the roadway.

**What it means:** Hitchhiking is not named. Section 257 is aimed at selling things or seeking work from drivers in the roadway. Thumbing a free ride from the shoulder is not caught by it. Soliciting a paid ride while standing in the lane could arguably count as "business", so stand on the shoulder.

### Motor Vehicles Act s. 1: Definitions of "highway" and "roadway"

**Source:** [Government of the Northwest Territories, Motor Vehicles Act (office consolidation PDF)](https://gnwt.ca/sites/default/files/legacy_justice/files/legislation/motor-vehicles/motor-vehicles.a.pdf)

> "highway" means a road, place, bridge or structure, whether publicly or privately owned, that the public is ordinarily entitled or permitted to use for the passage of vehicles and includes
> (a) a privately or publicly owned area that is designed and primarily used for the parking of vehicles, other than the driveway of a private dwelling,
> (b) where a plan of survey or other instrument establishes a highway, the area between the boundary lines of the highway as shown on the plan of survey or instrument,
> (c) a sidewalk, pathway, ditch or shoulder adjacent to and on either side of the travelled portion of the road or place and the area between the sidewalk, pathway, ditch or shoulder and the travelled portion of the road or place, and
> (d) a road on a frozen body of water or water course or a road that can be used for only a portion of a year; (route)
>
> [...]
>
> "roadway" means the part of a highway that is improved, designed or ordinarily used for the passage of vehicles, but does not include the shoulder of a highway; (chaussée)

**What it means:** The shoulder is expressly not part of the roadway. Ice roads and seasonal roads count as highways, so the same pedestrian rules apply there.

### Motor Vehicles Act ss. 336 and 338: Offence and general punishment

**Source:** [Government of the Northwest Territories, Motor Vehicles Act (office consolidation PDF)](https://gnwt.ca/sites/default/files/legacy_justice/files/legislation/motor-vehicles/motor-vehicles.a.pdf)

> 336. Every person who contravenes this Act or the regulations is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to the punishment set out in this Act.
>
> [...]
>
> 338. Subject to section 337, every person who is found guilty of an offence under this Act or the regulations is liable to a fine not exceeding $5,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to both.

**What it means:** Pedestrian-rule violations are summary offences with a high ceiling. The actual ticket amount is set separately (see open questions).

jurisdictions.statusLine: Legal. Nunavut's Traffic Safety Act, formerly the Motor Vehicles Act, bans pedestrians from being on the roadway to solicit **employment or business** (s. 257), but it says nothing about rides. Ordinary pedestrian rules apply.

sections.summary:
Nunavut inherited the Northwest Territories Motor Vehicles Act in 1999 and later renamed it the Traffic Safety Act. The pedestrian sections are the same as in the NWT: no hitchhiking rule, and a ban on soliciting "employment or business" from the roadway. The Act has no freeway or controlled-access highway provisions.

What applies to hitchhikers:

- **Walk on the sidewalk** where one is usable. Otherwise walk on the left-hand side of the roadway or the shoulder (s. 255).
- **Stay off the roadway** while soliciting anything. The shoulder is not part of the roadway.
- **Municipal by-laws** may regulate pedestrians (s. 347), so check local rules in Iqaluit and other communities.

Offences carry a maximum fine of $5,000 or up to six months in jail (s. 338).
sections.laws:
### Traffic Safety Act ss. 255 to 257: Pedestrians

**Source:** [Nunavut Legislation, Consolidation of Traffic Safety Act (PDF)](https://nunavutlegislation.ca/en/file-download/download/public/8180) (consolidation current to December 6, 2019. The site notes later amendments by S.Nu. 2020, c. 15; 2021, c. 10; 2021, c. 20; 2025, c. 15; and 2026, c. 7. I checked the texts of 2021, c. 10; 2025, c. 15, s. 50; and 2026, c. 7, s. 23, and none of them changes ss. 255 to 257 or s. 338.)

> 255. (1) A pedestrian shall not walk or run on a roadway if there is a sidewalk that is usable on either side of the roadway.
>
> (2) Where there is no sidewalk that is usable on either side of a roadway, a pedestrian shall, unless it is impracticable, walk or run on the left-hand side of the roadway or the shoulder of the highway.
>
> 256. (1) No person who is outside of a vehicle shall
> (a) hold onto a vehicle that is in motion, or
> (b) hold onto a vehicle that is stationary,
> for the purpose of being towed.
>
> (2) No driver shall knowingly tow a person that is holding onto the vehicle he or she is driving.
>
> 257. No pedestrian shall be on a roadway for the purpose of soliciting employment or business with an occupant of a vehicle using the roadway.

**What it means:** Asking for a free ride is not mentioned anywhere. Section 257 targets selling or job-seeking from the roadway. Stand on the shoulder or the roadside and you are clear of it.

### Traffic Safety Act s. 1: Definitions of "highway" and "roadway"

**Source:** [Nunavut Legislation, Consolidation of Traffic Safety Act (PDF)](https://nunavutlegislation.ca/en/file-download/download/public/8180) (current to December 6, 2019)

> "highway" means a road, place, bridge or structure, whether publicly or privately owned, that the public is ordinarily entitled or permitted to use for the passage of vehicles and includes
> (a) a privately or publicly owned area that is designed and primarily used for the parking of vehicles, other than the driveway of a private dwelling,
> (b) where a plan of survey or other instrument establishes a highway, the area between the boundary lines of the highway as shown on the plan of survey or instrument,
> (c) a sidewalk, pathway, ditch or shoulder adjacent to and on either side of the travelled portion of the road or place and the area between the sidewalk, pathway, ditch or shoulder and the travelled portion of the road or place, and
> (d) a road on a frozen body of water or water course or a road that can be used for only a portion of a year; (route)
>
> [...]
>
> "roadway" means the part of a highway that is improved, designed or ordinarily used for the passage of vehicles, but does not include the shoulder of a highway; (chaussée)

**What it means:** The shoulder is not part of the roadway. Ice roads and seasonal trails open to vehicles count as highways.

### Traffic Safety Act ss. 336 and 338: Offence and general punishment

**Source:** [Nunavut Legislation, Consolidation of Traffic Safety Act (PDF)](https://nunavutlegislation.ca/en/file-download/download/public/8180) (current to December 6, 2019)

> 336. Every person who contravenes this Act or the regulations is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to the punishment set out in this Act.
>
> [...]
>
> 338. Subject to section 337, every person who is found guilty of an offence under this Act or the regulations is liable to a fine not exceeding $5,000 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to both.

**What it means:** A breach of the pedestrian rules is a summary offence. The $5,000 figure is the maximum, not a typical fine.
sections.history:
### Renamed from Motor Vehicles Act to Traffic Safety Act

**Source:** [Nunavut Legislation, current consolidated laws, "T"](https://nunavutlegislation.ca/en/consolidated-law/current?title=T)

The listing for the Traffic Safety Act consolidation states "Formerly: Motor Vehicles Act." An older consolidation (PDF file dated 2005), then titled the Motor Vehicles Act (Nunavut), already contained the same s. 257 wording on soliciting employment or business, with no mention of rides.

**What it means:** Older references to the Nunavut "Motor Vehicles Act" refer to this same law.

sections.summary:
Every source of the Yukon Motor Vehicles Act text blocked automated retrieval. That includes the official site laws.yukon.ca, CanLII and the Internet Archive. Under this project's rule of quoting only primary text actually retrieved, no Yukon law is quoted on this page. Do not read this page as saying hitchhiking is legal or illegal in Yukon.

What I could confirm:

- **City of Whitehorse:** the office consolidation of the [Whitehorse Traffic Bylaw 2013-34](https://www.whitehorse.ca/whitehorse_bylaws/traffic-bylaw/) contains no provision on soliciting rides or hitchhiking. I searched the full text for "solicit", "hitch" and "ride".
- **National parks (Kluane):** the federal [National Parks Highway Traffic Regulations, C.R.C., c. 1126](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/C.R.C.,_c._1126/FullText.html) (current to 2026-10-19) contain no provision on soliciting rides. I searched the full text for "solicit" and "hitch".

- **Motor Vehicles Act, R.S.Y. 2002, c. 153, Part on pedestrians.** Search results suggest it includes sections titled "Pedestrians on roadway" and "Pedestrians crossing roadway". Its wording, and whether it has a "solicit a ride" or "solicit employment or business" clause, still needs to be retrieved from [laws.yukon.ca](https://laws.yukon.ca/cms/images/LEGISLATION/PRINCIPAL/2002/2002-0153/2002-0153.pdf) by someone with browser access. The same applies to the definitions of "roadway" and "highway" and the general penalty section.
- **Freeway pedestrians.** Yukon has no freeways in the usual sense. Whether the Act or any regulation bans pedestrians on any class of highway, such as the Alaska Highway, is unconfirmed.
